title: Engineering correlated phases through manipulation of Van Hove singularities
summary: Controlling the ordered phases of correlated electron systems remains a central challenge in quantum materials design. Divergences in the electronic density of states, known as Van Hove singularities (VHSs), are one obvious route to such control. It is clear from recent work that the exact functional form of these divergences can profoundly affect which phases are realized; a full picture, however, remains elusive. In this work, we use both the hot-spot parquet renormalization group and the truncated-unity functional renormalization group to theoretically study the emergent correlated states of a two-dimensional square-lattice Hubbard model with VHSs at or near the Fermi level. By varying a single hopping parameter, $t_3$, we are able to change the strength of the VHS divergence in the density of states from logarithmic (for $t_3 < t_{3c}$) to power-law (for $t_3 = t_{3c}$). Further increase of $t_3$ ($t_3 > t_{3c}$) causes each original Van Hove point to split into two, both of the conventional logarithmic type. We show that which of these regimes we are in strongly influences the predicted ordered states. We also study the dependence on doping, and find that the ferromagnetic state that occurs at Van Hove filling in these models is unstable to very small shifts in the Fermi level, often giving way to distinct ordered states depending on whether the model is electron- or hole-doped. These results highlight the importance of tuning VHS properties to control ordered states in correlated materials, and offer design rules to engineer these phases in novel systems.

AI.tldr: This paper uses parquet and functional renormalization group methods to study a square-lattice Hubbard model where a single hopping parameter t3 tunes the Van Hove singularity (VHS) from logarithmic to power-law divergences. They find the type of VHS divergence strongly influences the emergent ordered states, and that ferromagnetic order at Van Hove filling is highly sensitive to doping, giving way to distinct phases depending on electron vs. hole doping.
AI.motivation: Controlling ordered phases of correlated electron systems is a central challenge. Van Hove singularities offer a route to such control, and recent work shows the exact functional form of VHS divergences can profoundly affect which phases are realized. A full picture of how VHS properties control emergent ordered states remains elusive, motivating this systematic study.

They vary a single hopping parameter t3 to tune the VHS divergence strength from logarithmic (t3 < t3c) to power-law (t3 = t3c), and beyond t3c the original Van Hove points split into two conventional logarithmic-type VHSs. They also investigate doping dependence.
AI.result: The predicted ordered states depend strongly on which VHS divergence regime the system is in (logarithmic vs. power-law vs. split VHSs). At Van Hove filling, the ferromagnetic state is unstable to very small Fermi-level shifts. Depending on whether the model is electron- or hole-doped, distinct ordered states emerge instead.
AI.conclusion: Tuning VHS properties is key to controlling ordered states in correlated materials. The results provide design rules for engineering correlated phases by adjusting the functional form of the density-of-states divergences in novel quantum materials.

title: Metallic Gross-Neveu criticality and superconductivity on the $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ SLAC fermion
summary: The realization of Dirac criticality beyond the conventional Gross-Neveu-Yukawa (GNY) paradigm has become a major frontier in condensed matter physics. In this work, we introduce an $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-symmetric bilayer SLAC fermion model with tunable inter-layer interactions that exhibits a rich quantum phase diagram. As the interaction strength increases, the system undergoes two distinct phase transitions. The primary transition is a continuous boundary separating a Dirac semimetal (DSM) from an $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-broken ordered phase. Crucially, this transition evades the standard GNY universality class because the emergent order only gaps out a subset of the itinerant fermions. Using large-scale quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations, we establish that this transition belongs to the Gross-Neveu-$\mathrm{SO}(3)$ universality class with $N=6$ irreducible Dirac cones and precisely extract the corresponding critical exponents. At stronger couplings, a second transition drives the system into an inter-layer $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-symmetric superconducting (SC) state. We provide strong numerical evidence that this transition is a quantum-fluctuation-driven first-order transition. Our study provides new insights into the exploration of Dirac criticality beyond the standard GNY universality class, and also offers a novel platform to realize superconductivity featuring $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ symmetry.

The authors seek a new platform where emergent order gaps only a subset of itinerant fermions, evading the standard GNY universality class and enabling new critical phenomena.

They use large-scale quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations to investigate the quantum phase diagram, including locating phase boundaries, extracting critical exponents, and determining the nature of transitions.

AI.conclusion: The study provides new insights into Dirac criticality beyond the standard GNY universality class and establishes a novel platform for realizing superconductivity featuring SO(3) symmetry.

title: Quantum geometric localization length and localization criticality in an ideally flat Chern band
comment: 8 pages and 4 figures for the main text; 13 pages, 8 figures and 2 tables for SM
summary: We propose that the localization length in an isolated, ideally flat Chern band is set by quantum geometry. We explore the corresponding localization transition and its critical scaling by applying transfer matrix calculations in the maximally localized hybrid Wannier basis, whose spatial spread is exactly characterized by a quantum geometric length. Remarkably, upon tuning the quantum metric of the Chern band, we observe a crossover from a universal regime controlled by the Dirac fixed point to a non-universal regime with continuously varying critical exponents. Within the universal regime, the localization length exhibits a pronounced linear dependence on the quantum geometric length, supporting its quantum geometric nature. These findings provide a novel quantum geometric perspective on the localization in quantum Hall systems such as twisted moiré superlattices, and shed new light on the long-standing controversy over the criticality of the integer quantum Hall transition.

AI.motivation: To understand the mechanism controlling localization in flat Chern bands and to resolve the long-standing controversy over the criticality of the integer quantum Hall transition by linking localization to band quantum geometry.
AI.method: Transfer matrix calculations performed in the maximally localized hybrid Wannier basis, where the spatial spread of the basis is exactly characterized by a quantum geometric length; the quantum metric of the Chern band is tuned to explore the localization transition and its critical scaling.

title: Momentum-Selective Electron and Spin Dynamics under Ultrafast Photoexcitation
summary: Recent advances in time-resolved spectroscopies have enabled direct access to the momentum-selective nonequilibrium dynamics of correlated quantum materials, revealing a strongly momentum-dependent response of electrons and collective excitations. Interpreting these observations requires a real-time theoretical framework that consistently captures the interplay between strong local electronic correlations and nonlocal collective fluctuations, a capability that remains beyond state-of-the-art nonequilibrium approaches. Using a recently developed real-time many-body framework, we resolve the momentum-selective ultrafast dynamics of a photoexcited correlated electron system. We predict a transient nodal-antinodal anisotropy in electronic heating, providing a microscopic explanation for the momentum-dependent response debated in time-resolved photoemission and Raman experiments, and identify the nonthermal spectral-weight transfer responsible for the transient antinodal in-gap states observed in ultrafast photoemission. We further uncover a momentum-selective magnetic response, in which antiferromagnetic fluctuations undergo a strongly nonthermal, quench-like excitation far above the electronic temperature while preserving their correlation length, before relaxing through a momentum-space magnon cascade toward lower-momentum modes. Finally, by tracking the real-time local spin susceptibility, we identify a dynamical, experimentally accessible signature of local-moment formation and its photoinduced melting. Our results establish a unified microscopic picture of ultrafast electronic and magnetic dynamics, providing a framework for interpreting momentum-resolved pump-probe experiments.

AI.tldr: Using a real-time many-body framework, the authors resolve momentum-selective ultrafast dynamics of photoexcited correlated electron systems, uncovering transient nodal-antinodal electronic heating anisotropy, nonthermal in-gap states, anti-ferromagnetic fluctuations with quench-like behavior, and dynamical signatures of local-moment formation.
AI.motivation: Time-resolved spectroscopies reveal strongly momentum-dependent nonequilibrium responses in correlated quantum materials, but interpreting them requires a real-time theoretical framework that simultaneously captures strong local electronic correlations and nonlocal collective fluctuations, a capability lacking in existing nonequilibrium approaches.
AI.method: A recently developed real-time many-body framework is applied to model photoexcited correlated electron systems, capturing electron-electron correlations and nonlocal collective fluctuations in the time domain.
AI.result: Predictions include: (1) transient nodal-antinodal anisotropy in electronic heating explaining momentum-dependent responses in time-resolved photoemission/Raman; (2) nonthermal spectral-weight transfer creating transient antinodal in-gap states; (3) momentum-selective magnetic response with quench-like nonthermal excitation of antiferromagnetic fluctuations above electronic temperature while preserving correlation length, followed by a momentum-space magnon cascade; and (4) a real-time local spin susceptibility signature of local-moment formation and its photoinduced melting.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a unified microscopic picture of ultrafast electronic and magnetic dynamics in correlated materials, offering a theoretical framework for interpreting momentum-resolved pump-probe experiments.

title: Effects of high-pressure synthesis on phase formation and superconducting properties of PrFeAsO1-xFx
summary: Motivated by recent reports of enhanced superconducting performance in several families of iron-based superconductors (IBS) processed by high-pressure (HP) synthesis, we investigate the influence of high gas pressure and high-temperature synthesis (HP-HTS) process on the structural, microstructural, electrical transport, and magnetic properties of Pr-based oxypnictide PrFeAsO1-xFx (Pr1111) using the processing conditions of 0.5 GPa for 1 h previously optimized for other IBS families. Representative underdoped (x = 0.2), optimal doped (x = 0.3), and overdoped (x = 0.5) compositions from the ambient-pressure electronic phase diagram of Pr1111 are selected to evaluate its composition-dependent effects of HP-HTS. The results demonstrate that HP-HTS enhances fluorine incorporation, improves phase formation, and produces a denser microstructure with improved grain connectivity in the underdoped and optimal doped compositions. Magnetic measurements reveal increased in the superconducting transition temperature (Tc) of ~1 K for x = 0.2 and ~6 K for x = 0.3, whereas only a marginal improvement in the critical current density is observed. Electrical resistivity measurements of the underdoped composition show a slight increase in Tc accompanied by a broader resistive transition, indicating residual structural inhomogeneity. In contrast, the overdoped composition exhibits increased impurity phase segregation, accompanied by suppression of superconductivity. These results demonstrate that the effectiveness of HP-HTS in Pr1111 is strongly composition dependent and governed by the interplay among fluorine incorporation, phase stability, and microstructural evolution, highlighting the need for further optimization of the HP-HTS processing conditions.

AI.tldr: This study investigates the effect of high-pressure high-temperature synthesis (HP-HTS) at 0.5 GPa on PrFeAsO1-xFx (Pr1111) iron-based superconductors across three doping levels (x=0.2, 0.3, 0.5). HP-HTS enhances fluorine incorporation, phase formation, and densification in underdoped/optimal doped compositions, raising Tc by ~1 K and ~6 K respectively, but shows marginal critical current density improvement and suppresses superconductivity in the overdoped composition due to impurity segregation.
AI.motivation: Recent reports show enhanced superconducting performance in iron-based superconductors processed by high-pressure synthesis. The authors aim to determine whether the same HP-HTS processing conditions (0.5 GPa, 1 h) previously optimized for other IBS families benefit Pr1111, and to understand how composition-dependent effects influence the outcome.
AI.method: PrFeAsO1-xFx samples at three doping levels (underdoped x=0.2, optimal x=0.3, overdoped x=0.5) were processed via HP-HTS at 0.5 GPa for 1 hour. Structural, microstructural, electrical transport, and magnetic properties were characterized to compare HP-processed samples against ambient-pressure counterparts.
AI.result: HP-HTS improves fluorine incorporation, phase formation, and grain connectivity in underdoped/optimal doped samples. Tc increases by ~1 K (x=0.2) and ~6 K (x=0.3), with only marginal critical current density improvement. The underdoped sample shows broader resistive transitions indicating structural inhomogeneity. The overdoped composition suffers increased impurity segregation and suppressed superconductivity.
AI.conclusion: The effectiveness of HP-HTS in Pr1111 is strongly composition-dependent, governed by the interplay between fluorine incorporation, phase stability, and microstructural evolution. Further optimization of HP-HTS conditions is needed for this material family.

title: Oxygen Reduction Reaction on Platinum Nanocatalysts Produces Long-Lived, Hysteretic Oxygenated Adsorbates
summary: Aqueous electrocatalysis generates oxygenated intermediates at catalyst surfaces. While intermediate species on single-crystal catalysts have been observed, the nature and evolution of surface oxygenated species on industrially relevant nanoparticle (NP) catalysts remain largely unknown. Here, using in situ Raman spectroscopy, we tracked the formation and potential-dependent evolution of oxygenated adsorbates in alkaline media on NP catalysts with an active platinum (Pt) surface. By comparing spectroscopic features in Ar- vs O2-saturated electrolytes, we determined three key intermediates produced by the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR): adsorbed OOH, OH, and O2. In contrast to the conventional wisdom that intermediates exist only during catalytic reactions, we found these oxygenated adsorbates to be highly long-lived and hysteretic, and to persist even after the termination of ORR. This adsorbate-retention effect exhibits a modest dependence on the surface oxidation state and the electrolyte cations (K+ vs Li+), and is likely facilitated by the heterogeneous nature of the catalyst surface. The results highlight the complexity of surface adsorption structures on realistic catalysts, which often extends beyond that captured by measurements or simulations on model single-crystal surfaces.

AI.tldr: Using in situ Raman spectroscopy, this study identifies three long-lived oxygenated intermediates (adsorbed OOH, OH, and O2) on platinum nanoparticle catalysts during the oxygen reduction reaction in alkaline media, revealing that these adsorbates persist even after the reaction terminates—contradicting conventional understanding that intermediates exist only during catalysis.
AI.motivation: While oxygenated intermediates have been observed on single-crystal catalysts, the nature and evolution of such species on industrially relevant nanoparticle catalysts remain poorly understood, limiting our understanding of realistic electrocatalytic systems.
AI.method: In situ Raman spectroscopy was used to track the formation and potential-dependent evolution of oxygenated adsorbates in alkaline media on nanoparticle catalysts with active platinum surfaces. Spectroscopic features were compared between Ar- and O2-saturated electrolytes to identify reaction intermediates, and the effects of surface oxidation state and electrolyte cations (K+ vs Li+) were examined.
AI.result: Three key ORR intermediates were identified: adsorbed OOH, OH, and O2. These oxygenated adsorbates were found to be highly long-lived and hysteretic, persisting after ORR termination. The adsorbate-retention effect showed modest dependence on surface oxidation state and electrolyte cations, likely facilitated by the heterogeneous nature of the nanoparticle surface.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight that surface adsorption structures on realistic nanoparticle catalysts are more complex than those captured by measurements or simulations on model single-crystal surfaces, underscoring the need to account for adsorbate persistence and heterogeneity in practical electrocatalysis.

title: Defect-Controlled Multiferroicity via Stacking Control in Nonmagnetic van der Waals Bilayers
summary: We present a general paradigm that directly couples vacancy-localized magnetism to interfacial sliding ferroelectricity in nonmagnetic van der Waals (vdWs) bilayers. Utilizing bilayer hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) as a prototypical vdWs host system, we use first-principles calculations to show that a single vacancy acts as a local registry sensor, lifting the degeneracy between polar sliding partners via a defect-centered polarization offset. For interlayer vacancy pairs, we discover a defect selectivity where the hosting sublattice fully dictates the interlayer exchange, stabilizing either ferrimagnetic or antiferromagnetic configurations. Applying an out-of-plane electric field selects the polar registry and drives an amplitude modulation of the compensated Néel order parameter. These findings establish a robust, sublattice-dependent engineering of multiferroic functionality via stacking control across a wide class of nonmagnetic 2D heterostructures.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a general paradigm coupling vacancy-localized magnetism to interfacial sliding ferroelectricity in nonmagnetic van der Waals bilayers. Using bilayer hBN as a prototypical system, first-principles calculations show a single vacancy acts as a local registry sensor, lifting degeneracy between polar sliding partners. For interlayer vacancy pairs, host sublattice dictates interlayer exchange, stabilizing ferrimagnetic or antiferromagnetic states. An out-of-plane electric field selects polar registry and modulates the compensated Néel order parameter, enabling sublattice-dependent multiferroic engineering via stacking control.
AI.motivation: To establish a general mechanism for introducing magnetism into nonmagnetic 2D van der Waals heterostructures by coupling vacancy-localized spins to interfacial sliding ferroelectricity, enabling multiferroic functionality in otherwise nonmagnetic materials.
AI.method: First-principles calculations on bilayer hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) with single and paired vacancies, analyzing defect-centered polarization offsets, sublattice-dependent interlayer exchange interactions, and electric-field controlled polar registry switching.
AI.result: A single vacancy lifts the degeneracy of polar sliding states via a defect-centered polarization offset. Interlayer vacancy pairs exhibit sublattice-dependent magnetic exchange, stabilizing either ferrimagnetic or antiferromagnetic configurations. An out-of-plane electric field modulates the compensated Néel order parameter by selecting the polar registry.
AI.conclusion: The findings establish a robust, sublattice-dependent route to engineer multiferroic functionality via stacking control across a wide class of nonmagnetic 2D heterostructures, generalizing vacancy-localized magnetism coupled to sliding ferroelectricity.

title: Fermionic Lattice Supersolidity in the Attractive Three-Color Fermi-Hubbard Model
summary: The recent experimental realization of the half-filled three-color Fermi-Hubbard model on a square optical lattice provides a novel platform for exploring exotic states of matter beyond conventional SU(2) systems. In this Letter, we investigate the three-color Fermi-Hubbard model with color-dependent attractive interactions using determinant quantum Monte Carlo simulations. We find that, at quantum degenerate temperatures, a lattice Fermi supersolid state emerges from the interplay between a moderately-to-strongly interacting two-color subsystem and a weakly coupled third-color environment. This supersolid state, characterized by the coexistence of charge-density-wave and color-superfluid orders, is highly promising for experimental detection with current techniques. Our results demonstrate that the attractive three-color Fermi-Hubbard model on a square optical lattice offers an experimentally accessible system for exploring the supersolidity of ultracold lattice fermions, requiring only a simple lattice geometry and easily tunable onsite interactions.

AI.tldr: The paper theoretically predicts a lattice Fermi supersolid state in the three-color Fermi-Hubbard model on a square optical lattice with color-dependent attractive interactions, using determinant quantum Monte Carlo simulations. The supersolid arises from the interplay between a strongly interacting two-color subsystem and a weakly coupled third-color environment, coexisting charge-density-wave and color-superfluid orders.
AI.motivation: Recent experimental realization of the half-filled three-color Fermi-Hubbard model on a square optical lattice offers a new platform to explore exotic quantum states beyond conventional SU(2) systems, motivating theoretical investigation of novel emergent phases in this experimentally accessible system.
AI.method: Determinant quantum Monte Carlo (DQMC) simulations of the three-color Fermi-Hubbard model with color-dependent attractive interactions on a square optical lattice.
AI.result: At quantum degenerate temperatures, a lattice Fermi supersolid state emerges from the interplay between a moderately-to-strongly interacting two-color subsystem and a weakly coupled third-color environment. The supersolid is characterized by the coexistence of charge-density-wave and color-superfluid orders and is highly promising for experimental detection.
AI.conclusion: The attractive three-color Fermi-Hubbard model on a square optical lattice provides an experimentally accessible system for exploring supersolidity of ultracold lattice fermions, requiring only a simple lattice geometry and easily tunable onsite interactions.

title: Quantum Metric Induced Critical Current Anomaly in Flat Band Josephson Junctions
summary: In well-established theories of Josephson junctions, the superconducting critical current \( I_\mathrm{c} \) increases as the normal state conductance \( \mathcal{G} \) increases. However, in a recent experiment in twisted bilayer graphene (TBG) based Josephson junctions, unexpectedly, it was observed that the increase of the critical current is accompanied by a decrease of the normal state conductance. We call this phenomenon the critical current anomaly. In this work, we point out that in the TBG-based Josephson junction, due to the suppression of the conventional Josephson current by the flatness of the band and the quantum metric enabled Josephson current (QMJC), the critical current anomaly can occur. The QMJC appears if the quantum metric length is comparable or longer than the junction length. We show that both \( \mathcal{G} \) and \( I_\mathrm{c} \) have the conventional and the quantum metric contributions, and there are parameter regimes in which \( I_\mathrm{c} \) increases even when \( \mathcal{G} \) decreases. We first demonstrate the critical current anomaly by a simple modified Lieb-lattice model both analytically and numerically. The incredible consistency with the experimental results is demonstrated using a realistic six-band model of twisted bilayer graphene. Therefore, we suggest that the critical current anomaly observed in the experiment provide strong evidence of QMJC which were ignored in well-established theories of Josephson junctions.

AI.tldr: The paper explains the "critical current anomaly" observed in twisted bilayer graphene Josephson junctions, where the superconducting critical current increases despite the normal state conductance decreasing. The authors show that quantum metric enabled Josephson current (QMJC), arising when the quantum metric length is comparable to or longer than the junction length, can explain this anomaly, providing evidence for QMJC that standard Josephson junction theories ignore.
AI.motivation: Recent experiments in twisted bilayer graphene (TBG) Josephson junctions report an unexpected behavior: the critical current increases while the normal state conductance decreases, contradicting well-established Josephson junction theories where critical current scales with conductance. The authors aim to explain this anomaly by invoking the quantum metric enabled Josephson current (QMJC).
AI.method: The authors first demonstrate the critical current anomaly using a simplified modified Lieb-lattice model, analyzed both analytically and numerically. They then validate their findings using a realistic six-band model of twisted bilayer graphene, showing that both the conductance and critical current have conventional and quantum metric contributions, and identifying parameter regimes where \( I_\mathrm{c} \) increases while \( \mathcal{G} \) decreases.
AI.result: The authors find that the suppression of conventional Josephson current due to the flatness of the TBG band, combined with the quantum metric enabled Josephson current (QMJC), can produce the critical current anomaly. Their Lieb-lattice model reproduces the effect, and the realistic six-band TBG model shows remarkable consistency with experimental observations.
AI.conclusion: The critical current anomaly observed in TBG-based Josephson junctions provides strong evidence for the existence of quantum metric enabled Josephson current, a contribution that has been neglected in well-established theories of Josephson junctions.

title: A comparative study of sum-connectivity and product-connectivity Gourava indices for benzenoid hydrocarbons
summary: This study evaluates the sum-connectivity ($SGO$) and product-connectivity ($PGO$) Gourava indices as molecular descriptors for benzenoid hydrocarbons. Using a dataset of 30 benzenoid structures, we compare least-squares regression models for predicting $π$-electronic energies ($E_π$) and find that $SGO$ yields a markedly better fit than $PGO$ across molecular edge types. The indices are further assessed using three validation designs: (i) correlation analysis, in which $SGO$ exhibits strong yet non-perfect inverse correlations with standard descriptors ($M_1, M_2, SO, DSO,$ and $ABS$; $r\in[-0.9923,-0.8936]$), suggesting complementary structural information; (ii) degeneracy analysis on Octane, Nonane, and order-$10$ tree datasets, where $SGO$ attains low degeneracy rates (22.22\%, 40.00\%, and 42.45\%); and (iii) structure-sensitivity analysis on trees of order $n=10$, showing 74\% higher sensitivity than $DSO$ while maintaining a high structure-abruptness ratio ($SA = 0.474386$). Overall, $SGO$ offers a favorable balance between discriminative power and numerical stability, supporting its applicability in QSPR modeling and related theoretical studies.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates two recently proposed molecular descriptors—sum-connectivity (SGO) and product-connectivity (PGO) Gourava indices—for benzenoid hydrocarbons. SGO outperforms PGO in predicting π-electronic energies across 30 benzenoid structures and demonstrates strong discriminative power through correlation, degeneracy, and structure-sensitivity analyses, offering a favorable balance between discriminative power and numerical stability for QSPR modeling.
AI.motivation: To assess the utility of sum-connectivity (SGO) and product-connectivity (PGO) Gourava indices as molecular descriptors for benzenoid hydrocarbons, testing their predictive performance for π-electronic energies and their overall discriminative power for QSPR applications.
AI.method: Using a dataset of 30 benzenoid structures, least-squares regression models were compared for predicting π-electronic energies (E_π) using SGO and PGO. The indices were further validated through three designs: (i) correlation analysis against standard descriptors (M_1, M_2, SO, DSO, ABS), (ii) degeneracy analysis on Octane, Nonane, and order-10 tree datasets, and (iii) structure-sensitivity analysis on trees of order n=10.
AI.result: SGO yields a markedly better fit than PGO for predicting E_π across molecular edge types. SGO shows strong but non-perfect inverse correlations with standard descriptors (r ∈ [-0.9923, -0.8936]), low degeneracy rates (22.22%, 40.00%, and 42.45% on Octane, Nonane, and order-10 trees respectively), and 74% higher structure sensitivity than DSO with a structure-abruptness ratio of SA = 0.474386.
AI.conclusion: SGO offers a favorable balance between discriminative power and numerical stability, supporting its applicability in QSPR modeling and related theoretical studies of benzenoid hydrocarbons.

title: Understanding the Oxygen Reduction Reaction and Oxygen Evolution Reaction in Metal Intercalated Biphenylene Bilayers
summary: We conducted an {\it ab initio} study of the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) and oxygen evolution reaction (OER) in metal-encapsulated biphenylene bilayers, B/M/B, with M = Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Nb, Ru, W, Os and Pt. In most systems, the intercalated metal sits at the square carbon sites (C$^{468}$) of the biphenylene lattice. Using a computational hydrogen electrode approach, we evaluated the reaction energetics at these active sites. Several B/M/B systems show competitive ORR and OER performance. Among the investigated systems, Cu, Pt, Ru, and Mn exhibit the lowest ORR overpotentials of 0.42, 0.44, 0.50, and 0.56 V, respectively, while Fe is identified as the most active catalyst for OER with an overpotential of 0.44 V. To understand the catalytic trends, we looked at the electronic structure through the metal $d-$band centers, the C$^{468}$ $p_z-$band centers, and the corresponding orbital charge populations. The band centers did not give a simple polynomial dependence on the overpotentials, though they did point to favorable electronic ranges for the best catalysts. The $d-$orbital charge population of the encapsulated metal, however, correlated most clearly with activity-especially for OER-yielding volcano-type plots. From these, B/Fe/B emerges as the best OER catalyst, while B/Mn/B lies closest to the ORR optimum. The $p-$orbital population at the active carbon site also captures the main trends, albeit less strongly. Overall, these results show that straightforward electronic descriptors can predict catalytic behavior in metal-encapsulated biphenylene bilayers and guide the search for efficient catalysts where the carbon framework itself drives the reactivity.

AI.tldr: An ab initio study of ORR and OER in metal-encapsulated biphenylene bilayers (B/M/B) evaluating 13 transition metals. Cu, Pt, Ru, Mn show best ORR overpotentials (0.42-0.56 V), Fe is the best OER catalyst (0.44 V). The metal d-orbital charge population best correlates with catalytic activity, yielding volcano-type plots, while band centers show no simple polynomial dependence.
AI.motivation: To identify efficient catalysts for oxygen reduction and oxygen evolution reactions by exploring metal-encapsulated biphenylene bilayers as a novel carbon-based catalytic framework, and to establish simple electronic descriptors that can predict and guide catalyst design.
AI.method: Ab initio (DFT-based) calculations combined with a computational hydrogen electrode (CHE) approach. Metals (Ti to Pt, 13 total) are intercalated into biphenylene bilayers at square carbon sites (C468). Reaction energetics evaluated for ORR and OER. Electronic structure analyzed via metal d-band centers, C468 pz-band centers, and orbital charge populations to correlate with overpotentials.
AI.result: Cu, Pt, Ru, and Mn give the lowest ORR overpotentials (0.42, 0.44, 0.50, 0.56 V); Fe is the best OER catalyst (0.44 V). Band centers do not show simple polynomial relationships with overpotentials but indicate favorable ranges. The metal d-orbital charge population correlates most clearly with activity, especially for OER, producing volcano-type plots. B/Fe/B is the best OER catalyst and B/Mn/B is closest to the ORR optimum. The carbon p-orbital population captures trends less strongly.
AI.conclusion: Simple electronic descriptors, particularly the metal d-orbital charge population, can reliably predict ORR/OER catalytic behavior in metal-encapsulated biphenylene bilayers. This framework can guide the search for efficient carbon-driven catalysts.

title: Composite-State Localization Beyond the External Landscape in Non-Hermitian Quasicrystals
summary: A composite excitation need not inherit the localization behavior of its constituents. We show that an interacting non-Hermitian quasiperiodic ladder realizes a controllable and reversible localization inversion between composite and unbound excitations, where internal configuration, rather than only the external potential, becomes a control parameter for localization. Opposite complex potentials on the two legs cancel at first order for a same-rung pair but act directly on separated particles, allowing extended composite states to persist while the unpaired sector becomes localized. A strong-coupling theory identifies the composite state as an emergent weakly modulated non-Hermitian quasicrystal generated by virtual unpaired configurations. Breaking the potential antisymmetry restores a direct modulation of the composite band and reverses the localization hierarchy. Engineering configuration-space pathways further stabilizes an extended composite band embedded within a localized continuum, the inverse of the conventional bound-state-in-the-continuum scenario. Our results establish internal configuration as a reversible control parameter for localization.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that composite excitations in an interacting non-Hermitian quasiperiodic ladder can realize a controllable and reversible localization inversion between composite and unbound excitations, where internal configuration becomes a control parameter for localization. Opposite complex potentials on the two legs cancel at first order for same-rung pairs but act on separated particles, allowing extended composite states while the unpaired sector localizes.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to show that composite excitations need not inherit the localization behavior of their constituents, and to establish internal configuration—rather than only the external potential—as a reversible control parameter for localization.
AI.method: The study uses an interacting non-Hermitian quasiperiodic ladder with opposite complex potentials on the two legs. A strong-coupling theory identifies the composite state as an emergent weakly modulated non-Hermitian quasicrystal generated by virtual unpaired configurations. The authors also engineer configuration-space pathways to stabilize composite states within a localized continuum.
AI.result: Extended composite states persist while the unpaired sector becomes localized due to first-order cancellation of opposite complex potentials for same-rung pairs. Breaking potential antisymmetry restores direct modulation of the composite band and reverses the localization hierarchy. Engineering configuration-space pathways stabilizes an extended composite band embedded within a localized continuum—the inverse of the conventional bound-state-in-the-continuum scenario.
AI.conclusion: The results establish internal configuration as a reversible control parameter for localization, demonstrating that composite excitations can exhibit localization behavior independent of and even opposite to their constituents.

title: Plasmon modes in quadratic and cubic nodal line semimetals
summary: Nodal line semimetals (NLSMs) host distinctive topological properties and unconventional collective excitations. While plasmons in linear NLSMs are well studied, those of higher-order dispersive NLSMs remain poorly understood. We investigate plasmon modes in 3D quadratic and cubic NLSMs within the random phase approximation (RPA), valid for $r_s\ll1$ but breaking down in the small-doping cubic regime where the density of states diverges. Deriving the one-loop polarizability and evaluating its coefficients numerically from the full 3D Lindhard integral, we find distinct carrier-density scaling laws: quadratic NLSMs exhibit $ω_p\sim n^{1/2}$, while cubic NLSMs show $ω_p\sim n^{2/3}$ at large doping crossing over to $ω_p\sim n^{3/4}$ at small doping. The $n^{3/4}$ law is not quantitatively reliable: the diverging density of states drives $r_s>1$ already at $n\sim10^{18}$ cm$^{-3}$, limiting the observable window to at most $10^{18}\lesssim n\lesssim10^{19}$ cm$^{-3}$; below this, beyond-RPA correlations are essential. These scalings originate from the power-law density of states and intraband (Drude) response, and are analogous in phase-space power counting to bilayer and trilayer graphene, respectively. The long-wavelength intraband polarization dominates the plasmon frequency, while interband contributions are subleading (two to three orders of magnitude smaller for $Ω\llμ$). Both systems share a plasmon anisotropy $Ω_p^z/Ω_p^\perp\to\sqrt{2}$ in the thin-ring limit, a generic consequence of the torus Fermi-surface geometry. This $\sqrt{2}$ doublet, though observable by HREELS, cannot distinguish quadratic from cubic dispersion; the density scaling exponent is the true distinguishing signature. Our results provide a framework for the collective dynamics of higher-order dispersive NLSMs and suggest experimentally testable signatures accessible by HREELS.

Both systems share a √2 plasmon anisotropy ratio in the thin-ring limit, which cannot distinguish quadratic from cubic dispersion—the density scaling exponent serves as the distinguishing signature.

title: Excitron-Induced Pair Fluctuations Reveal Superconductivity in the Electron Gas
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures. Supplemental Material (7 pages, takada_SM.pdf) included
summary: Understanding how superconductivity can emerge in dilute electronic systems remains a central challenge in condensed matter physics. By performing first-principles calculations of the electron self-energy Σ(k,iw_n) in the low-density three-dimensional electron gas, we identify a sharp divergence at r_s ~ 8 and T ~ 10^{-4}E_ F, signaling a second-order phase transition. This critical behavior originates from one-dimensional superconducting fluctuations mediated by virtual excitations of an excitron---a quasi-1D electronic composite formed by an electron and longitudinal electron-hole pairs. Although the superconducting mechanism itself is plasmon-mediated, the excitron channel provides a unique window into its fluctuation dynamics. Near the transition, we observe a pseudogap and a linear-in-T inverse electron lifetime, reminiscent of phenomena in high-T_c materials. These results reveal an unexpected route by which plasmon-driven superconductivity manifests in the dilute 3D electron gas through quasi-1D excitron dynamics.

The transition is signaled by a sharp divergence in the electron self-energy at r_s ~ 8 and exhibits pseudogap and linear-in-T scattering behavior reminiscent of high-T_c materials.

AI.method: First-principles calculations of the electron self-energy Σ(k,iw_n) in the low-density three-dimensional electron gas are performed to investigate the emergence of superconductivity.

The critical behavior originates from one-dimensional superconducting fluctuations mediated by virtual excitations of an excitron. title: Chemical potentials from structure factors: I. Neutral multi-component mixtures
summary: The chemical potentials of multi-component mixtures underlie many physical and chemical phenomena, but remain challenging to compute. The S0 method enables the computation of chemical potentials from equilibrium molecular dynamics simulations, by leveraging the thermodynamic relationship between particle number fluctuations and derivatives of chemical potentials, followed by numerical integration along different compositions. Here we generalize the S0 method from two-component mixtures to neutral multi-component mixtures. We first extend the statistical mechanical formalism to high-dimensional compositional space, and then introduce a Gaussian process integration scheme combined with active learning to efficiently integrate chemical potentials and sample diverse compositions. We use this method to compute the mixing free energies of a molten metal alloy, and the solubilities of two paracetamol polymorphs in water-ethanol solvents. The extended S0 method provides a practical and scalable route for computing chemical potentials in neutral bulk multi-component mixtures from atomistic simulations.

AI.tldr: The paper generalizes the S0 method for computing chemical potentials in neutral multi-component mixtures by extending its statistical mechanics formalism to high-dimensional compositional space and introducing a Gaussian process integration scheme with active learning. The method is validated on a molten metal alloy and paracetamol polymorph solubility in water-ethanol solvents.
AI.motivation: Computing chemical potentials of multi-component mixtures is challenging but essential for understanding many physical and chemical phenomena. The existing S0 method only works for two-component mixtures, limiting its applicability to more complex systems.
AI.method: The authors generalize the S0 method by (1) extending the statistical mechanical formalism from binary to neutral multi-component mixtures in high-dimensional compositional space, and (2) introducing a Gaussian process integration scheme combined with active learning to efficiently integrate chemical potentials and explore diverse compositions.
AI.result: The extended S0 method successfully computes mixing free energies of a molten metal alloy and solubilities of two paracetamol polymorphs in water-ethanol solvents, demonstrating its practical applicability and scalability.
AI.conclusion: The extended S0 method provides a practical and scalable route for computing chemical potentials in neutral bulk multi-component mixtures from atomistic simulations.

title: Sn-Doping in LPCVD-Grown (010) $β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ Films
summary: In this work, Sn-doped (010) $β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ homoepitaxial films were grown by low-pressure chemical vapor deposition (LPCVD), and the influence of Sn incorporation on their structural, morphological, and electrical properties was systematically investigated. Controlled room-temperature carrier concentrations ranging from $1.17 \times 10^{17}$ to $3.06 \times 10^{18}$ cm$^{-3}$ were achieved, with corresponding Hall mobilities decreasing from 113 to 63 cm$^2$ V$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$. The films exhibited the monoclinic $β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ phase, near-stoichiometric composition, and well-defined step-flow morphology, with a minimum rocking-curve FWHM of 68.4 arcsec and an RMS roughness of 2.63 nm. Film thicknesses ranging from 1.66 to 11.3 $μ$m were obtained at growth rates of 6.4 to 16.6 $μ$m h$^{-1}$, demonstrating the ability of LPCVD to produce thick epitaxial layers. The sample with a room-temperature carrier concentration of $1.17 \times 10^{17}$ cm$^{-3}$ exhibited room-temperature and low-temperature Hall mobilities of 113 cm$^2$ V$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$ and 380 cm$^2$ V$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$ at 84 K, respectively. Both represent the highest reported values for LPCVD-grown Sn-doped $β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$. Transport modeling of the same sample yielded a shallow donor activation energy of 32.7 meV, a deeper donor level at 95 meV, and a low compensating acceptor concentration of $2.0 \times 10^{16}$ cm$^{-3}$, indicating efficient donor activation and a low degree of compensation. These results demonstrate that LPCVD enables controlled Sn doping while maintaining excellent structural and electrical quality, providing a viable route for realizing thick $β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ epitaxial drift layers.

The best film achieved record-high Hall mobilities for LPCVD-grown Sn-doped β-Ga₂O₃ (113 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹ at 300 K, 380 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹ at 84 K), with shallow donor activation energy of 32.7 meV, a deeper donor at 95 meV, and low compensation, demonstrating LPCVD as a viable route for thick epitaxial drift layers.
