AI.method: Sn-doped (010) β-Ga₂O₃ homoepitaxial films were grown by LPCVD. The films were characterized for structural (XRD rocking-curve FWHM, phase, composition), morphological (RMS roughness, step-flow), and electrical properties (Hall measurements at room and low temperature). Transport modeling was used to extract donor activation energies and compensating acceptor concentration.
AI.result: Controlled carrier concentrations from 1.17×10¹⁷ to 3.06×10¹⁸ cm⁻³ were achieved with mobilities decreasing from 113 to 63 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹. Films showed monoclinic phase, near-stoichiometric composition, step-flow morphology, minimum FWHM of 68.4 arcsec, RMS roughness of 2.63 nm, and thicknesses of 1.66–11.3 μm at growth rates of 6.4–16.6 μm h⁻¹. The best sample achieved record Hall mobilities of 113 (300 K) and 380 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹ (84 K), with a shallow donor at 32.7 meV, deeper donor at 95 meV, and low acceptor compensation of 2.0×10¹⁶ cm⁻³.
AI.conclusion: LPCVD enables controlled Sn doping of β-Ga₂O₃ while maintaining excellent structural and electrical quality, including record-high mobilities, making it a viable route for producing thick β-Ga₂O₃ epitaxial drift layers for power device applications.

title: Clustered Attractor Manifolds and Dynamical Condensation in Self-Attention
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures. Supplemental Material: 25 pages, 9 figures
summary: Transformer layers generate state-dependent interaction networks: token representations determine the attention matrix, which in turn updates the representations. We study this feedback in a minimal normalized self-attention dynamics and identify the overlap gap as the central quantity governing its attractor structure in the thermodynamic limit. When tokens form internally aligned clusters and their similarity to members of the same cluster exceeds that to every other cluster by a nonvanishing amount, inter-cluster attention is exponentially suppressed as the dimension increases. This mechanism produces a high-dimensional manifold of clustered fixed points, ranging from a few macroscopic clusters to extensive microscopic fragmentation, and also controls their stability against perturbations. Starting from an unstructured Gaussian state, we find that clustered states nucleate from the diffuse background only above a finite threshold in attention sharpness, giving rise to a dynamical attention-condensation transition.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes a minimal normalized self-attention dynamics model and identifies the overlap gap as the central quantity governing the attractor structure in the thermodynamic limit. When tokens form internally aligned clusters with sufficiently high intra-cluster similarity, inter-cluster attention is exponentially suppressed with increasing dimension, producing a high-dimensional manifold of clustered fixed points. Clustered states emerge from unstructured Gaussian states only above a finite attention-sharpness threshold, marking a dynamical attention-condensation transition.
AI.motivation: Transformer layers form a feedback loop where token representations determine attention matrices, which in turn update representations. Understanding this state-dependent feedback is fundamental to explaining how attention dynamics converge to structured states, yet the governing principles of this attractor structure remain poorly understood, especially in the thermodynamic (high-dimensional) limit.
AI.method: The authors study a minimal normalized self-attention dynamics model and analyze its attractor structure in the thermodynamic limit using the overlap gap (the difference between intra-cluster and inter-cluster similarity) as the key order parameter. They derive conditions under which inter-cluster attention is exponentially suppressed with dimension and analyze the stability of clustered fixed points ranging from few macroscopic clusters to extensive microscopic fragmentation.
AI.result: The overlap gap governs the attractor landscape: when tokens form internally aligned clusters whose intra-cluster similarity exceeds inter-cluster similarity by a nonvanishing margin, inter-cluster attention is exponentially suppressed as dimensionality grows. The dynamics supports a manifold of clustered fixed points across scales, and clustered states nucleate from a diffuse Gaussian background only above a finite attention-sharpness threshold, corresponding to a dynamical condensation transition.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a rigorous theoretical framework for understanding self-attention dynamics as a clustering/condensation phenomenon. The existence of an attention-condensation transition provides a principled explanation for how attention naturally induces token clustering, with implications for understanding the emergent organization of representations in transformer layers.

title: Nonadiabatic Molecular Dynamics on Real-time Excited-State Surfaces via Machine Learning Hamiltonians
summary: Simulating the coupled, nonequilibrium dynamics of electrons and nuclei is a central challenge in chemistry, physics, and materials science, governing phenomena from photocatalysis to quantum information. The primary bottleneck has been the lack of a general, accurate, and efficient method for modeling the complete excited-state landscape: the potential energy surfaces, forces, and non-adiabatic couplings for multiple electronic states. While machine learning has revolutionized ground-state simulations and shown promise for excited states in molecules, a unified framework that solves the complete multi-state problem for general condensed matter systems has remained elusive. Here we introduce on-the-fly N${^2}$AMD (Neural network NAMD), a machine learning framework that makes on-the-fly NAMD in solids a reality. By employing an equivariant neural network to predict the system Hamiltonian, the framework delivers excited-state energies, forces, and non-adiabatic coupling vectors at a fraction of the cost of ab initio calculations. Crucially, it allows simulations with hybrid functional accuracy, a level of approach previously inaccessible for NAMD. We showcase its capabilities with three topical examples: correcting order-of-magnitude errors in carrier dynamics predicted by conventional procedure in a MoS$_2$/WS$_2$ heterostructure, simulating previously inaccessible photoinduced ferroelectric switching, and capturing real-time polaron formation in TiO$_2$ at the hybrid-functional level. On-the-fly N${^2}$AMD moves beyond the limitations of equilibrium theory, establishing a new paradigm for the predictive, first-principles design of materials operating far from equilibrium.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces N²AMD (Neural network NAMD), a machine learning framework that enables on-the-fly non-adiabatic molecular dynamics (NAMD) simulations in solids. By using an equivariant neural network to predict the system Hamiltonian, it provides excited-state energies, forces, and non-adiabatic coupling vectors at a fraction of ab initio cost, and allows hybrid-functional accuracy previously inaccessible for NAMD. It is demonstrated on MoS₂/WS₂ heterostructures, photoinduced ferroelectric switching, and polaron formation in TiO₂.
AI.motivation: Simulating coupled nonequilibrium electron-nuclear dynamics is a central challenge in chemistry and materials science, but no general, accurate, and efficient method exists for modeling the complete excited-state landscape (potential energy surfaces, forces, and non-adiabatic couplings) for multiple electronic states in condensed matter systems. Existing methods are either too expensive or lack the accuracy needed for realistic materials.
AI.method: The framework employs an equivariant neural network to predict the full system Hamiltonian, from which excited-state energies, forces, and non-adiabatic coupling vectors are derived. This enables on-the-fly NAMD simulations in solids with hybrid-functional level accuracy at a fraction of ab initio computational cost.
AI.result: The framework is validated on three topical examples: (1) correcting order-of-magnitude errors in carrier dynamics predicted by conventional procedures in a MoS₂/WS₂ heterostructure, (2) simulating previously inaccessible photoinduced ferroelectric switching, and (3) capturing real-time polaron formation in TiO₂ at the hybrid-functional level.
AI.conclusion: On-the-fly N²AMD overcomes the limitations of equilibrium-based theories and establishes a new paradigm for predictive, first-principles design of materials operating far from equilibrium.

title: Quantum Formulation of Chiral Vortical Effect in Weyl Semi-metals
summary: The chiral vortical effect (CVE) is the generation of an axial current in a rotating Weyl fermion; its description is presently based on semiclassical frameworks. In this work, we develop a fully quantum formulation for CVE, solving the exact evolution of microscopic spinful wavefunctions, which enables a bottom-up quantitative test of semi-classical theories and postulated distributions $f_{\text{CVE}}$ in different reference frames. Notably, it shows that $f_{\text{CVE}}$ is over a ground-state-free Floquet spectrum, qualitatively distinct from a thermal equilibrium distribution (i.e., fermi form $f_F$), underscoring CVE as a non-equilibrium phenomenon, distinguished from other chiral transports. The $f_F$ only approximately holds when three conditions are simultaneously fulfilled: (1) slow rotation $ωR/v_F\ll 1$, (2) high chemical potential $μ/(\hbar v_F R)\gg 1$, (3) isotropic symmetry, where $R$ is the size, $v_F$ is fermi velocity. In these conditions, the theory recovers established semiclassical results, including the current-response coefficients and the magnetization contribution; otherwise, it uncovers quantum phenomena such as ``void states", deviation from the semiclassical formula $j_{\text{CVE}} \sim μ^2$, a $v_F$-independent charge pumping. The theory is based on semimetals, providing more experimentally accessible detection than fundamental Weyl particles.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a fully quantum formulation for the chiral vortical effect (CVE) by solving the exact evolution of microscopic spinful wavefunctions, revealing that the postulated distribution f_CVE is defined over a ground-state-free Floquet spectrum and is qualitatively distinct from a thermal Fermi distribution. The semiclassical theory is recovered only under simultaneous conditions of slow rotation, high chemical potential, and isotropic symmetry; otherwise, quantum phenomena such as void states, deviations from j_CVE ~ μ², and v_F-independent charge pumping emerge. The theory based on semimetals offers more experimentally accessible detection than fundamental Weyl particles.
AI.motivation: The current description of the chiral vortical effect relies on semiclassical frameworks, lacking a fully quantum treatment. The authors aim to build a quantum formulation that can quantitatively test semiclassical theories and the postulated distribution f_CVE in different reference frames, while also resolving whether CVE is an equilibrium or non-equilibrium phenomenon.
AI.method: The authors derive a fully quantum formulation for CVE by solving the exact time evolution of microscopic spinful wavefunctions in a rotating Weyl fermion system. They compare the resulting distribution against semiclassical predictions and the proposed f_CVE distribution under various parameter regimes, systematically varying rotation frequency, chemical potential, and symmetry conditions. The theory is built on semimetal systems for experimental accessibility.
AI.result: The analysis shows f_CVE is defined over a ground-state-free Floquet spectrum, qualitatively distinct from a thermal Fermi distribution, establishing CVE as a non-equilibrium phenomenon. The Fermi-form distribution holds only when slow rotation (ωR/v_F ≪ 1), high chemical potential (μ/(ℏv_F R) ≫ 1), and isotropic symmetry are simultaneously satisfied. Outside these conditions, novel quantum effects emerge, including void states, deviations from the semiclassical j_CVE ~ μ² scaling, and v_F-independent charge pumping.
AI.conclusion: CVE is fundamentally a non-equilibrium effect, distinct from other chiral transport phenomena. The semiclassical theory serves only as a limiting case under specific conditions. The quantum formulation uncovers new physics (void states, modified scaling, v_F-independent pumping) and, by grounding the theory in semimetals, proposes a more experimentally accessible route to detecting CVE compared to fundamental Weyl particles.

title: Prediction of BaBiO$_3$-like superconducting perovskites in K-doped SrAsO$_3$
summary: Using first-principles calculations, we predict a new perovskite compound SrAsO$_3$ . The undoped cubic phase has pronounced soft-phonon instabilities, which are gradually suppressed upon K doping the Sr site. The cubic phase becomes dynamically stable for K-doping levels above approximately 60%, and the stabilized K-doped phases are metallic with predicted conventional phonon mediated superconductivity. Moreover, the inclusion of nonlocal exchange interactions broadens the electronic bandwidth, enhances the electron-phonon coupling (EPC) strength, and increases the superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$) of these doped compounds. In particular, the HSE06 hybrid exchange-correlation functional corrected EPC constant $λ$ reaches 1.41 for Sr$_{0.4}$K$_{0.6}$AsO$_3$, corresponding to a predicted $T_c$ of 44.3 K. These results suggest that SrAsO$_3$ is a BaBiO$_3$-like superconducting perovskite driven by strong electron-phonon coupling.

AI.tldr: First-principles calculations predict a new perovskite compound SrAsO₃ that becomes dynamically stable and superconducting when K-doped above ~60%, with a predicted T_c of 44.3 K for Sr₀.₄K₀.₆AsO₃, driven by strong electron-phonon coupling.
AI.motivation: To discover and characterize a new perovskite oxide superconductor, SrAsO₃, by investigating its lattice stability, electronic structure, and superconducting properties upon doping.
AI.method: First-principles calculations using density functional theory, including soft-phonon instability analysis, K-doping effects on the Sr site, hybrid HSE06 exchange-correlation functional for nonlocal exchange corrections, and electron-phonon coupling calculations within the conventional phonon-mediated superconductivity framework.
AI.result: The undoped cubic SrAsO₃ has soft-phonon instabilities that are suppressed by K doping above ~60%, yielding dynamically stable metallic phases with phonon-mediated superconductivity. The HSE06 functional increases the EPC constant to λ=1.41 for Sr₀.₄K₀.₆AsO₃, corresponding to a predicted T_c of 44.3 K, significantly higher than standard functional predictions.
AI.conclusion: SrAsO₃ is identified as a BaBiO₃-like superconducting perovskite with strong electron-phonon coupling, where nonlocal exchange effects play a critical role in enhancing the superconducting transition temperature.

title: Finite-Temperature Spin-Adapted ROKS and TDDFT
summary: Finite-temperature conditions constitute a central regime of interest in quantum chemistry. Nonetheless, a consistent incorporation of finite-temperature effects into density functional theory (DFT) for both ground and excited states, while rigorously preserving the spin-symmetry associated with the $\hat{S}^2$ operator, has not yet been achieved. In this work, we develop a finite-temperature extension of restricted open-shell Kohn-Sham (ROKS) theory and spin-adapted time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT), providing unified frameworks for the description of ground and excited states, respectively. For finite-temperature ROKS, we construct a canonical ensemble by using integer high-spin ROKS components, where each component $I$ has the same spin number $|SS \rangle$ and its weight $w_I$ follows the Boltzmann distribution. For finite-temperature spin-adapted TDDFT, every integer component $I$ supplies an ordinary zero-temperature spin-adapted TDDFT matrix pair $(\Mmat_I,\Nmat_I)$. These matrices are arranged in one unified spatial-orbital order and then averaged. In the zero-temperature single-component limit, the theory reduces to ordinary high-spin ROKS and the corresponding spin-adapted TDDFT. As a numerical application, we apply the theory to a diradicaloid and use the calculated excitations to interpret the thermally activated absorption observed in variable-temperature UV/Vis spectroscopy.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a finite-temperature extension of restricted open-shell Kohn-Sham (ROKS) theory and spin-adapted time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT), enabling unified descriptions of ground and excited states under finite-temperature conditions while rigorously preserving spin symmetry. The theory is constructed via a canonical ensemble of integer high-spin ROKS components with Boltzmann-distributed weights, and the spin-adapted TDDFT matrices are averaged across components. The approach is validated on a diradicaloid system, interpreting thermally activated absorption observed in variable-temperature UV/Vis spectroscopy.
AI.motivation: Finite-temperature effects are crucial in quantum chemistry, yet no consistent incorporation of them into DFT for both ground and excited states exists while rigorously preserving the spin symmetry associated with the S^2 operator. This gap limits the accurate description of systems at finite temperatures, especially for thermally activated electronic processes.
AI.method: The authors construct a finite-temperature canonical ensemble using integer high-spin ROKS components, where each component I has the same spin number |SS⟩ and its weight w_I follows a Boltzmann distribution. For finite-temperature spin-adapted TDDFT, each integer component provides an ordinary zero-temperature spin-adapted TDDFT matrix pair (M_I, N_I), which are arranged in a unified spatial-orbital order and averaged. In the zero-temperature single-component limit, the theory reduces to ordinary high-spin ROKS and corresponding spin-adapted TDDFT.
AI.result: The theory is applied numerically to a diradicaloid system, and the calculated excitations are used to interpret thermally activated absorption observed in variable-temperature UV/Vis spectroscopy, demonstrating the practical utility of the approach.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a unified finite-temperature framework for both ground and excited states in open-shell DFT that rigorously preserves spin symmetry, extending ROKS and spin-adapted TDDFT to canonical ensembles at finite temperature and validating the approach on a diradicaloid system against experimental UV/Vis data.

title: Spin selective non-van der Waal electride nature in manganese under ambient pressure
summary: Electrides are an unusual class of ionic materials in which electrons localized in non-nuclear, interstitial regions act as anions within the crystal lattice. Here, we employ first-principles quantum mechanical calculations to investigate the structural, electronic, magnetic, and electride characteristics of elemental manganese (Mn) at an ambient pressure (0 GPa), focusing on its three crystalline phases: cubic ($α$)-Mn ($I\bar{4}3m,no.217$), cubic ($β$)-Mn ($P4_132, no.213$), and hexagonal ($hex$)-Mn ($P6_3/mmc, no.194$). Our calculations reveal pronounced interstitial-electron character in all three phases, accompanied by spin-selective electron localization function (ELF), establishing elemental Mn as a non-van der Waals electride system. Bader charge analysis indicates substantial electron redistribution from the Mn host framework toward the interstitial anionic-electron (IAE) regions, with an effective charge transfer of approximately $-1.645e$, $-1.477e$, and $-1.083e$ per interstitial basin in $α$-Mn, $β$-Mn, and $hex$-Mn, respectively. The electride character is further supported by the electronic density of states, where the IAE-associated states exhibit finite contributions near the Fermi level ($E_F$) and coexist with Mn-derived states, demonstrating their direct participation in the low-energy electronic structure. The combined electron localization function (ELF), effective charge transfer, and electron population due to IAE at $E_F$ therefore provide consistent evidence for interstitial anionic electrons in elemental Mn. To the best of our knowledge, this work provides the first systematic identification of spin-selective electride character in elemental Mn at ambient pressure, highlighting the possibility of exploiting its interstitial-electron states for unconventional electronic and magnetic functionalities.

AI.tldr: First-principles calculations reveal that elemental manganese (Mn) exhibits spin-selective electride character in all three of its ambient-pressure crystalline phases (α, β, and hexagonal), with electrons localized in interstitial anionic regions showing substantial charge transfer and finite contributions near the Fermi level.
AI.motivation: To systematically investigate whether elemental Mn, despite being a conventional transition metal, exhibits electride-like behavior with interstitial anionic electrons at ambient pressure, and to characterize this behavior across its three crystalline phases.
AI.method: First-principles quantum mechanical calculations examining structural, electronic, magnetic, and electride properties of Mn in its three phases (α-Mn, β-Mn, hex-Mn), using electron localization function (ELF), Bader charge analysis, and electronic density of states calculations.
AI.result: All three Mn phases exhibit pronounced interstitial-electron character with spin-selective ELF. Bader analysis shows effective charge transfer of approximately -1.645e, -1.477e, and -1.083e per interstitial basin for α-Mn, β-Mn, and hex-Mn, respectively. IAE-associated states contribute finitely near the Fermi level, coexisting with Mn-derived states.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the first systematic identification of spin-selective electride character in elemental Mn at ambient pressure, establishing Mn as a non-van der Waals electride system and suggesting potential for unconventional electronic and magnetic functionalities.

title: Coordinate-Residual Physics-Driven Neural Network for Electromagnetic Inverse Scattering
summary: Electromagnetic inverse scattering is a nonlinear and ill-posed problem, where accurate reconstruction is challenging due to measurement limitations, noise, and high computational costs, especially for 3-D imaging. Although physics-driven neural networks (PDNNs) reduce the dependence on labeled training data, existing accelerated PDNN frameworks often rely on preliminary reconstruction-based region selection, which may introduce instability when the selected region is inaccurate. In this paper, a coordinate-residual physics-driven neural network (CRPDNN) is proposed for 3-D electromagnetic inverse scattering. The proposed solver directly reconstructs the unknown contrast distribution using normalized spatial coordinates and a residual convolutional network, without requiring a preliminary reconstruction. For the reported noise-free 3-D synthetic cases, CRPDNN achieves an average relative error of 2.10\%, compared with 7.97\% for CSI and 3.99\% for $L_{2/3}$-FBE-WCIE, while providing approximately 5.5- and 12.1-fold speedups over the two baselines, respectively. Supplementary 2-D comparisons further confirm its stability and computational efficiency relative to existing PDNN frameworks. CRPDNN also maintains reliable reconstruction performance under noisy measurements, and the 3-D Fresnel experiments further indicate its potential for practical imaging applications. The related code is available at https://github.com/Physics-driven-methods.

AI.tldr: CRPDNN is a coordinate-residual physics-driven neural network for 3-D electromagnetic inverse scattering that directly reconstructs contrast distributions without preliminary region selection, achieving 2.10% average relative error and 5.5-12.1x speedups over baselines.
AI.motivation: Electromagnetic inverse scattering is nonlinear and ill-posed with high computational costs, especially for 3-D imaging. Existing accelerated PDNN frameworks rely on preliminary reconstruction-based region selection which is unstable when the selected region is inaccurate.
AI.method: The proposed CRPDNN directly reconstructs unknown contrast distribution using normalized spatial coordinates and a residual convolutional network, eliminating the need for preliminary reconstruction-based region selection.
AI.result: On noise-free 3-D synthetic cases, CRPDNN achieves 2.10% average relative error compared to 7.97% for CSI and 3.99% for L2/3-FBE-WCIE, with approximately 5.5x and 12.1x speedups respectively. It shows stability and computational efficiency in 2-D comparisons, maintains performance under noise, and demonstrates practical potential in 3-D Fresnel experiments.
AI.conclusion: CRPDNN provides a stable and efficient alternative to existing PDNN frameworks for 3-D electromagnetic inverse scattering, offering improved accuracy, computational speed, and robustness to noise without requiring preliminary reconstruction, with potential for practical imaging applications.

title: Elementary magnons and interacting multi-magnon quasiparticles in the effective spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ kagome-staircase magnet Co$_{3}$V$_{2}$O$_{8}$
summary: The excitation spectrum of an anisotropic magnet provides a direct link between its microscopic Hamiltonian and interaction-driven quasiparticles. Here we use high-resolution time-domain terahertz spectroscopy to map the magnetic excitations of the three-dimensional kagome-staircase compound Co$_{3}$V$_{2}$O$_{8}$ as functions of temperature and magnetic field. At low energies, polarization-resolved spectra identify magnetic-dipole-active one-magnon modes and track their evolution across the ferromagnetic and spin-density-wave phases. Combining their field dependence with previously reported inelastic-neutron-scattering dispersions, we determine an effective spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ Hamiltonian with strongly anisotropic exchange that quantitatively reproduces the one-magnon spectrum. This model provides a noninteracting benchmark for the high-energy response, where we observe sharp branches with field slopes that are two to four times those of the one-magnon modes, together with anticrossings between branches of different magnon numbers. Their sharpness, polarization dependence, and departure from the calculated multi-magnon continua identify them as interacting multi-magnon quasiparticles that can be stabilized by strong exchange anisotropy.

AI.tldr: High-resolution time-domain terahertz spectroscopy maps magnetic excitations in the kagome-staircase compound Co3V2O8. Polarization-resolved spectra identify one-magnon modes across ferromagnetic and spin-density-wave phases, enabling determination of an effective spin-1/2 Hamiltonian with strongly anisotropic exchange. Sharp high-energy branches with field slopes 2-4 times those of one-magnon modes, alongside anticrossings between different magnon-number branches, are identified as interacting multi-magnon quasiparticles stabilized by strong exchange anisotropy.
AI.motivation: To establish a direct link between the microscopic Hamiltonian of an anisotropic magnet and its interaction-driven quasiparticles by mapping the magnetic excitation spectrum of Co3V2O8, a three-dimensional kagome-staircase compound.
AI.method: High-resolution time-domain terahertz spectroscopy was used to map magnetic excitations as functions of temperature and magnetic field. Polarization-resolved spectra identified magnetic-dipole-active one-magnon modes. Field-dependent data were combined with inelastic-neutron-scattering dispersions to determine an effective spin-1/2 Hamiltonian with strongly anisotropic exchange. High-energy branches were analyzed against multi-magnon continuum calculations.
AI.result: An effective spin-1/2 Hamiltonian with strongly anisotropic exchange quantitatively reproduces the one-magnon spectrum. Sharp high-energy branches exhibit field slopes two to four times those of one-magnon modes, with anticrossings between branches of different magnon numbers. Their sharpness, polarization dependence, and deviation from calculated multi-magnon continua identify them as interacting multi-magnon quasiparticles.
AI.conclusion: Strong exchange anisotropy can stabilize interacting multi-magnon quasiparticles that persist as sharp, well-defined excitations rather than broadening into continua, providing a noninteracting benchmark for the high-energy magnetic response.

title: Exchange-induced suppression of superconductivity in a nano-skyrmion lattice - superconductor hybrid
summary: Engineered magnet-superconductor hybrids have recently been identified as promising platforms for the investigation of topological superconductivity. Beyond ferro- and antiferromagnetic structures, coupling non-collinear spin textures, such as skyrmion lattices, to superconductors offers an exciting route for creating and manipulating unconventional superconducting states. In this work, by preparing monolayer Fe on Ir(111) thin films grown epitaxially on a Nb(110) surface, we realize a hybrid system of a nano-skyrmion lattice proximitized to a superconducting substrate. Scanning tunneling spectroscopy shows that superconductivity becomes suppressed by the Fe nano-skyrmion lattice, with both the superconducting gap and coherence peaks disappearing. Tight-binding calculations reveal that with increasing exchange coupling, the gap is progressively filled up and eventually superconductivity gets quenched. These results reveal microscopic constraints for designing topologically non-trivial states based on magnet-superconducting heterostructures.

AI.tldr: A Fe/Ir(111) nano-skyrmion lattice grown on Nb(110) suppresses superconductivity via strong exchange coupling, filling the superconducting gap and quenching it entirely, revealing design constraints for topological hybrid systems.
AI.motivation: Magnet-superconductor hybrids are promising platforms for topological superconductivity. While ferro- and antiferromagnetic structures have been studied, coupling non-collinear spin textures like skyrmion lattices to superconductors could enable new routes to unconventional superconducting states, but this regime remains unexplored experimentally.
AI.method: Monolayer Fe was grown epitaxially on Ir(111) thin films on a Nb(110) substrate to create a nano-skyrmion lattice proximitized to a superconductor. Scanning tunneling spectroscopy (STS) characterized the superconducting state, complemented by tight-binding calculations tracking gap evolution as a function of exchange coupling.
AI.result: STS showed suppression of superconductivity by the Fe nano-skyrmion lattice, with both the superconducting gap and coherence peaks vanishing. Tight-binding calculations demonstrated that increasing exchange coupling progressively fills the gap until superconductivity is completely quenched.
AI.conclusion: Strong exchange coupling from nano-skyrmion lattices can destroy superconductivity, establishing microscopic constraints that must be considered when designing topologically non-trivial states in magnet-superconducting heterostructures.

title: Bayesian Localization and Uncertainty Quantification of Trace Species in Two-Dimensional SIMS Imaging
summary: To enable accurate localization of trace species on material surfaces, we propose a Bayesian framework for analyzing two-dimensional (2D) secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS) imaging data. SIMS is widely used in semiconductor manufacturing, materials science, geology, environmental science, and life sciences because of its high sensitivity and excellent elemental and isotopic specificity. However, precise localization remains challenging because of primary ion beam broadening, overlap between neighboring ion distributions, and limited ion counts. The underlying distribution of trace species is modeled as a superposition of two-dimensional Gaussian peaks. To account for the stochastic nature of low-count measurements, the detected ion counts are assumed to follow a Poisson likelihood within a Bayesian framework. Posterior distributions of the peak parameters are estimated using replica-exchange Monte Carlo (REMC), enabling stable inference together with quantitative uncertainty estimation under low-count conditions. The proposed method is first validated using synthetic datasets with known ground truth and is then applied to SIMS measurements of semiconductor samples containing regularly arranged gold (Au) dots with diameters ranging from 0.4 to 2.0~$μ$m, using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images as the reference. Optimization of the measurement conditions reduced the relative localization error for 0.4~$μ$m dots from 5.1$\%$ to 1.9$\%$. These results demonstrate accurate submicrometer localization with statistically rigorous uncertainty quantification in 2D SIMS imaging.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Bayesian framework for localizing trace species in 2D SIMS imaging, modeling the underlying distribution as a superposition of 2D Gaussian peaks with Poisson likelihood and replica-exchange Monte Carlo for posterior estimation. Validated on synthetic data and applied to semiconductor samples with Au dots (0.4-2.0 μm), it reduced relative localization error from 5.1% to 1.9% for 0.4 μm dots.
AI.motivation: Precise localization of trace species on material surfaces using SIMS is challenging due to primary ion beam broadening, overlap between neighboring ion distributions, and limited ion counts. Current methods lack statistically rigorous ways to handle these issues under low-count conditions.
AI.method: The underlying trace species distribution is modeled as a superposition of 2D Gaussian peaks. Detected ion counts are assumed to follow a Poisson likelihood within a Bayesian framework. Posterior distributions of peak parameters are estimated using replica-exchange Monte Carlo (REMC), enabling stable inference with quantitative uncertainty estimation under low-count conditions.
AI.result: Validation on synthetic datasets with known ground truth confirmed the method's effectiveness. Application to SIMS measurements of semiconductor samples with Au dots (0.4-2.0 μm diameter) using SEM images as reference showed that optimization of measurement conditions reduced the relative localization error for 0.4 μm dots from 5.1% to 1.9%.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Bayesian framework enables accurate submicrometer localization with statistically rigorous uncertainty quantification in 2D SIMS imaging, demonstrating reliable trace species localization under low-count conditions.

title: Metastability limit of pristine 2D noble metals with high-energy facet: dominance of the Bell-Evans-Polanyi principle
summary: Using density functional theory, we predict that ultrathin (110) sheets of Rh, Pd, Ag, and Ir tend to transform into their (100) counterparts via lattice contraction. An approximately linear relationship between the transformation barrier and the energy difference between (110) and (100) sheets is revealed, demonstrating that the Bell-Evans-Polanyi (BEP) principle dominates. Furthermore, the critical thicknesses for these metals are also described by the BEP principle: below these thicknesses, the (110) sheets are no longer metastable and undergo spontaneous structural transformation.

AI.tldr: DFT calculations predict that ultrathin (110) sheets of Rh, Pd, Ag, and Ir spontaneously transform to (100) sheets via lattice contraction. A linear BEP-type relationship governs both the transformation barrier and critical thickness for these structural transitions.
AI.motivation: To understand the structural stability and transformation behavior of ultrathin metal sheets with different surface orientations, which is important for nanomaterial applications.
AI.method: Density functional theory (DFT) calculations to predict structural transformations between (110) and (100) ultrathin sheets of Rh, Pd, Ag, and Ir, combined with analysis of transformation barriers and energy differences using the Bell-Evans-Polanyi (BEP) principle.
AI.result: Ultrathin (110) sheets of these metals transform to (100) sheets via lattice contraction. A near-linear relation exists between the transformation barrier and the (110)-(100) energy difference, confirming BEP behavior. Critical thicknesses below which (110) sheets become thermodynamically unstable are also described by the BEP principle.
AI.conclusion: The BEP principle provides a unified framework for predicting both transformation barriers and critical thicknesses governing the spontaneous structural transformation of ultrathin metal sheets, offering a predictive tool for designing stable 2D metal structures.

title: Magnetotransport evolution and nonlinear Hall effect in altermagnetic MnTe
summary: Hexagonal MnTe is a prototypical semiconducting altermagnet whose properties are heavily influenced by intrinsic disorder, yet how the resulting diverse transport regimes shape its magnetotransport behavior remains to be clarified alongside the role of relativistic spin-orbit coupling (SOC). Here, we present a systematic study of the anisotropic magnetoresistance (AMR), planar Hall effect (PHE), and nonlinear transport in MnTe bulk single crystals. Below the Néel temperature (TN ~ 304 K), the emergence of high-order harmonics in AMR and PHE within the high-temperature metallic regime reveals the interplay of magnetic order, crystalline symmetry, and SOC. At relatively lower temperatures, the disappearance of higher-order symmetries coincides with a transport crossover into the hopping conduction regime, suggesting that carrier localization diminishes the transport sensitivity to the Fermi-surface topology. In addition, we detect distinct second-order nonlinear Hall signals, providing evidence for a macroscopic inversion-asymmetric response in altermagnetic MnTe. Extending the investigations into the localized regime provides key insights into the subtle role of disorder and SOC in macroscopic charge transport. Our work thus underscores the necessity of exploring magnetotransport across diverse conducting regimes to comprehensively understand altermagnetic properties.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a systematic study of anisotropic magnetoresistance (AMR), planar Hall effect (PHE), and nonlinear transport in MnTe bulk single crystals, revealing how transport regimes (metallic vs. hopping) and spin-orbit coupling shape magnetotransport behavior in this semiconducting altermagnet.
AI.motivation: Hexagonal MnTe is a prototype semiconducting altermagnet heavily influenced by intrinsic disorder, yet how its diverse transport regimes shape magnetotransport behavior and the role of relativistic spin-orbit coupling (SOC) remain unclear.
AI.method: Systematic measurements of AMR, PHE, and nonlinear transport in MnTe bulk single crystals across different temperature regimes (above and below the Néel temperature TN ~ 304 K).
AI.result: High-order harmonics in AMR and PHE emerge in the high-temperature metallic regime reflecting magnetic order, crystalline symmetry, and SOC interplay. These higher-order symmetries vanish at lower temperatures with a crossover to hopping conduction, indicating carrier localization reduces Fermi-surface sensitivity. Distinct second-order nonlinear Hall signals provide evidence for macroscopic inversion-asymmetric response in altermagnetic MnTe.
AI.conclusion: Exploring magnetotransport across diverse conducting regimes is essential to comprehensively understand altermagnetic properties, highlighting the subtle roles of disorder and SOC in macroscopic charge transport.

title: Autonomous Lindblad Realizability of Nonunitary Linear Dynamics with a Carleman Lattice Boltzmann Application
summary: Carleman lifting converts nonlinear polynomial dynamics into finite linear systems, but the resulting truncations are generally nonunitary and need not correspond to physical quantum evolution. We prove that a finite linear endpoint admits an autonomous Gorini--Kossakowski--Sudarshan--Lindblad (GKSL) realization on vacuum coherences if and only if it is invertible and power bounded. The construction is explicit and realizes the nonunitary map directly as open-system dynamics, with no endpoint postselection and with one encoding and one decoding over repeated timesteps. We apply the result to the complete D2Q9 multiple-relaxation-time lattice Boltzmann (LB) timestep by compiling collision and periodic streaming into a single Carleman endpoint. The resulting GKSL evolution reproduces the classical Carleman trajectory over multiple timesteps, while the remaining discrepancy from nonlinear LB dynamics is the expected Carleman truncation error. The result establishes a general criterion for autonomous open-quantum realization of finite nonunitary dynamics, with Carleman--LB dynamics as a concrete example.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that a finite linear endpoint from Carleman lifting admits an autonomous GKSL (Lindblad) open-quantum realization on vacuum coherences if and only if it is invertible and power bounded. The construction is explicit, requires no endpoint postselection, and uses one encoding and one decoding over repeated steps. The result is applied to a complete D2Q9 MRT lattice Boltzmann timestep, where a single Carleman endpoint is compiled and the resulting GKSL evolution reproduces the classical Carleman trajectory, with deviation from the full nonlinear LB dynamics being just the expected Carleman truncation error.
AI.motivation: Carleman lifting maps nonlinear polynomial dynamics to finite linear systems, but the resulting truncations are generally nonunitary and therefore cannot be directly interpreted as physical quantum evolution. The paper aims to find a general criterion and constructive method for realizing such finite nonunitary linear maps as genuine open-quantum (GKSL) dynamics without resorting to postselection.
AI.method: The authors derive a necessary and sufficient condition—invertibility plus power boundedness—for a finite linear endpoint to admit an autonomous GKSL realization on vacuum coherences. They provide an explicit construction that encodes once, decodes once over repeated timesteps, and avoids endpoint postselection. They compile the complete D2Q9 multiple-relaxation-time lattice Boltzmann timestep (collision plus periodic streaming) into a single Carleman endpoint and construct the corresponding GKSL evolution.
AI.result: The resulting GKSL evolution reproduces the classical Carleman trajectory over multiple timesteps. The only discrepancy relative to the true nonlinear LB dynamics is the expected Carleman truncation error. This establishes a concrete example of autonomous open-quantum realization of finite nonunitary dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a general criterion (invertible and power bounded) for an autonomous open-quantum realization of finite nonunitary dynamics, with the Carleman–LB dynamics serving as a concrete and complete demonstration.

title: Revisiting the Coupling of Thermodynamics and Electromagnetics
summary: We revisit the coupling of continuum thermodynamics and electromagnetic theory for polarisable and magnetisable matter in motion. Two routes are followed and then compared. The first route is the axiomatic bulk theory of Dreyer, Guhlke and Müller, in which universal balance laws are closed by an entropy principle. We show that the source of the internal energy balance must be built with the non-convective electric current, that the polarisation current and the Lorentz magnetisation enter through one single identity, which Dreyer et al.\ do not write down, and that this identity fixes both the admissible entropy variables and the signs of the bound-current ansatz. The second route is the statistical-mechanical one of Mazur, in which the macroscopic Maxwell equations are obtained by ensemble averaging over a system of atoms with internal charge carriers. Mazur stops before the conservation laws, so we derive them, and we estimate the size of the mass-correction terms that appear. The comparison shows that after a redefinition of polarisation and magnetisation the two sets of equations agree structurally. The only irreducible difference is a momentum contribution from microscopic field fluctuations, which can not be reproduced in a purely macroscopic theory. We further show that the electromotive intensity $\mathcal{E}$ and the Lorentz magnetisation $\mathcal{M}$ are not modelling choices but appear by themselves, and that the asymmetric look of the entropy function is a consequence of the chosen energy variable and not a defect of the theory.

AI.tldr: This paper revisits the coupling of continuum thermodynamics with electromagnetic theory for moving polarisable and magnetisable matter by comparing two complementary approaches: the axiomatic bulk theory of Dreyer, Guhlke & Müller and the statistical-mechanical approach of Mazur. After redefining polarisation and magnetisation, both formalisms yield structurally identical equations. The only irreducible difference is a momentum contribution from microscopic field fluctuations that cannot be reproduced macroscopically. The paper shows that the electromotive intensity and Lorentz magnetisation emerge naturally (not as modelling choices), and that the seemingly asymmetric entropy function stems from the chosen energy variable.
AI.motivation: To clarify and reconcile two competing theoretical frameworks describing the coupling between thermodynamics and electromagnetism in moving, polarisable and magnetisable media, and to resolve ambiguities regarding energy balance sources, entropy variables, magnetisation definitions, and the origin of certain field quantities.
AI.method: Two routes are followed and compared: (1) the axiomatic bulk thermodynamic theory of Dreyer, Guhlke and Müller, closed via an entropy principle, where the authors show the internal energy balance source must use the non-convective electric current, and that polarisation current and Lorentz magnetisation are linked by a previously unidentified identity that fixes entropy variables and bound-current signs; (2) the statistical-mechanical approach of Mazur, extending it by deriving the missing conservation laws and estimating mass-correction terms.
AI.result: After redefining polarisation and magnetisation, the two sets of equations agree structurally. The only irreducible difference is a momentum contribution from microscopic field fluctuations, which cannot be reproduced in a purely macroscopic theory. The electromotive intensity and Lorentz magnetisation arise naturally from the formalism, and the asymmetric form of the entropy function is a consequence of the energy variable choice rather than a theory defect.
AI.conclusion: The two frameworks—axiomatic thermodynamics and statistical mechanics—are structurally reconcilable for polarisable and magnetisable matter in motion, provided a consistent redefinition of polarisation and magnetisation. The inherent limitation of macroscopic theory is the loss of momentum contributions from micro-field fluctuations, and several quantities previously thought to be modelling choices are in fact unavoidable consequences of the formalism.

title: Optimally embedded tight binding for reproducing geometry dependent observables
comment: Main: 18 pages, 7 figures, Appendix: 10 pages, 6 figures
summary: In tight-binding models, the position operator is reduced to intra-cell orbital positions (embeddings). While accurately reproducing band structures, such models often fail for geometry dependent responses depending on the position operator. To address this, we investigate the role of these embeddings and introduce the general framework of optimally embedded tight binding. Treating the embeddings as geometric tuning parameters to be fixed against a reference response (obtained from ab-initio computation or experiment), we obtain tight-binding models of GaAs and CdS which quantitatively reproduce non-linear optical responses at no cost to band structure accuracy. The optimal embeddings are determined efficiently using position derivatives obtained from decomposing tight-binding observables into a geometry independent and dependent part, and explicit derivatives are provided for key quantities such as the quantum geometric tensor. The decomposition reveals where geometric effects dominate, and we show in both toy models and in the Chern insulator V2O3 how geometry can dramatically alter the local metric trace. Our results highlight that orbital embeddings should be treated as a genuine model parameter which should be explicitly fixed against physical data to get accurate minimal models.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "optimally embedded tight binding," treating orbital embeddings (intra-cell position operator reductions) as geometric tuning parameters to be fixed against reference responses. This framework quantitatively reproduces non-linear optical responses in GaAs and CdS without sacrificing band structure accuracy, and reveals how geometry dramatically impacts responses in toy models and the Chern insulator V2O3.
AI.motivation: Tight-binding models reduce the position operator to intra-cell orbital positions (embeddings), which accurately reproduce band structures but often fail for geometry-dependent responses. The paper addresses the need to properly treat embeddings to accurately capture such responses.
AI.method: Treat embeddings as geometric tuning parameters fixed against reference responses from ab-initio computation or experiment. Use position derivatives from decomposing tight-binding observables into geometry-independent and geometry-dependent parts. Provide explicit derivatives for key quantities such as the quantum geometric tensor, and apply the framework to GaAs, CdS, and a Chern insulator V2O3.
AI.result: Tight-binding models of GaAs and CdS quantitatively reproduce non-linear optical responses with no loss in band structure accuracy. The framework identifies where geometric effects dominate, and demonstrates in toy models and V2O3 that geometry can dramatically alter the local metric trace.
AI.conclusion: Orbital embeddings should be treated as genuine model parameters explicitly fixed against physical data to achieve accurate minimal tight-binding models for geometry-dependent responses.

title: Nonequilibrium dynamics of doped Chern ferromagnets: a case study for false vacuum decay
summary: Even though metastable false vacuum decay is ubiquitous in physics, its underlying dynamics are still not well understood. Dissipative state preparation in moiré quantum materials provides an exceptional setting for exploring this physics since it allows the possibility of generating exotic quantum states that are not the ground state of the system Hamiltonian. Motivated by recent experiments demonstrating steady-state optical orientation of the spin-valley degree of freedom of holes, here we investigate dynamics of itinerant and Chern ferromagnets in the presence of an opposing magnetic field. Optical pumping using a circularly polarized Laguerre-Gauss beam allows us to deterministically prepare a true vacuum bubble embedded inside a metastable state. Depending on its initial size controlled by the pump power, we observe that the bubble collapses or expands due to an interplay between domain wall and bulk dynamics. For external magnetic fields comparable to the coercive field of ferromagnetism, we observe up to two-orders-of-magnitude prolongation of the spin polarization decay time at commensurate fillings corresponding to integer and fractional Chern insulator states. Our experiments reveal that the nonequilibrium dynamics of the ferromagnetic domains is substantially more sensitive to the precise filling factor around Chern insulator states than standard transport or optical measurements.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates nonequilibrium dynamics of metastable false vacuum decay in moiré quantum materials by optically preparing true vacuum bubbles embedded in metastable ferromagnetic states using circularly polarized Laguerre-Gauss beams. The bubble collapses or expands depending on its initial size, and at magnetic fields comparable to the coercive field, spin polarization decay times are prolonged by up to two orders of magnitude at commensurate fillings corresponding to integer and fractional Chern insulator states.
AI.motivation: The underlying dynamics of metastable false vacuum decay are not well understood despite being ubiquitous in physics. Dissipative state preparation in moiré quantum materials offers a unique platform to explore this physics by enabling the generation of exotic quantum states that are not ground states of the system Hamiltonian.
AI.method: Optical pumping using a circularly polarized Laguerre-Gauss beam deterministically prepares a true vacuum bubble embedded inside a metastable state. The bubble's initial size is controlled by the pump power, allowing observation of collapse or expansion dynamics governed by the interplay between domain wall and bulk dynamics. The system consists of itinerant and Chern ferromagnets in an opposing magnetic field, motivated by experiments on steady-state optical orientation of hole spin-valley degrees of freedom.
AI.result: The bubble either collapses or expands depending on its initial size. At external magnetic fields comparable to the coercive field, up to two-orders-of-magnitude prolongation of spin polarization decay time is observed at commensurate fillings corresponding to both integer and fractional Chern insulator states. The nonequilibrium domain dynamics show substantially higher sensitivity to precise filling factors around Chern insulator states than standard transport or optical measurements.
AI.conclusion: The experiments demonstrate that dissipative state preparation in moiré quantum materials provides an exceptional setting to explore false vacuum decay dynamics, and the nonequilibrium ferromagnetic domain dynamics are highly sensitive probes of Chern insulator states, offering information beyond what conventional transport or optical measurements can reveal.

title: Revealing Hidden Unconventional Pairing through Nonreciprocal Transport
summary: Identifying the pairing symmetry of Cooper pairs is a fundamental step toward understanding the microscopic mechanisms of unconventional superconductors. However, experimental identification remains a formidable challenge, particularly when unconventional pairing is obscured by a dominant $s$-wave component that masks its spectroscopic signatures. Here, we develop a symmetry-resolved framework to identify superconducting pairing symmetry through nonreciprocal conductance upon exchanging source and detector terminals in multiterminal devices. We show that nonreciprocal transport arises from symmetry-breaking components of the superconducting order parameter and exhibits a characteristic angular dependence that encodes the momentum-space structure of the pairing gap. In particular, time-reversal-breaking singlet pairing induces nonreciprocal charge transport, while spin-triplet pairing generates nonreciprocal spin responses, providing distinct transport fingerprints of the underlying order. We demonstrate this mechanism using representative models of iron-based and noncentrosymmetric superconductors and outline experimental protocols for multiterminal measurements. Our results advance the theoretical understanding of nonreciprocal transport in superconductors, and establish it as a symmetry-selective probe for identifying hidden unconventional pairing in a wide range of superconducting materials.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a symmetry-resolved framework to identify superconducting pairing symmetry via nonreciprocal conductance in multiterminal devices. It shows that symmetry-breaking components of the order parameter (time-reversal-breaking singlet and spin-triplet pairings) generate distinct nonreciprocal charge and spin transport signatures with characteristic angular dependence, demonstrated on iron-based and noncentrosymmetric superconductors.
AI.motivation: Identifying Cooper pair pairing symmetry is fundamental for understanding unconventional superconductors, yet experimental identification is challenging, especially when unconventional pairing is masked by a dominant s-wave component that hides its spectroscopic signatures.
AI.method: The authors develop a symmetry-resolved theoretical framework that connects nonreciprocal conductance upon source-detector terminal exchange in multiterminal devices to symmetry-breaking components of the superconducting order parameter, and demonstrate the mechanism using representative models of iron-based and noncentrosymmetric superconductors.
AI.result: Time-reversal-breaking singlet pairing induces nonreciprocal charge transport, while spin-triplet pairing generates nonreciprocal spin responses, each providing distinct transport fingerprints with characteristic angular dependence encoding the momentum-space structure of the pairing gap. Experimental protocols for multiterminal measurements are outlined.
AI.conclusion: The results advance the theoretical understanding of nonreciprocal transport in superconductors and establish it as a symmetry-selective probe for identifying hidden unconventional pairing across a wide range of superconducting materials.

title: Analytical Nuclear Gradients and Hessians on Quantum Hardware via Orbital-Optimized VQE with Error Mitigation
summary:
Nuclear gradients and Hessians are fundamental quantities in computational chemistry, essential for a wide range of applications including geometry optimization, vibrational spectroscopy, and molecular property calculations. In this work, we present their analytical implementation on quantum hardware. The methodology is formulated within an active-space framework combining orbital optimization and linear-response theory.
  On the quantum-computing side, the approach employs the tiled unitary product state (tUPS) ansatz to directly evaluate the tensor elements required for solving the response equations. Moreover, the expectation values are corrected using an adapted confusion-matrix error-mitigation scheme in combination with post-selection criteria. The resulting workflow is assessed on molecular hydrogen and on water through the calculation of potential energy surfaces, nuclear gradients, Hessians, and vibrational frequencies, enabling the evaluation of both its capabilities and current limitations.
  The results demonstrate good performance for the hydrogen molecule, whereas the water molecule provides a more demanding test of quantum-hardware resources and highlights the trade-offs associated with error-mitigation strategies. The quantified analysis of the results identify the main sources of errors, suggesting improvement directions for more accurate quantum computer applications.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first analytical implementation of nuclear gradients and Hessians on quantum hardware, using an active-space framework with orbital optimization and linear-response theory, the tUPS ansatz for tensor evaluation, and an adapted confusion-matrix error-mitigation scheme with post-selection. The workflow is benchmarked on H₂ and H₂O, achieving good performance on hydrogen while identifying hardware-resource trade-offs and error sources on water.
AI.motivation: Nuclear gradients and Hessians are essential for geometry optimization, vibrational spectroscopy, and molecular property calculations, yet their analytical implementation on quantum hardware has not been demonstrated. This work aims to fill that gap by providing a rigorous quantum-hardware implementation of these fundamental quantities.
AI.method: The methodology combines (1) an active-space framework with orbital optimization and linear-response theory, (2) the tiled unitary product state (tUPS) ansatz for directly evaluating tensor elements in the response equations, and (3) an adapted confusion-matrix error-mitigation scheme combined with post-selection criteria for correcting expectation values.
AI.result: The workflow was benchmarked on molecular hydrogen (H₂) and water (H₂O) by computing potential energy surfaces, nuclear gradients, Hessians, and vibrational frequencies. H₂ showed good performance, while H₂O posed a significantly more demanding test of quantum-hardware resources, revealing trade-offs in error-mitigation strategies and identifying dominant error sources.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates a working analytical implementation of nuclear gradients and Hessians on quantum hardware, validates the approach on hydrogen, and provides a quantified error analysis for water that points toward concrete improvement directions for more accurate quantum-computing-based molecular property calculations.

title: Gate-tunable electronic properties of epitaxial Bi (111) films using a printable hexagonal boron nitride ionogel
summary: Achieving effective electrostatic control of carrier transport in semimetals remains challenging due to strong screening and multiband effects. We report efficient low voltage top gated control of electronic transport in epitaxial Bi (111) thin films grown on GaAs (111) substrates using a printable hexagonal boron nitride ionogel. Magnetotransport measurements reveal pronounced nonlinear Hall conductivities arising from multiband electron and hole contributions. Remarkably, the application of a small gate voltage (less than 0.4 V in magnitude) leads to a systematic evolution of the low field Hall conductivity slope and the electron-hole compensation point. The response to gate voltage depends upon thickness and temperature. The observed behavior cannot be explained by a conventional Fermi level shift with rigid bands and instead indicates a non rigid band response associated with multiband effects and a gat tunable Rashba spin orbit coupling. Our results establish printable ionogel gating as a powerful approach to tune multiband transport in topological semimetals.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates efficient low-voltage top-gated electrostatic control of electronic transport in epitaxial Bi(111) thin films on GaAs(111) substrates using a printable hexagonal boron nitride ionogel. Small gate voltages (<0.4 V) systematically tune the Hall conductivity slope and electron-hole compensation point via a non-rigid band response involving multiband effects and gate-tunable Rashba spin-orbit coupling.
AI.motivation: Achieving effective electrostatic control of carrier transport in semimetals is challenging due to strong screening and multiband effects. The authors aim to overcome this limitation by establishing a gating approach suitable for semimetallic systems.
AI.method: Epitaxial Bi(111) thin films grown on GaAs(111) substrates are gated with a printable hexagonal boron nitride ionogel. Magnetotransport measurements are used to probe nonlinear Hall conductivities arising from multiband electron and hole contributions, with gate voltage, thickness, and temperature dependence characterized.
AI.result: Applying gate voltages of magnitude less than 0.4 V produces systematic evolution of the low-field Hall conductivity slope and the electron-hole compensation point. The response is thickness- and temperature-dependent, and cannot be explained by a conventional rigid-band Fermi level shift, indicating a non-rigid band response with gate-tunable Rashba spin-orbit coupling.
AI.conclusion: Printable ionogel gating is established as a powerful approach to tune multiband transport in topological semimetals, offering low-voltage electrostatic control despite the strong screening typically encountered in such systems.

title: Multiphysics Modeling of Thermo-Viscoelastic Damage in Functionally Graded Abradable Coatings with Probabilistic Geometric Tolerance Analysis
summary: In aircraft engines, functionally graded abradable coatings are used to control blade-tip clearance, but their durability is governed by effects that are often treated separately in existing models, including temperature-dependent viscoelastic softening, progressive damage, deposition-induced microstructural modulation, and geometric tolerances. This study integrates these effects within a unified multiphysics--probabilistic framework. The solved domain is a local through-thickness coating column driven by prescribed strain and temperature histories that include thermal eigenstrain and coating--substrate expansion mismatch. The results show that periodic property modulation increases end-of-cycle damage relative to the monotonic gradient and concentrates the maximum stress within a localized modulation crest. Propagating symmetric geometric tolerances through the coupled solver produces a strongly right-skewed damage distribution and a higher classification-level exceedance probability for the modulated gradient than for the monotonic gradient. This exceedance behavior cannot be obtained from a deterministic analysis performed at nominal geometry. The implementation is verified through spatial and temporal refinement, closed-form unit tests, nested Monte Carlo convergence with Wilson confidence intervals, and a hold-out-validated polynomial response surface. Numerical verification is clearly distinguished from experimental validation, and the simulated case is presented as a generic benchmark rather than an identified material model. The framework links deposition parameters and tolerance bands to damage-exceedance risk, supporting reliability-oriented screening of graded and multilayer coating systems.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a unified multiphysics-probabilistic framework for functionally graded abradable coatings in aircraft engines, integrating temperature-dependent viscoelastic softening, progressive damage, deposition-induced microstructural modulation, and geometric tolerances. Results show periodic property modulation increases end-of-cycle damage and stress concentration, produces right-skewed damage distributions with higher exceedance probabilities than monotonic gradients, and links deposition parameters and tolerance bands to damage-exceedance risk for reliability-oriented screening.
AI.motivation: Existing models treat durability-affecting effects in abradable coatings (viscoelastic softening, progressive damage, microstructural modulation, geometric tolerances) separately, but these effects interact in reality. A unified framework is needed to capture their coupling and assess reliability in blade-tip clearance control.
AI.method: A unified multiphysics-probabilistic framework solves a local through-thickness coating column driven by prescribed strain and temperature histories including thermal eigenstrain and coating-substrate expansion mismatch. It integrates viscoelasticity, damage progression, deposition-induced property modulation, and geometric tolerances, with verification via spatial/temporal refinement, closed-form unit tests, nested Monte Carlo convergence with Wilson confidence intervals, and hold-out-validated polynomial response surfaces.
