Propagating symmetric geometric tolerances yields strongly right-skewed damage distributions and higher classification-level exceedance probability for the modulated gradient, a result unattainable from deterministic analysis at nominal geometry.
AI.conclusion: The framework links deposition parameters and tolerance bands to damage-exceedance risk, supporting reliability-oriented screening of graded and multilayer coating systems. Numerical verification is distinguished from experimental validation, and the simulated case serves as a generic benchmark rather than an identified material model.

title: Hexagonal Stacking Maximizes Proton Configurational Entropy among Ice-I Polytypes
comment: 14 pages, 4 figures. Supplemental Material included as appendices S1-S7
summary: Ice I admits cubic, hexagonal, and mixed layer stackings, but rigorous entropy comparisons have focused on the two ideal endmembers. We represent every cyclic uniform-registry stacking by a word in a nonnegative transfer operator K and its transpose. For every such even-length word, applying the Schatten-Hölder inequality proves that alternating hexagonal stacking maximizes the ice-rule count at every common finite cross-section; the configuration constant is therefore maximal among all periodic uniform-registry polytypes. We obtain the lower endpoint by restricting Nagle's positive even-subgraph expansion to exactly enumerated disjoint blocks. Finner's degree-two hypergraph Hölder inequality and rational Collatz-Wielandt certificates for two-replica prism transfer operators give the upper endpoints. These constructions yield $1.503360 \le w \le 1.540196$, with $w(\mathrm{Ic}) \le 1.527699$.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the configurational entropy (configuration constant) of ice polytypes by representing cyclic uniform-registry stackings as words in a nonnegative transfer operator K. It proves that alternating hexagonal stacking maximizes ice-rule counts, and establishes rigorous bounds 1.503360 ≤ w ≤ 1.540196, with w(Ic) ≤ 1.527699, using Schatten-Hölder, Finner's hypergraph Hölder inequality, and Collatz-Wielandt certificates.
AI.motivation: To rigorously compare the configurational entropy of different ice polytypes (cubic, hexagonal, and mixed layer stackings), going beyond previous analyses that focused only on the two ideal endmembers.
AI.method: Represent every cyclic uniform-registry stacking by a word in a nonnegative transfer operator K and its transpose. Use the Schatten-Hölder inequality to prove alternating hexagonal stacking maximizes ice-rule counts at every finite cross-section. Restrict Nagle's positive even-subgraph expansion to enumerated disjoint blocks for the lower bound. Use Finner's degree-two hypergraph Hölder inequality and rational Collatz-Wielandt certificates for two-replica prism transfer operators for upper bounds.
AI.result: The configuration constant (exponential growth rate) is bounded by 1.503360 ≤ w ≤ 1.540196, with the specific cubic stacking w(Ic) bounded by w(Ic) ≤ 1.527699. Alternating hexagonal stacking is proven to maximize the ice-rule count among all periodic uniform-registry polytypes.
AI.conclusion: Alternating hexagonal stacking yields the maximal configuration constant among all periodic uniform-registry ice polytypes, and rigorous numerical bounds for the entropy constant are established, tightening previously known estimates.

title: Ferroelectric-controllable spin-orbit torque in two-dimensional multiferroic heterostructure
summary: Spin-orbit torque (SOT), which enables electrical control of magnetization, plays a crucial role in the development of next-generation spintronic devices. Realizing SOT in two-dimensional van der Waals systems, together with achieving efficient nonvolatile manipulation via ferroelectricity, would be highly beneficial for the implementation of tunable logic devices with enhanced storage density. In this work, based on first-principles calculation and using a multiferroic Fe$_{3}$GeTe$_{2}$/In$_{2}$Se$_{3}$ heterostructure as a representative example, we demonstrate that switching the ferroelectric polarization of the In$_{2}$Se$_{3}$ layer induces a pronounced modification in the magnetization-dependent distribution of torkance within the heterostructure. Specifically, when the magnetization is in the plane, where the torque is maximal, reversing the polarization of In$_{2}$Se$_{3}$ from upward to downward enhances the total torkance to more than 150% of its original value. This substantial variation primarily originates from the polarization-induced modulation of the $z$ component of the time-reversal-odd torkance, which is mainly associated with an approximately 233% change in the atomic-resolved torque contributed from the middle Fe layer in Fe$_{3}$GeTe$_{2}$ layer. Further analysis reveals that the electronic states near $Γ$ on the Fermi surface undergo significant reconstruction upon polarization switching, which is responsible for the observed variation in the time-reversal-odd torque. Our results not only provide new insights into the functional potential of van der Waals multiferroic heterostructures, but also offer a viable strategy for achieving electrically tunable SOT, paving the way for future programmable spintronic devices.

AI.tldr: Using first-principles calculations on a Fe3GeTe2/In2Se3 van der Waals multiferroic heterostructure, the authors demonstrate that switching the ferroelectric polarization of In2Se3 dramatically enhances spin-orbit torque (SOT)—specifically increasing total torkance by over 150% when the magnetization is in-plane. This effect stems from polarization-induced reconstruction of electronic states near the Γ point on the Fermi surface, primarily through modulation of the time-reversal-odd torkance, with the middle Fe layer contributing ~233% change in atomic-resolved torque.
AI.motivation: To achieve electrically tunable spin-orbit torque in two-dimensional van der Waals systems, combining SOT functionality with ferroelectric nonvolatile manipulation would enable programmable and reconfigurable spintronic devices with enhanced storage density.
AI.method: First-principles calculations based on density functional theory on a Fe3GeTe2/In2Se3 multiferroic heterostructure, analyzing torkance distributions for different ferroelectric polarization states and decomposing torque contributions atomically and by symmetry (time-reversal-odd components).
AI.result: Reversing In2Se3 polarization from upward to downward enhances the total torkance to more than 150% of its original value for in-plane magnetization. The change primarily arises from modulation of the z-component of the time-reversal-odd torkance, driven by ~233% change in atomic-resolved torque from the middle Fe layer. The underlying mechanism is significant reconstruction of electronic states near the Γ point on the Fermi surface upon polarization switching.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates a viable strategy for electrically tunable SOT via ferroelectric polarization switching in van der Waals multiferroic heterostructures, offering new insights into their functional potential and paving the way for future programmable spintronic devices.

title: Geometrical approach and topological electron density in the $p_x + ip_y$ superconductor
summary: We present an analysis on the geometrical and physical nature of the $p_x + ip_y$ superconductor on the square lattice, with an emphasis on the topological phase transition at half-filling. We develop a local topological marker from specific Dirac points within the Brillouin zone, which is introduced via the addition of two one-dimensional (1D) $\mathbb{Z}$ $(\mathbb{Z}_2$) invariants defined on the Bloch sphere. We relate this topological marker to the electron spectral function integrated on frequency through the local momentum-resolved electron density, which may be measured via Angle Resolved Photoemission Spectroscopy (ARPES), and show that it remains well-protected including temperature effects. Integrating on a small area around a specific point in momentum space associated to the measure uncertainty, this also reveals the Van Hove logarithmic profile of the density of states in the derivative of the local marker while preserving the topological information. Topological transitions correspond to a protected semi-metal. We analyse the real space representation of this topological marker from correlation functions. We present physical responses such as the topological superfluid density.

AI.tldr: An analysis of the geometrical and physical nature of the p_x + ip_y superconductor on the square lattice, focusing on the topological phase transition at half-filling via a local topological marker constructed from Dirac points and 1D Z/Z2 invariants on the Bloch sphere, linked to ARPES-measurable quantities.
AI.motivation: To understand the topological phase transition in the p_x + ip_y superconductor on the square lattice at half-filling, and to develop a physically measurable local topological marker that remains robust against thermal effects and measurement uncertainty.
AI.method: The authors construct a local topological marker from specific Dirac points in the Brillouin zone, built by adding two 1D Z (Z2) invariants defined on the Bloch sphere. They relate this marker to the frequency-integrated electron spectral function (local momentum-resolved electron density), measurable via ARPES. They analyze its real-space representation from correlation functions and study its behavior under temperature, momentum-integration uncertainty (revealing Van Hove logarithmic structure), and topological phase transitions (protected semi-metals). Physical responses such as the topological superfluid density are also computed.
AI.result: The local topological marker remains well-protected including temperature effects. Integrating over a small momentum area around specific points reveals the Van Hove logarithmic profile of the density of states in the derivative of the local marker while preserving topological information. Topological transitions correspond to a protected semi-metal, and the marker is analyzable in real space via correlation functions. Physical responses such as topological superfluid density are presented.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a robust, ARPES-accessible local topological marker for the p_x + ip_y superconductor that retains topological protection under thermal fluctuations and measurement uncertainty, with topological transitions occurring via a protected semi-metal, and offers physical responses like the topological superfluid density as observable signatures.

title: Superconductivity, pseudogap and marginal Fermi liquid in a relative-momentum-local theory
summary: Cuprate superconductors host \(d\)-wave superconductivity (SC), a pseudogap (PG) with Fermi arcs and a strange metal (SM) with incoherent excitations and temperature-linear resistivity. These regimes emerge from the same doped Mott system but are usually described separately. Here a relative-momentum-local (RML) theory is constructed, with the exact spin-singlet Cooper representation of antiferromagnetic superexchange in the \(t\)-\(J\) model serving as a common thread. Pair correlations organize the low-energy behaviour of this Cooper channel into phase-coherent static SC, phase-incoherent quasi-static PG and phase-incoherent dynamic SM. A static RML prescription yields an exactly solvable PG Hamiltonian with nodal electron poles, antinodal gaps, resolution-broadened Fermi arcs and gapless charge-\(2e\) Cooper surfaces. A Cooper-surface Lifshitz transition generates logarithmic enhancements in the specific-heat coefficient and charge response without a spin singularity. The particle-particle continuum at finite centre-of-mass momentum produces Ohmic damping, while a dynamic RML prescription yields a one-loop self-energy with marginal-Fermi-liquid scaling. Spectral-weight transfer in the physical pair spectrum diagnoses the PG--SM crossover, whereas nonzero phase stiffness and global phase coherence identify SC. The RML theory relates single-particle, pair-sensitive and thermodynamic probes to three infrared organizations of one Cooper channel. A decisive experimental signature would be zero-energy Cooper-surface ridges in two-electron angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (2e-ARPES).

AI.tldr: A relative-momentum-local (RML) theory based on the spin-singlet Cooper representation of superexchange in the t-J model unifies the three regimes of cuprate superconductors—d-wave SC, pseudogap with Fermi arcs, and strange metal—through three infrared organizations of the same Cooper channel.
AI.motivation: The three regimes of cuprates (d-wave SC, pseudogap with Fermi arcs, strange metal) emerge from the same doped Mott system but are typically described by separate frameworks; a unified theoretical description is missing.
AI.method: Constructs a relative-momentum-local (RML) theory using the exact spin-singlet Cooper representation of antiferromagnetic superexchange in the t-J model. Static RML yields an exactly solvable PG Hamiltonian (nodal poles, antinodal gaps, Fermi arcs, gapless charge-2e Cooper surfaces), a Cooper-surface Lifshitz transition generates logarithmic enhancements, and a dynamic RML prescription gives a one-loop self-energy with marginal-Fermi-liquid scaling.
AI.result: The theory organizes pair correlations into phase-coherent static SC, phase-incoherent quasi-static PG, and phase-incoherent dynamic SM. It produces Ohmic damping from the particle-particle continuum, marginal-Fermi-liquid self-energy, and spectral-weight transfer diagnosing the PG-SM crossover. Predicted experimental signature is zero-energy Cooper-surface ridges in 2e-ARPES.
AI.conclusion: The RML theory relates single-particle, pair-sensitive, and thermodynamic probes to three infrared organizations of one Cooper channel, providing a unified description of cuprate phenomenology with a testable experimental prediction.

title: Self-consistent double-hybrid density functional theory via one-body second-order Møller-Plesset perturbation theory and projection-based embedding
summary: We present the development of self-consistent one-body double-hybrid (OBDH) density functional theory (DFT). In this approach, the one-body second-order Møller-Plesset (OBMP2) perturbation potential is embedded directly in the generalized Kohn-Sham framework, allowing orbitals to be optimized in the presence of MP2-level dynamic correlation. Unlike existing orbital-optimized double hybrids, OBDH requires neither the optimized effective potential nor perturbative orbital relaxation corrections. The energy functional combines a semilocal exchange-correlation functional, exact exchange, and OBMP2 correlation, from which the effective Hamiltonian and self-consistent-field equations are systematically derived. To reduce computational cost, projector-based embedding with concentric localization truncation is applied to the OBMP2 component, termed sub-OBDH. OBDH and sub-OBDH are benchmarked on diatomic potential energy curves, self-interaction errors, dihedral torsions of organic molecules, and interaction energies in non-covalent charged systems. Across all systems, OBDH consistently outperforms standard DFT, demonstrating its potential for accurate and practical electronic structure calculations.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces one-body double-hybrid (OBDH) DFT, which embeds an MP2-level perturbation potential directly into the generalized Kohn-Sham framework, allowing self-consistent orbital optimization without optimized effective potentials or perturbative corrections. A computationally cheaper variant (sub-OBDH) uses projector-based embedding with concentric localization. Benchmarks show OBDH outperforms standard DFT across diatomic curves, self-interaction errors, torsional barriers, and non-covalent interactions.
AI.motivation: Existing orbital-optimized double-hybrid functionals require either optimized effective potentials or perturbative orbital relaxation corrections, which are computationally and methodologically expensive. The goal is to develop a self-consistent double-hybrid approach that naturally optimizes orbitals in the presence of MP2-type correlation within a generalized Kohn-Sham framework, without these auxiliary steps.
AI.method: The OBMP2 perturbation potential is embedded directly in the generalized Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian. The energy functional combines a semilocal exchange-correlation functional, exact exchange, and OBMP2 correlation; the effective Hamiltonian and SCF equations are derived systematically from this functional. To reduce cost, projector-based embedding with concentric localization truncation is applied to the OBMP2 component (sub-OBDH).
AI.result: OBDH and sub-OBDH were benchmarked on diatomic potential energy curves, self-interaction errors, dihedral torsions of organic molecules, and interaction energies in non-covalent charged systems. Across all test systems, OBDH consistently outperforms standard DFT.
AI.conclusion: OBDH provides a self-consistent, accurate, and practical alternative to standard DFT for electronic structure calculations, with sub-OBDH offering a lower-cost route while retaining the benefits of the approach.

title: Predicting large-supercell defect formation energies from machine-learning charge density models trained on small supercells
summary: First-principles defect calculations are often limited by the cost of the large supercells required to suppress image interactions. Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) provide another alternative, but training defect MLIPs typically requires thousands of structures and weeks of data generation. Since charge density is the key to density-functional-theory (DFT), we propose a machine-learning charge density (MLCD) route for predicting defect formation energies with higher data efficiency. We optimize the training set by integrating small supercells of varying sizes for better extrapolation, allocating their proportions based on spatial charge-density analysis. With only 96 supercells containing 16--96 atoms as the dataset, MLCD accurately predicts the formation energies of four intrinsic defects in 360-atom supercells, with defect-wise mean absolute error below 0.05 eV. In contrast, MLIPs trained on the same dataset can err by more than 1 eV. These results show that charge-density learning enables more robust cross-size transfer than direct energy-force fitting and that mixed-size data design can substantially reduce the cost of defect prediction.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a machine-learning charge density (MLCD) approach for predicting defect formation energies, achieving high accuracy with only 96 small supercells (16–96 atoms) by training on charge density rather than direct energy-force fitting. It accurately predicts four intrinsic defects in 360-atom supercells with defect-wise mean absolute error below 0.05 eV, far outperforming MLIPs trained on the same data (>1 eV error).
AI.motivation: Defect calculations in DFT are limited by the computational cost of large supercells needed to suppress image interactions. While MLIPs offer an alternative, they require thousands of training structures and weeks of data generation. The authors aim to develop a more data-efficient approach by leveraging charge density—the fundamental quantity in DFT—to enable robust cross-size transfer in defect prediction.
AI.method: The authors propose a machine-learning charge density (MLCD) framework. They optimize the training set by integrating small supercells of varying sizes for improved extrapolation, and allocate data proportions based on spatial charge-density analysis. The training set consists of only 96 supercells ranging from 16 to 96 atoms.
AI.result: MLCD accurately predicts formation energies of four intrinsic defects in 360-atom supercells, achieving defect-wise mean absolute error below 0.05 eV. In contrast, MLIPs trained on the same dataset exhibit errors exceeding 1 eV, demonstrating the superiority of charge-density learning for cross-size transfer.
AI.conclusion: Charge-density learning enables more robust cross-size transfer than direct energy-force fitting, and mixed-size data design can substantially reduce the cost of defect prediction while maintaining high accuracy.

title: Fuzzy Spectroscopy of Bound States in Massive Quantum Field Theories
summary: Mesons and glueballs are paradigmatic bound states of confining quantum field theories (QFTs), but their nonperturbative spectroscopy in the continuum remains challenging beyond one spatial dimension. Here we perform such spectroscopy for the Ising QFT using a recently developed regularization based on noncommutative ``fuzzy'' geometry. On a thin fuzzy torus, we reproduce the universal low-lying $\mathbb E_8$ meson masses of the magnetically perturbed $(1{+}1)\mathrm{D}$ Ising QFT. By increasing the torus aspect ratio, we continuously track the second-lightest $\mathbb E_8$ meson as the system effectively crosses over from 1D to 2D. On the 2D fuzzy torus and sphere, we find a subthreshold scalar level and above-threshold response features consistent with previous estimates of glueball masses. The same excitations are revealed away from equilibrium using quench dynamics. Our results establish fuzzy geometries as nonperturbative spectroscopic probes of massive QFTs, including their bound-state evolution through dimensional crossover.

AI.tldr: The paper uses noncommutative "fuzzy" geometry regularization to perform nonperturbative bound-state spectroscopy of the Ising quantum field theory (QFT). On thin fuzzy tori, it reproduces the universal E8 meson masses of the 1+1D magnetically perturbed Ising QFT, tracks the second-lightest E8 meson through a dimensional crossover from 1D to 2D, and finds subthreshold scalar levels and above-threshold response features consistent with glueball mass estimates on 2D fuzzy tori and spheres. The same excitations are observed in quench dynamics away from equilibrium.
AI.motivation: Nonperturbative spectroscopy of mesons and glueballs in confining quantum field theories remains challenging beyond one spatial dimension in the continuum. The authors aim to overcome this by employing fuzzy geometry regularization, which provides a finite-dimensional Hilbert space approximation to continuous manifolds, enabling nonperturbative bound-state computations in higher-dimensional QFTs.
AI.method: The authors use a regularization scheme based on noncommutative (fuzzy) geometry to discretize spacetime. They implement the Ising QFT on a thin fuzzy torus to reproduce 1+1D universal E8 meson masses, then increase the torus aspect ratio to interpolate between 1D and 2D physics. They further place the theory on 2D fuzzy tori and spheres to compute mass spectra, and employ quench dynamics to extract the same excitations nonperturbatively.
AI.result: The low-lying E8 meson masses are accurately reproduced on the thin fuzzy torus. The second-lightest E8 meson is continuously tracked as the system crosses from effectively 1D to 2D. On 2D fuzzy surfaces, a subthreshold scalar state and above-threshold response features are observed that agree with previous glueball mass estimates. Quench dynamics reveals the same spectral excitations.
AI.conclusion: Fuzzy geometries are validated as effective nonperturbative spectroscopic probes for massive QFTs, enabling bound-state evolution to be tracked through dimensional crossover. This establishes a new computational framework for glueball and meson spectroscopy in confining field theories beyond one spatial dimension.

title: Dynamical quantum phase transitions in a hybrid quantum dot system with superconducting and ferromagnetic leads
summary: We theoretically explore the non-equilibrium dynamics of a single quantum dot system coupled to both ferromagnetic and superconducting electrodes. To investigate its time evolution, we utilize the time-dependent numerical renormalization group technique, which captures the system's response to abrupt parameter changes in a fully non-perturbative manner. Our analysis focuses on dynamics following a sudden modification in the couplings to the leads or a shift of the orbital level. In particular, we calculate the time evolution of the induced local superconducting pairing correlations and magnetization. In this context, the relevant energy spectra are examined. Moreover, we study the behavior of the Loschmidt echo and the return function to shed light on the signatures of dynamical quantum phase transitions. The determined dependencies reveal non-trivial competition between relevant correlations, involving superconducting pairing and ferromagnetic-contacted induced exchange field, and deepen our understanding of nanoscale hybrid systems' dynamical behavior.

AI.tldr: This paper theoretically investigates the non-equilibrium dynamics of a quantum dot coupled to ferromagnetic and superconducting electrodes using time-dependent numerical renormalization group (TD-NRG) techniques. It examines the time evolution of local superconducting pairing correlations and magnetization following sudden parameter changes, and analyzes Loschmidt echo and return functions to identify dynamical quantum phase transitions.
AI.motivation: To understand the non-equilibrium dynamical behavior of nanoscale hybrid systems, specifically the competition between superconducting correlations and ferromagnetic-induced exchange fields in a quantum dot coupled to ferromagnetic and superconducting leads.
AI.method: The authors employ the time-dependent numerical renormalization group (TD-NRG) technique, a fully non-perturbative method, to simulate the system's response to abrupt changes in lead couplings or orbital level shifts. They compute the time evolution of local superconducting pairing correlations, magnetization, Loschmidt echo, and return function.
AI.result: The calculated time-dependent quantities reveal non-trivial competition between superconducting pairing correlations and the ferromagnetic-contact-induced exchange field, with signatures of dynamical quantum phase transitions identified via the Loschmidt echo and return function analyses.
AI.conclusion: The work deepens understanding of the dynamical behavior of nanoscale hybrid systems involving quantum dots coupled to ferromagnetic and superconducting electrodes, highlighting the intricate interplay between competing correlations in the non-equilibrium regime.

title: Spin Polarization of a Two-Dimensional Electron Liquid
summary: We show experimentally that the longitudinal resistance of a strongly correlated two-dimensional electron system provides a direct quantitative measure of its spin polarization. Using electrically detected electron spin resonance as an independent calibration of the spin state, we establish a parameter-free relation between magnetotransport and spin polarization, enabling spin polarization to be reconstructed from transport measurements alone. The extracted spin polarization quantitatively explains the magnetic field and temperature dependence of the electrically detected spin-resonance signal and allows the magnetic state of the electron liquid to be mapped over a broad range of carrier densities and magnetic fields.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that the longitudinal resistance of a strongly correlated 2D electron system can provide a direct, quantitative measure of its spin polarization. Using electrically detected electron spin resonance as an independent calibration, the authors establish a parameter-free relation between magnetotransport and spin polarization, enabling transport-based spin polarization reconstruction that quantitatively explains ESR signals and allows mapping of the magnetic state across densities and fields.
AI.motivation: To find a direct, quantitative method for measuring spin polarization in strongly correlated two-dimensional electron systems, which is a key parameter governing their magnetic and transport properties.
AI.method: The authors combine magnetotransport measurements (longitudinal resistance) with electrically detected electron spin resonance (ESR) as an independent calibration of the spin state. They establish a parameter-free relationship connecting longitudinal resistance to spin polarization, using the ESR signal to validate and calibrate the correspondence.
AI.result: The extracted spin polarization quantitatively reproduces the magnetic field and temperature dependence of the electrically detected spin-resonance signal, and enables mapping of the electron liquid's magnetic state over a broad range of carrier densities and magnetic fields.
AI.conclusion: Longitudinal resistance alone can serve as a direct quantitative probe of spin polarization in strongly correlated 2D electron systems, validated by electrically detected ESR, offering a simplified yet accurate pathway to reconstruct spin polarization and map magnetic phases from transport measurements.

title: Layer-Locked Chiral Topological Superconductivity
summary: We uncover a universal mechanism for realizing layer-locked topological phases. Guided by it, we investigate the realization of layer-locked chiral topological superconductivity-the superconducting analogue of the quantum anomalous layer Hall effect-in a nonsymmorphic bilayer antiferromagnetic system with s-wave pairing. We identify three distinct gate-tunable topological phases and establish a direct correspondence between the nearly quantized layer-resolved Chern numbers and the layer-locking behavior of chiral Majorana edge states, vortex-core Majorana zero modes, and nearly quantized thermal Hall responses.

AI.tldr: The paper uncovers a universal mechanism for realizing layer-locked topological phases and applies it to demonstrate layer-locked chiral topological superconductivity in a nonsymmorphic bilayer antiferromagnetic system with s-wave pairing, revealing three gate-tunable topological phases with layer-resolved Chern numbers linked to chiral Majorana edge states, vortex-core Majorana zero modes, and nearly quantized thermal Hall responses.
AI.motivation: To establish a universal mechanism for realizing layer-locked topological phases and to explore whether these phases can be extended to topological superconductivity, specifically the superconducting analogue of the quantum anomalous layer Hall effect.
AI.method: The authors identify a universal mechanism for layer-locked topological phases and apply it to a nonsymmorphic bilayer antiferromagnetic system with s-wave pairing. They compute layer-resolved Chern numbers and analyze the resulting edge states, Majorana zero modes, and thermal Hall responses as a function of gate voltage.
AI.result: Three distinct gate-tunable topological phases are identified, with a direct correspondence established between nearly quantized layer-resolved Chern numbers and the layer-locking behavior of chiral Majorana edge states, vortex-core Majorana zero modes, and nearly quantized thermal Hall responses.
AI.conclusion: Layer-locked chiral topological superconductivity can be realized as the superconducting analogue of the quantum anomalous layer Hall effect, with gate voltage serving as a tuning knob to switch among distinct topological phases whose layer-resolved topological invariants directly govern observable transport and edge-state phenomena.

title: Real-Time Approach to the Dynamical Bethe-Salpeter Equation for Finite Systems
summary: We present a real-time linear-response approach to solving the dynamical Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE). The polarization part of the screened interaction is obtained from time-dependent Hartree propagation of the one-particle density matrix within an orbital basis-set representation. The frequency convolution defining the dynamical kernel is evaluated as a product in time, avoiding numerical integration and storage of the full screened Coulomb operator. The resulting nonlinear eigenvalue problem is then solved directly, going beyond the static screening approximation with full-frequency dependence in the screened interaction. While the deterministic scaling remains $\mathcal{O}(N^6)$, the time propagation formulation is readily compatible with grid-based stochastic sampling methods, which will open the possibility for dynamical BSE calculations of very large systems.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a real-time linear-response approach to solving the dynamical Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE), where the screened interaction is obtained from time-dependent Hartree propagation of the density matrix, and the frequency convolution is evaluated as a product in time. This avoids numerical integration and storage of the full screened Coulomb operator, going beyond static screening with full-frequency dependence. Although deterministic scaling remains O(N^6), the time-propagation formulation is compatible with grid-based stochastic sampling, enabling dynamical BSE for very large systems.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to overcome the limitations of the static screening approximation in Bethe-Salpeter equation calculations by developing an approach that captures full-frequency dependence in the screened interaction, while also providing a formulation amenable to stochastic methods for large-scale systems.
AI.method: The method uses a real-time linear-response formalism for the dynamical BSE. The polarization part of the screened interaction is computed via time-dependent Hartree propagation of the one-particle density matrix in an orbital basis-set representation. The frequency convolution of the dynamical kernel is evaluated as a product in the time domain, eliminating the need for numerical frequency integration and storage of the full screened Coulomb operator. The resulting nonlinear eigenvalue problem is solved directly.
AI.result: The approach achieves full-frequency dependence in the screened interaction, going beyond the static screening approximation, while maintaining O(N^6) deterministic scaling. Crucially, the real-time formulation is compatible with grid-based stochastic sampling methods, opening the path to dynamical BSE calculations for very large systems.
AI.conclusion: The real-time formulation provides a practical and scalable route to dynamical BSE calculations, solving the nonlinear eigenvalue problem directly and avoiding costly frequency-domain integrations, with the added potential for stochastic acceleration to treat very large systems.

title: Local coordination and migration-network topology shape Li-ion transport and delithiation in the low-energy $\varepsilon$-LiMnO$_2$ polymorph
summary: In rocksalt-derived oxide cathodes, the local Li-migration environment around an O4 tetrahedral intermediate is commonly classified by the number of face-sharing transition-metal (TM) neighbors. In LiMnO2, the TM species is Mn, and 0-TM denotes the absence of face-sharing Mn neighbors. However, migration and delithiation may also depend on higher-shell coordination and tetrahedral connectivity. Using the recently reported low-energy epsilon-LiMnO2 polymorph as a model, we examine these factors through bond-valence site-energy and bond-valence pathway analyses combined with first-principles calculations. The resulting migration maps and tetrahedral statistics reveal distinct topologies and dimensionalities across four LiMnO2 polymorphs. Although the epsilon phase and the lithiated-spinel phase Li2Mn2O4 (hereafter spinel) have identical tetrahedral-type fractions, their 0-TM motifs form quasi-one-dimensional chains and a three-dimensional network, respectively. Climbing-image nudged elastic band calculations further distinguish the two structures: epsilon-phase barriers are 0.35-0.36 eV, compared with 0.41-0.53 eV in spinel, a difference that may be associated with distinct next-nearest corner-sharing shells. Ab initio molecular dynamics yields an apparent activation energy of 0.32 eV, while direction-resolved mean-squared displacements show preferential Li migration along c, supporting low-barrier quasi-one-dimensional diffusion. Delithiation calculations show that differences in 0-TM connectivity and Li-Li separation between the epsilon phase and spinel are associated with Li-site evolution and calculated voltage steps, suggesting that motif connectivity may influence voltage response. These results link the local environments and spatial connectivity of 0-TM motifs to Li migration and delithiation, providing insights into the design of metastable cathode structures.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates Li migration and delithiation in rocksalt-derived oxide cathodes (specifically LiMnO2 polymorphs), showing that beyond local 0-TM (no face-sharing Mn neighbors) classification, the higher-shell coordination and spatial connectivity of tetrahedral motifs critically determine migration pathways, dimensionality, and voltage response. The low-energy epsilon-LiMnO2 polymorph exhibits quasi-one-dimensional 0-TM chains with low barriers (0.35-0.36 eV), whereas lithiated-spinel Li2Mn2O4 has a 3D 0-TM network with higher barriers (0.41-0.53 eV), despite identical tetrahedral-type fractions.
AI.motivation: Conventional classification of Li-migration environments in rocksalt-derived oxide cathodes relies solely on the local 0-TM descriptor (number of face-sharing transition-metal neighbors around an O4 tetrahedral intermediate). However, this ignores higher-shell coordination and tetrahedral connectivity, which may also govern migration and delithiation. The study aims to systematically examine these overlooked factors using the recently reported low-energy epsilon-LiMnO2 polymorph as a model system.
AI.method: The authors employ a multi-scale computational approach: (1) bond-valence site-energy and bond-valence pathway analyses to construct migration maps and tetrahedral statistics; (2) first-principles calculations; (3) climbing-image nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) calculations to quantify migration barriers; (4) ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) to extract apparent activation energies and direction-resolved mean-squared displacements; and (5) delithiation calculations to track Li-site evolution and voltage steps across the epsilon phase and lithiated-spinel phase.
AI.result: Four LiMnO2 polymorphs exhibit distinct 0-TM motif topologies and dimensions. Despite identical tetrahedral-type fractions, epsilon-LiMnO2 and spinel Li2Mn2O4 differ fundamentally: the epsilon phase has quasi-one-dimensional 0-TM chains with CI-NEB barriers of 0.35-0.36 eV and an AIMD apparent activation energy of 0.32 eV with preferential migration along c, while the spinel phase forms a 3D 0-TM network with higher barriers (0.41-0.53 eV). The distinct next-nearest corner-sharing shells account for this barrier difference. Delithiation calculations reveal that 0-TM connectivity and Li-Li separation differences correlate with Li-site evolution and calculated voltage steps.
AI.conclusion: The spatial connectivity of 0-TM motifs — not just their local density — plays a decisive role in determining Li migration barriers, diffusion dimensionality, and voltage response in rocksalt-derived cathodes. This establishes motif connectivity as a key design principle for metastable cathode structures, suggesting that engineering 0-TM chain connectivity could enable low-barrier quasi-1D Li diffusion with advantageous electrochemical properties.

title: Lee-Yang Theory Guided Force Field Refinement Based on Phase Diagrams
summary: We propose a general framework for automatic force field refinement guided by phase diagrams, grounded in Lee-Yang phase transition theory. The central idea is to directly use the partition function modulus as a phase-diagram-guided optimization target. Evaluating the modulus at points close to the real axis, where the Lee-Yang zeros are mostly associated with the phase transition, is more physically meaningful and avoids the numerical difficulty of explicitly solving for the zeros. This approach requires no system-specific order parameters or response properties for characterizing phase transition points, making it universal across various discontinuous phase transitions and material systems. We validate the method on refining parameters of a Lennard-Jones potential covering both gas-liquid and solid-liquid transitions, and a Cu embedded-atom method potential based on experimental melting curves. The refined force fields reproduce the target phase diagrams with significant improvement across all systems. For Cu, the refinement simultaneously improves predictions of enthalpy and heat capacity, which are observables beyond the optimization target. These results establish Lee-Yang theory as a practical tool for contemporary force field development.

AI.tldr: A general framework for automatic force field refinement is proposed, using the partition function modulus near the real axis (rooted in Lee-Yang phase transition theory) as a phase-diagram-guided optimization target. It requires no system-specific order parameters or response properties, and is validated on Lennard-Jones potentials (gas-liquid and solid-liquid transitions) and a Cu embedded-atom method potential, significantly improving phase diagram reproduction and even non-target observables like enthalpy and heat capacity.
AI.motivation: Force field accuracy in reproducing phase diagrams is critical for materials simulation, but existing refinement approaches often require system-specific order parameters or response properties to locate phase transition points, limiting their generality and applicability across different material systems and transition types.
AI.method: The method uses the partition function modulus as the optimization target, evaluated at points close to the real axis where Lee-Yang zeros associated with phase transitions reside. This avoids explicit zero-solving numerical difficulties and eliminates the need for system-specific order parameters or response functions, making the framework universal across discontinuous phase transitions.
AI.result: The refined Lennard-Jones and Cu EAM potentials reproduce target phase diagrams with significant improvement. For Cu, refinement also simultaneously improves predictions of enthalpy and heat capacity—observables beyond the optimization target—demonstrating robust generalization.
AI.conclusion: Lee-Yang phase transition theory is established as a practical and universal tool for contemporary force field development, enabling automatic phase-diagram-guided refinement across diverse material systems and phase transition types.

title: Classical fractons with cosmological fixed points
summary: Classical fractons are Hamiltonian systems that can develop attractors after projection onto configuration or shape variables, although the full phase space admits none. We study a scale-invariant, dipole-conserving two-parameter family of fracton Hamiltonians $H_{α,β}$. By separating coordinates into scale and shape, we obtain autonomous shape dynamics that admit fixed points which leave a purely scale evolution of the form $R(t)\propto |t|^{α/(α-β)}$. The shape fixed points, which determine the distribution of the expanding particles, are central configurations of power-law Riesz potentials. The distinguished model $(α,β)=(-2,1)$ is unique: its scale evolution takes the Einstein-de Sitter form $R(t)\propto |t|^{2/3}$, its fixed-point equation is the equal-mass Newtonian central-configuration, its large-$N$ distribution is a homogeneous ball, and its homothetic trajectories admit a zero-energy Newtonian gravitational dual. The fixed points are locally stable, and simulations at moderate $N$ approach them from random initial data. Large $N$ simulations reveal a richer class of fixed-points: bound clusters of approximately fixed physical size retain internal motion, while their centers approach unequal-mass Newtonian central configurations and preserve large-scale homogeneity. A scale-separation conjecture yields an effective unequal-mass fracton dynamics for the centers and a corresponding zero-energy Newtonian gravitational dual. Trajectories generically exhibit a bidirectional arrow of time: scale and shape complexity grow away from a Janus point, while Boltzmann entropy grows logarithmically. Together, these features reproduce the salient structure of a flat matter-dominated cosmology. In the distinguished fracton model, all these cosmological analogues emerge as attractor properties, making it a toy model for cosmological dynamics without fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: This paper studies a class of dipole-conserving fracton Hamiltonians with scale-invariant two-parameter structure, showing that shape dynamics admit fixed points corresponding to central configurations of power-law Riesz potentials. The distinguished (α,β)=(-2,1) model uniquely reproduces Einstein-de Sitter cosmological expansion, Newtonian gravitational duality, and a bidirectional arrow of time, serving as an attractor-based toy model for flat matter-dominated cosmology without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: To understand how fracton systems, which have no attractors in full phase space, can develop attractors when projected onto shape/configuration variables, and to explore whether such systems can naturally reproduce cosmological-like dynamics (expansion, arrow of time, gravitational duals) as attractor properties rather than fine-tuned outcomes.
AI.method: The authors separate coordinates into scale and shape variables for a two-parameter family of fracton Hamiltonians H_{α,β}, obtaining autonomous shape dynamics. They identify fixed points as central configurations of power-law Riesz potentials, analyze their stability, perform moderate and large-N simulations from random initial data, and propose a scale-separation conjecture yielding effective unequal-mass fracton dynamics for bound cluster centers with a zero-energy Newtonian gravitational dual.
AI.result: The shape fixed points are locally stable and are approached from random initial data at moderate N. The distinguished model (α,β)=(-2,1) uniquely gives Einstein-de Sitter scale evolution R(t)∝|t|^{2/3}, equal-mass Newtonian central-configuration fixed points, homogeneous-ball large-N distribution, and zero-energy Newtonian gravitational dual. Large-N simulations reveal bound clusters whose centers approach unequal-mass Newtonian central configurations. Trajectories exhibit a bidirectional arrow of time with logarithmic Boltzmann entropy growth. The fixed points are locally stable and simulations converge to them.
AI.conclusion: The distinguished fracton model reproduces the salient structure of flat matter-dominated cosmology—expansion, arrow of time, gravitational duality—as generic attractor properties, making it a toy model for cosmological dynamics without fine-tuning.

title: Probing intermittent polariton vortex dynamics with two-point correlations
summary: Superconducting single-photon detectors with time resolution of 80 ps have been used to study the spatiotemporal dynamics of a trapped bosonic condensate of exciton-polaritons. Both second- and first-order correlation functions are found to exhibit pronounced oscillations in time governed by the dynamics of the polariton condensate in the trap. We have identified the intermittent regime of stochastic transitions between stationary and limit-cycle regimes near the Andronov-Hopf bifurcation manifested in asymmetric distortions of the correlation function. This rich interplay of deterministic and stochastic condensate dynamics is explained theoretically as a manifestation of mutually compensating self-repulsion and reservoir-mediated attraction.

AI.tldr: Using superconducting single-photon detectors with 80 ps time resolution, the study examines spatiotemporal dynamics of trapped exciton-polariton condensates, revealing oscillation in both second- and first-order correlation functions and identifying an intermittent regime of stochastic transitions near the Andronov-Hopf bifurcation, explained by mutually compensating self-repulsion and reservoir-mediated attraction.
AI.motivation: To understand the spatiotemporal dynamics of trapped bosonic condensates of exciton-polaritons, particularly the interplay between deterministic and stochastic dynamics near a bifurcation point, using high-time-resolution single-photon detection to capture correlation function oscillations.
AI.method: Superconducting single-photon detectors with 80 ps time resolution were used to measure both second- and first-order correlation functions of a trapped exciton-polariton condensate, probing its temporal dynamics.
AI.result: Both correlation functions exhibit pronounced time oscillations governed by condensate dynamics in the trap. An intermittent regime of stochastic transitions between stationary and limit-cycle regimes near the Andronov-Hopf bifurcation was identified, manifested as asymmetric distortions of the correlation function.
AI.conclusion: The observed deterministic-stochastic interplay is explained theoretically as arising from mutually compensating self-repulsion and reservoir-mediated attraction in the polariton condensate.

title: Uniaxial stress effects on magnetic and electric properties of the ground state in a centrosymmetric magnetic skyrmion host Gd$_2$PdSi$_3$
summary: We investigate effects of uniaxial stress to magnetic orders and electrical resistivity of the centrosymmetric magnetic skyrmion compound Gd$_2$PdSi$_3$, which has a hexagonal crystal structure composed of triangular lattice layers of magnetic Gd$^{3+}$ ions. This compound is known to exhibit the triple-$q$ magnetic skyrmion lattice phase with a giant topological Hall effect in the first field induced phase [T. Kurumaji $\textit{et al}$. Science $\textbf{365}$, 914-918 (2019)]. In contrast to the established picture of the field-induced phase, the ground state of this system still remains to be studied. Although previous studies reported the existence of the incommensurate magnetic modulations described by a magnetic modulation wave vector ${\bf q}=(q,0,0)$ where $q\sim 0.14$ and its equivalents, it is still unclear whether the magnetic structure is a single-$q$ structure or a multiple-$q$ structure. In the present study, we performed magnetization, resistivity and neutron diffraction measurements with a compressive uniaxial stress applied perpendicular to the $c$ axis. The observed data revealed that the system did not exhibit anisotropic magnetic and electric properties expected from a single-$q$ magnetic order, suggesting that the magnetic ground state of this system is a multi-$q$ magnetic order.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the magnetic ground state of the centrosymmetric skyrmion compound Gd₂PdSi₃ by applying compressive uniaxial stress perpendicular to the c-axis and measuring magnetization, resistivity, and neutron diffraction. The absence of anisotropic responses expected from a single-q magnetic order suggests the ground state is a multi-q magnetic order.
AI.motivation: While the field-induced triple-q skyrmion lattice phase of Gd₂PdSi₃ is well established, the nature of its zero-field magnetic ground state remains unresolved—specifically whether it is a single-q or multiple-q incommensurate magnetic structure.
AI.method: Magnetization, electrical resistivity, and neutron diffraction measurements were performed under compressive uniaxial stress applied perpendicular to the crystallographic c-axis, exploiting the expected anisotropic responses to discriminate between single-q and multi-q magnetic ordering.
AI.result: No anisotropic magnetic or electrical properties consistent with a single-q magnetic order were observed under uniaxial stress. The absence of such anisotropy indicates the ground state is a multi-q magnetic order.
AI.conclusion: The magnetic ground state of Gd₂PdSi₃ is a multi-q magnetic structure rather than a single-q one, contrasting with the field-induced triple-q skyrmion phase while revealing richer zero-field magnetic complexity in this system.

title: Nonadiabatic Forward-Flux Sampling of Rare Molecular Gas-Phase Ammonia Photodissociation
summary: Simulating rare events in photochemistry by brute-force surface hopping is computationally prohibitive: most propagated trajectories either remain nonreactive or follow dominant relaxation channels, while the reaction of interest may occur with very low probability. Path sampling methods have long addressed this problem for ground-state dynamics, but their extension to nonadiabatic processes has so far been limited to low-dimensional analytical models. Here, we demonstrate that our recently developed nonadiabatic forward-flux sampling (NAFFS) method can be applied to efficiently simulate rare-events in full-dimensional molecular systems. As a representative benchmark, we investigate the rare molecular photodissociation channel of gas-phase ammonia, NH$_3$ + h$ν\rightarrow$ NH + H$_2$. NAFFS samples reactive trajectories with the correct statistical weight, reproduces the reaction rate constant obtained in previous brute-force dynamical studies, provides direct access to mechanistic information through an averaged committor analysis, and reduces the simulation time per transition trajectory by up to three orders of magnitude. These results establish NAFFS as an efficient and statistically rigorous framework for investigating rare nonadiabatic processes in realistic molecular systems.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that the nonadiabatic forward-flux sampling (NAFFS) method can efficiently simulate rare photochemical events in full-dimensional molecular systems, using the photodissociation of gas-phase ammonia (NH3 → NH + H2) as a benchmark. NAFFS reproduces the correct reaction rate constant, provides mechanistic insights via committor analysis, and reduces simulation time per transition trajectory by up to three orders of magnitude compared to brute-force surface hopping.
AI.motivation: Brute-force surface hopping is computationally prohibitive for rare photochemical events because most trajectories are nonreactive or follow dominant relaxation channels. While path sampling methods have addressed rare events in ground-state dynamics, their extension to nonadiabatic processes was previously limited to low-dimensional analytical models.
AI.method: The authors apply their recently developed nonadiabatic forward-flux sampling (NAFFS) method to full-dimensional molecular systems. NAFFS samples reactive trajectories with correct statistical weighting and includes an averaged committor analysis for mechanistic information. The method is benchmarked on the rare molecular photodissociation channel of ammonia.
AI.result: NAFFS successfully reproduces the reaction rate constant obtained from previous brute-force dynamical studies, provides direct mechanistic information through committor analysis, and achieves up to three orders of magnitude reduction in simulation time per transition trajectory.
AI.conclusion: NAFFS is established as an efficient and statistically rigorous framework for investigating rare nonadiabatic processes in realistic molecular systems, extending rare-event sampling methodologies to photochemistry.

title: Multimodal deep learning framework to predict strain localization of Mg/LPSO two-phase alloys
summary: This study proposes a method for predicting three-dimensional (3D) local strain distribution under compressive deformation of as-cast Mg/LPSO two-phase alloys from 3D microstructure images. The 3D local strain distribution was obtained by applying the digital volume correlation method to X-ray CT images before and after compression tests. Three microstructure descriptors were extracted from the 3D microstructure images around each strain measurement point: volume fractions of the phases, persistent diagrams that can express the connectivity of the phases, and two-phase spatial correlation that can express the spatial distribution of the phases. A deep learning model was then constructed to predict local strain from the three microstructure descriptors. Since two types of descriptors were used in this study, numerical data and image data, multimodal deep learning was employed to make predictions. Thus, the use of multiple microstructure descriptors enabled predictions to be made with higher accuracy than when predictions were made from a single descriptor. Feature importance of the descriptors was assessed through correlation analysis and occlusion sensitivity analysis. The results revealed that high strain tended to occur in the region where the hard phase, LPSO phase, had a large elongated phase oriented at a 45° direction to the loading direction. This result is consistent with other previous studies and indicates that the proposed method is effective in elucidating the relationship between the microstructure and the deformation behavior of the material.

AI.tldr: A multimodal deep learning approach using multiple 3D microstructure descriptors (phase volume fractions, persistent diagrams, and two-phase spatial correlations) predicts 3D local strain distribution in as-cast Mg/LPSO two-phase alloys under compression, achieving higher accuracy than single-descriptor models and revealing that high strain correlates with large elongated LPSO phases oriented at 45° to the loading direction.
AI.motivation: To understand the relationship between three-dimensional microstructure and local deformation behavior in Mg/LPSO two-phase alloys, a multi-step framework was needed to predict 3D local strain distribution from microstructure images. Existing approaches using single microstructure descriptors lacked accuracy, motivating the use of multiple complementary descriptors and multimodal deep learning.
AI.method: The method pipelines X-ray CT images before and after compression tests through digital volume correlation to obtain 3D local strain maps. Three microstructure descriptors (phase volume fractions, persistent diagrams for phase connectivity, and two-phase spatial correlations for spatial distribution) are extracted around each strain measurement point. A multimodal deep learning model integrates these numerical and image-based descriptors to predict local strain. Feature importance is assessed via correlation analysis and occlusion sensitivity analysis.
AI.result: Multimodal predictions using multiple descriptors outperformed single-descriptor models in accuracy. Occlusion sensitivity analysis identified that high strain regions correspond to areas where the hard LPSO phase forms large elongated structures oriented at 45° to the loading direction, consistent with prior findings.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multimodal deep learning framework effectively links 3D microstructure to local deformation behavior, and the descriptor importance analysis validates its reliability by reproducing known microstructure-strain relationships in Mg/LPSO alloys.

title: Turning angle analysis reveals hidden anisotropies in the anomalous diffusion of molecules in live cells
comment: Main text: 17 pages, 6 figures; Supplementary information: 14 pages, 5 figures
summary: Molecular motion within living cells provides a window into the physical principles underlying intracellular organization and transport. Yet a fundamental limitation remains: measured trajectories are often short, noisy, and randomly oriented, rendering spatial anisotropies inaccessible to conventional analyses. We show that turning-angle statistics provide a robust approach for uncovering anisotropies in anomalous diffusion. Using a two-dimensional anisotropic fractional Brownian motion model with random orientations, we show theoretically and through simulations that turning-angle distributions preserve signatures of anisotropy. We apply this approach to single-particle tracking data, including quantum dots in the cytoplasm of HeLa cells and membrane proteins in hippocampal neurons. Turning angles reveal hidden anisotropies in the motion of quantum dots and Nav 1.6 channels, and in specific dynamical states of glycoprotein CD4. These results establish turning-angle analysis as a powerful strategy for detecting organization in complex environments and reveal that anisotropic anomalous diffusion is an overlooked feature of intracellular dynamics.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces turning-angle statistics as a robust method for detecting hidden anisotropies in anomalous diffusion from short, noisy, and randomly oriented single-particle tracking trajectories. The approach is validated theoretically and via simulations using an anisotropic fractional Brownian motion model, and applied to quantum dots in HeLa cells and membrane proteins (Nav 1.6 channels, CD4) in hippocampal neurons, revealing previously overlooked anisotropic diffusion in intracellular dynamics.
AI.motivation: Measured single-particle trajectories in living cells are often short, noisy, and randomly oriented, making spatial anisotropies inaccessible through conventional trajectory analyses. The authors aim to develop a robust method to uncover anisotropies in anomalous diffusion despite these limitations.
AI.method: The authors use turning-angle statistics applied to a two-dimensional anisotropic fractional Brownian motion model with random orientations. They demonstrate both theoretically and through simulations that turning-angle distributions preserve signatures of anisotropy, then apply this approach to experimental single-particle tracking data.
AI.result: Turning-angle analysis revealed hidden anisotropies in the motion of quantum dots in HeLa cell cytoplasm, Nav 1.6 channels, and in specific dynamical states of glycoprotein CD4 in hippocampal neurons. The method successfully detected anisotropic diffusion in complex biological environments.
AI.conclusion: Turning-angle analysis is established as a powerful strategy for detecting spatial organization in complex environments, revealing that anisotropic anomalous diffusion is an overlooked feature of intracellular dynamics.

title: All-electrical Coherent Control of a Single Rare-earth Spin Qubit
summary: Electrical control of single spin qubits is a major frontier for nanoscale, high-speed, and scalable quantum devices. Yet, extending it to highly shielded rare-earth 4f electrons remains an experimental challenge across solid-state platforms. Here we demonstrate all-electrical coherent control of a single Er electron spin, which is exchange-coupled to a nearby Ti atom. Scanning tunneling microscopy-based electron spin resonance with three-dimensional magnetic-field control enables comprehensive mapping of the resonance and Rabi frequencies, revealing pronounced anisotropies in both the Er g-tensor and the Er-Ti exchange interaction. The electrical modulation of the anisotropic Er-Ti coupling results in an efficient drive of the Er spin, allowing us to achieve near-gigahertz Rabi frequencies - a ten-fold improvement over the present record for rare-earth spin qubits. By establishing anisotropic exchange as a general resource for electrically accessing shielded rare-earth spins, our results open a new route to ultrafast and local control of rare-earth spins in solid-state quantum devices.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates all-electrical coherent control of a single Er electron spin exchange-coupled to a nearby Ti atom, using STM-based electron spin resonance with 3D magnetic-field control. The electrical modulation of the anisotropic Er-Ti exchange coupling enables near-gigahertz Rabi frequencies—a ten-fold improvement over the previous record for rare-earth spin qubits—establishing anisotropic exchange as a general resource for electrically accessing shielded rare-earth spins.
AI.motivation: Extending electrical control of single spin qubits to highly shielded rare-earth 4f electrons has remained a major experimental challenge across solid-state platforms, limiting the development of nanoscale, high-speed, and scalable quantum devices based on these systems.
AI.method: The authors used scanning tunneling microscopy-based electron spin resonance (STM-ESR) with three-dimensional magnetic-field control to map the resonance and Rabi frequencies of a single Er spin exchange-coupled to a nearby Ti atom, revealing anisotropies in both the Er g-tensor and the Er-Ti exchange interaction. Electrical modulation of this anisotropic Er-Ti coupling was employed to drive the Er spin coherently.
AI.result: The approach achieved near-gigahertz Rabi frequencies, a ten-fold improvement over the previous record for rare-earth spin qubits, with comprehensive mapping of resonance and Rabi frequencies revealing pronounced anisotropies in both the Er g-tensor and the Er-Ti exchange interaction.
AI.conclusion: Anisotropic exchange is established as a general resource for electrically accessing shielded rare-earth spins, opening a new route to ultrafast and local control of rare-earth spins in solid-state quantum devices.

title: Robust spin pseudogap and spin-charge separation in the $σt$-$J$ model
summary: The $σt$-$J$ model, obtained from the usual $t$-$J$ model by flipping the sign of the spin-down hopping term, has been proposed to eliminate the strong interference between doped holes and the spin background, known as the phase string effect. In this work, we investigate the finite-temperature properties of the $σt$-$J$ model using infinite projected entangled-pair state (iPEPS) algorithms, in comparison with the $t$-$J$ model and its easy-plane variants. We show that these models share similar spin-pseudogap thermodynamics, with a maximum in the spin susceptibility at $T^* \sim J$ and a broad specific-heat peak. Tensor network renormalization (TNR) further provides strong evidences for a Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transition in the spin sector of the $σt$-$J$ model at a lower temperature $T_\text{BKT} < T^*$ due to its reduced $\mathrm{U}(1)$ spin-rotation symmetry. Crucially, in contrast to the $t$-$J$ model and to its easy-plane variants that also exhibit BKT transitions, these signatures remain robust upon doping: the doped holes preserve and even enhance the antiferromagnetic correlations in the $xy$ spin plane, leading to a weak doping dependence of both $T^*$ and $T_\text{BKT}$. Finally, we develop a slave-fermion mean-field theory for the $σt$-$J$ model, whose projective symmetry group (PSG) is selected based on numerically determined hopping and pairing correlations, and show that it explains the robust spin pseudogap upon doping.

AI.tldr: The σt-J model, which removes the phase string effect from the t-J model, is studied via iPEPS and TNR at finite temperature. It shares spin-pseudogap thermodynamics with t-J models (spin susceptibility peak at T*~J, broad specific-heat peak) and exhibits a BKT transition at lower temperature. Unlike t-J and easy-plane variants, these features remain robust upon doping, as holes preserve/enhance xy-plane antiferromagnetic correlations. A slave-fermion mean-field theory with PSG selected from numerics explains the doping-robust spin pseudogap.
AI.motivation: The σt-J model was proposed to eliminate the phase string effect—the strong interference between doped holes and the spin background—that complicates the standard t-J model. This work aims to determine whether this modified model preserves the key physics (spin pseudogap, BKT transition) while improving robustness against doping, and to develop a tractable theoretical description.
AI.method: Infinite projected entangled-pair state (iPEPS) algorithms are used to investigate finite-temperature properties, compared against the t-J model and its easy-plane variants. Tensor network renormalization (TNR) provides evidence for the BKT transition. Additionally, a slave-fermion mean-field theory is constructed, with its projective symmetry group (PSG) selected based on numerically computed hopping and pairing correlations.
AI.result: All studied models share spin-pseudogap thermodynamics (spin susceptibility maximum at T*~J, broad specific-heat peak). TNR gives strong evidence for a BKT transition in the spin sector of the σt-J model at TBKT<T*, due to reduced U(1) spin-rotation symmetry. Crucially, unlike the t-J model and easy-plane variants, these signatures are robust upon doping: holes preserve and enhance xy-plane antiferromagnetic correlations, yielding weak doping dependence of both T* and TBKT.
AI.conclusion: The σt-J model exhibits a robust spin pseudogap and BKT transition that survive hole doping, in contrast to the t-J and easy-plane models. The slave-fermion mean-field theory with numerically guided PSG selection successfully explains this doping-robust spin pseudogap, establishing the σt-J model as a cleaner framework for studying pseudogap physics without phase-string interference.

title: Probing crystal-field modulations with magnetic adatoms on the incipient charge-density-wave superconductor $2H$-NbS$_2$
summary: The interplay between multiple quantum phases in layered materials may lead to incipient quantum behavior, where the material's ground state is close to a phase transition and sensitive to local disorder. The transition metal dichalcogenide material $2H$-NbS$_2$ exhibits incipient charge-density-wave behavior along with a well-developed superconducting state, creating a scenario where the local lattice instabilities play a crucial role. Here we present how an individual magnetic atom on $2H$-NbS$_2$ can be applied as a local sensor to reveal hidden crystal-field modulations. By manipulating the adatom across the surface with the tip of a scanning tunneling microscope, we measure variations in the Yu-Shiba-Rusinov (YSR) excitation spectra and map the local environment around an intrinsic point defect. We find that while the superconducting state is spatially uniform, the YSR excitation energy strongly depends on the position of the atom. We determine that the main contribution to this effect originates from variations in the local crystal-field environment. These results establish a new approach to investigate crystal-field modulations at the atomic scale and reveal how defects and lattice instabilities shape the atomic landscape of an incipient charge-density-wave material.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates a new atomic-scale approach using a single magnetic adatom as a local sensor on the incipient charge-density-wave superconductor 2H-NbS2. By manipulating the adatom with an STM tip and measuring Yu-Shiba-Rusinov excitation spectra, the authors reveal hidden crystal-field modulations around an intrinsic point defect, showing that YSR excitation energy depends strongly on atomic position while the superconducting state remains spatially uniform.
AI.motivation: In materials where multiple quantum phases compete, such as 2H-NbS2 which exhibits incipient charge-density-wave behavior alongside superconductivity, local lattice instabilities play a crucial role. The authors aim to reveal hidden crystal-field modulations at the atomic scale that are otherwise difficult to probe, particularly in the presence of local disorder and defects.
AI.method: A single magnetic atom is deposited on 2H-NbS2 and used as a local sensor. The adatom is manipulated across the surface using an STM tip, and Yu-Shiba-Rusinov (YSR) excitation spectra are measured at each position. These spectra are used to map the local environment around an intrinsic point defect, with YSR excitation energy variations analyzed to extract crystal-field contributions.
AI.result: The superconducting state is found to be spatially uniform, yet the YSR excitation energy strongly depends on the adatom's position. The dominant contribution to this position-dependent energy shift originates from variations in the local crystal-field environment rather than from superconducting gap modulations.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes a new approach for investigating crystal-field modulations at the atomic scale, revealing how defects and lattice instabilities shape the atomic landscape of an incipient charge-density-wave material. The YSR-based sensing technique offers a powerful tool for probing local electronic and structural environments in correlated quantum materials.

title: Decoding Transient X-ray Absorption Spectra of Acetylacetone With Multireference Algebraic Diagrammatic Construction Theory
summary: Time-resolved X-ray absorption spectroscopy (TR-XAS) offers an element- and site-specific probe of coupled electronic and nuclear dynamics, but its interpretation requires methods that can treat multiconfigurational excited states across nonequilibrium nuclear ensembles. Here, we report time-resolved simulations of the acetylacetone (AcAc) transient X-ray absorption spectra by combining surface-hopping dynamics from complete active space second-order perturbation theory with multireference algebraic diagrammatic construction (MR-ADC). The simulated 20-200 fs spectra show a good agreement with experimental measurements and reveal that the TR-XAS response is governed by continuously evolving distributions of molecular geometries on the singlet potential energy surfaces (S2 and S1). In particular, absorption at 279.5-281.5 eV is enhanced for transient, nearly symmetric proton-sharing configurations, whereas the 284-286 eV profile reflects geometry-dependent C1s excitations modulated by proton transfer, bond alternation, and ring opening. For the long-time T_1 spectrum (7-10 ps), the principal features near 281.4 and 283.8 eV are assigned to central C 1s excitations into low-lying triplet pi-orbitals. Together, our simulations provide a more complete mechanistic picture of AcAc photorelaxation by directly linking ultrafast carbon K-edge signals to proton transfer, skeletal reorganization, internal conversion, and triplet formation.

AI.tldr: This paper reports time-resolved X-ray absorption spectroscopy (TR-XAS) simulations for acetylacetone (AcAc) by coupling surface-hopping dynamics from CASPT2 with multireference algebraic diagrammatic construction (MR-ADC). The simulations reproduce experimental spectra at 20-200 fs and reveal that the XAS response reflects continuously evolving molecular geometries on S2/S1 surfaces, with proton-sharing configurations enhancing absorption at 279.5-281.5 eV and geometry-dependent C1s excitations in the 284-286 eV region. Long-time T1 spectra are assigned to central carbon 1s excitations into low-lying triplet pi-orbitals, providing a comprehensive mechanistic picture of AcAc photorelaxation linking carbon K-edge signals to proton transfer, skeletal reorganization, internal conversion, and triplet formation.
AI.motivation: TR-XAS provides element- and site-specific probes of coupled electronic and nuclear dynamics, but its interpretation requires theoretical methods capable of treating multiconfigurational excited states across nonequilibrium nuclear ensembles—a capability that current methods lack for systems like acetylacetone undergoing complex photorelaxation.
AI.method: The authors combine surface-hopping nonadiabatic dynamics from complete active space second-order perturbation theory (CASPT2) with multireference algebraic diagrammatic construction (MR-ADC) to simulate time-resolved carbon K-edge X-ray absorption spectra of acetylacetone across ultrafast (20-200 fs) and long-time (7-10 ps) timescales.
AI.result: Simulated spectra agree well with experiments at 20-200 fs. The TR-XAS response is governed by evolving molecular geometries on S2 and S1 surfaces: absorption at 279.5-281.5 eV is enhanced for transient nearly symmetric proton-sharing configurations, while the 284-286 eV profile reflects geometry-dependent C1s excitations modulated by proton transfer, bond alternation, and ring opening. The long-time T1 spectrum assigns features at 281.4 and 283.8 eV to central carbon 1s excitations into low-lying triplet pi-orbitals.
AI.conclusion: The simulations provide a more complete mechanistic picture of AcAc photorelaxation by directly linking ultrafast carbon K-edge signals to proton transfer, skeletal reorganization, internal conversion, and triplet formation.

title: Machine Learning Framework for Magnetic Candidate Discovery in Cerium-Based Compounds
summary: Cerium (Ce), the most abundant lanthanide, offers significant potential for addressing shortages in high-performance magnetic materials, particularly through the discovery of compounds suitable for gap magnets. However, predicting Ce-based ferromagnets with uniaxial magnetic anisotropy remains challenging because their magnetic behavior depends strongly on crystal structure, exchange geometry, and electronic interactions. Here, we present a physics-guided computational framework to screen known Ce-based crystal structures and identify promising Ising ferromagnets for future synthesis. A Random Forest classifier uses seven structural and SOAP descriptors, including unit-cell volume, density, atomic sites, space group, atomic density, Ce SOAP overlap, and transition-metal SOAP overlap, to prioritize candidate compounds. Selected crystallographic structures are then analyzed using Ising-model Monte Carlo simulations to characterize phase behavior and critical properties. Critical exponents extracted from simulated phase transitions provide quantitative insight into magnetic regimes and anisotropy-related effects. We further employ autoencoders trained on affinity-based features from simulated spin configurations to identify latent signatures of phase evolution and transition behavior. Together, this framework integrates structural screening, statistical-mechanical simulation, and machine learning to accelerate the identification of promising Ce-based magnetic materials and provide candidates for experimental synthesis and validation.
