Near the phase boundaries, we observe fluctuating magnetic domains, providing direct microscopic evidence of phase coexistence between nearly degenerate competing ordered states. Together, these observations provide the first direct thermodynamic evidence for first order topological quantum phase transitions and establish a microscopic framework for understanding interaction driven topological quantum phase transitions through phase competition and coexistence.

AI.tldr: Using nanoSQUID-on-tip magnetometry, the authors directly image the local orbital magnetization of a spin-orbit-proximitized rhombohedral graphene quantum anomalous Hall (QAH) state with a record Chern number. Combined with self-consistent Hartree-Fock calculations, they demonstrate that transitions between layer antiferromagnetic, QAH, and layer polarized insulating states are first order, with discontinuous orbital magnetization changes and fluctuating magnetic domains near phase boundaries—providing the first direct thermodynamic evidence for first-order topological quantum phase transitions.
AI.motivation: While continuous gap closing/reopening drives topological phase transitions in non-interacting systems, strongly interacting systems are predicted to exhibit first-order transitions through competition between ordered states. This possibility had remained experimentally unresolved, and recent transport studies in rhombohedral graphene hinted at continuous transitions—motivating direct thermodynamic/microscopic investigation.
AI.method: NanoSQUID-on-tip magnetometry is used to locally image the orbital magnetization of a QAH state in spin-orbit-proximitized rhombohedral graphene, enabling real-space visualization of the QAH phase, reconstruction of the local thermodynamic gap, and tracking of magnetization across competing correlated states. These measurements are combined with self-consistent Hartree-Fock calculations.
AI.result: Sequential transitions between layer antiferromagnetic, QAH, and layer polarized insulating states are first order, with discontinuous changes in orbital magnetization. Near phase boundaries, fluctuating magnetic domains reveal phase coexistence between nearly degenerate competing ordered states, and the QAH phase exhibits the first real-space visualization with a record Chern number.
AI.conclusion: These observations provide the first direct thermodynamic evidence for first-order topological quantum phase transitions and establish a microscopic framework for understanding interaction-driven topological phase transitions through phase competition and coexistence.

title: An Automated Magnetron Sputtering Chamber for Ferroelectric Thin Film Deposition
summary: Optimization of next-generation materials synthesis and manufacturing processes can be accelerated by effective use of digital datasets. However, a majority of existing custom research infrastructure, including that for thin film deposition, is primarily manually operated and not compatible with this new research paradigm. Here, a template is provided for upgrading existing manual deposition chambers to enable automated and autonomous experimentation. As an example, the upgrade of an existing magnetron sputtering chamber dedicated to synthesis of wurtzite ferroelectrics is presented. Focus is placed on automation of instrumentation; system and deposition control; and synchronized and automated data collection strategies. An example use case of the system for semi-autonomous determination of process-property relationships is presented, specifically minimization of coercive field in wurtzite Al$_{1-x-y}$Sc$_x$B$_y$N thin films.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a template for upgrading existing manual thin film deposition chambers into automated, autonomous experimental systems. The upgrade of a magnetron sputtering chamber for wurtzite ferroelectrics synthesis is demonstrated, covering instrumentation automation, system/deposition control, and synchronized data collection. A semi-autonomous example optimizes process-property relationships by minimizing coercive field in AlScBN thin films.
AI.motivation: Accelerating next-generation materials synthesis via digital data requires automated infrastructure, but most existing research equipment, especially thin film deposition systems, is manually operated and incompatible with autonomous experimentation paradigms.
AI.method: The authors provide a template for retrofitting existing manual deposition chambers into automated systems. Using a magnetron sputtering chamber for wurtzite ferroelectrics as a case study, they focus on automation of instrumentation, system and deposition control, and synchronized automated data collection strategies. A semi-autonomous workflow is demonstrated to explore process-property relationships.
AI.result: A successful upgrade of an existing magnetron sputtering chamber enabling automated/autonomous experimentation is presented. The system is validated through a semi-autonomous optimization study of coercive field minimization in wurtzite Al1-x-yScxByN thin films.
AI.conclusion: Existing manual deposition infrastructure can be cost-effectively upgraded to support automated and autonomous research, enabling broader adoption of data-driven materials discovery while leveraging legacy equipment.

title: Nonisospectral Integrability and Exact Current Fluctuations in the Two-Dimensional SSEP
comment: Three figures, comments are very welcome. The supplementary material will be uploaded later
summary: We study annealed current fluctuations in the two-dimensional symmetric simple exclusion process across a circular passive counting boundary. The initial density is $ρ_1$ inside a disk of radius $R$ and $ρ_2$ outside, and the observable is the net decrease of the particle number in the disk over a finite time. Using convexity of the macroscopic fluctuation theory action and rotational averaging, we show that the minimizer of the full two-dimensional variational problem may be chosen radially symmetric. For the resulting radial problem, a suitable change of variables leads to a nonisospectral formulation on the half-line. Combining the associated scattering construction with a scalar factorization, we obtain a closed expression for the scaled cumulant generating function and hence the annealed large-deviation statistics of the current.

AI.tldr: The paper studies annealed current fluctuations in the two-dimensional symmetric simple exclusion process (SSEP) across a circular passive counting boundary with piecewise-constant initial density. By exploiting convexity of the macroscopic fluctuation theory (MFT) action and rotational averaging, the authors reduce the full two-dimensional variational problem to a radial one, which is then reformulated as a nonisospectral problem on the half-line. Combining scattering construction with scalar factorization yields a closed-form expression for the scaled cumulant generating function (SCGF) and hence the annealed large-deviation statistics of the current.
AI.motivation: To obtain exact large-deviation statistics for the current in a two-dimensional driven/diffusive system (the SSEP) with a circular counting boundary and a step-like initial density profile, which goes beyond known one-dimensional results and challenges posed by multi-dimensional variational problems.
AI.method: (1) Reformulate the problem using macroscopic fluctuation theory (MFT). (2) Use convexity of the MFT action and rotational averaging to prove the minimizer of the two-dimensional variational problem can be chosen radially symmetric. (3) Reduce the radial problem via a change of variables to a nonisospectral formulation on the half-line. (4) Apply a scattering construction combined with a scalar factorization to solve the spectral problem and obtain a closed expression for the SCGF.
AI.result: A closed-form expression for the scaled cumulant generating function of the annealed current fluctuations, yielding the associated large-deviation statistics for the two-dimensional SSEP across a circular passive counting boundary.
AI.conclusion: The annealed large-deviation statistics of the current in the two-dimensional SSEP with a circular boundary are exactly tractable through a reduction to a radial nonisospectral half-line problem equipped with scattering and factorization methods, demonstrating that symmetry reduction plus integrable tools can crack genuinely two-dimensional fluctuation problems.

title: Interaction between Rydberg Excitons in Cuprous Oxide Revealed through Resonant Second Harmonic Generation
summary: We report experimental and theoretical investigations of interacting excitons of the yellow series in cuprous oxide (Cu$_2$O) with principal quantum numbers up to by means of second harmonic generation (SHG). Using picosecond pulsed laser excitation up to 10 GW/cm$^2$ peak intensity we observe a pronounced change of the spectra with increasing pump laser intensity: an energetic shift to lower absolute energies and a spectral broadening. The absolute intensities of the spectral lines scale for low powers with the square of the pump power, but saturates at higher powers. At still higher powers the SHG intensity is actually reduced. To explain these results quantitively, we developed a semi-classical theory of resonant SHG where the process of SHG is fully coherent. The excitons are assumed to be bosons interacting by a distance dependent potential giving rise to both the changes in spectral line shape and the saturation by a $\it{Rydberg}$ blockade. The concomitant measurement of two-photon absorption allows to derive quantitative values for the exciton-exciton interaction. While the results agree in order of magnitude with those calculated by state-of-the art atomic-like van der Waals interaction theory, the scaling with principle quantum number is quite different. As a possible screening by an electron-hole plasma created by three-photon absorption into blue and violet band states could be ruled out, our results point toward fundamental differences between excitons and atoms.

AI.tldr: The paper reports experimental and theoretical studies of interacting yellow-series excitons in cuprous oxide (Cu2O) using second harmonic generation (SHG). Increasing pump intensity causes spectral shifts to lower energies, broadening, saturation, and eventually reduction of SHG intensity. A semi-classical theory with bosonic excitons interacting via a distance-dependent potential explains these effects, including Rydberg blockade saturation. Exciton-exciton interactions were quantified and shown to scale differently with principal quantum number than predicted by atomic-like van der Waals theory, revealing fundamental differences between excitons and atoms.
AI.motivation: To understand exciton-exciton interactions in cuprous oxide, particularly how they deviate from atomic-like van der Waals interaction predictions, and to explore fundamental differences between excitonic and atomic many-body systems.
AI.method: Experimental SHG with picosecond pulsed laser excitation up to 10 GW/cm² peak intensity on cuprous oxide, combined with a semi-classical theory of fully coherent resonant SHG. Excitons treated as bosons with a distance-dependent interaction potential, analyzed alongside two-photon absorption measurements to extract quantitative exciton-exciton interaction values. Screening by electron-hole plasma was ruled out as an alternative explanation.
AI.result: SHG intensity scales quadratically with pump power at low powers but saturates and then decreases at higher powers. Spectral lines shift to lower energies and broaden with increasing intensity. Exciton-exciton interaction values agree in order of magnitude with atomic-like van der Waals theory but show a markedly different scaling with principal quantum number.
AI.conclusion: The results suggest fundamental differences between excitons and atoms in their interaction behavior, as the principal-quantum-number scaling deviates from state-of-the-art atomic-like van der Waals interaction theory, while ruling out electron-hole plasma screening as the cause.

title: Microscopic Origin of Spin Splitting in Altermagnetic CrSb Thin Films
summary: Altermagnets have recently emerged as promising materials for spintronic applications owing to their momentum-dependent spin splitting. Among them, metallic CrSb is particularly attractive owing to its giant spin splitting and high Néel temperature. However, the microscopic origin of the distinct spin-splitting behaviors in bulk and thin-film CrSb remains unresolved. Here, we systematically investigate the electronic structures of CrSb slabs with different surface orientations using first-principles calculations. Although all considered slabs preserve spin-group symmetries compatible with altermagnetism, they exhibit markedly different electronic structures: the (2$\bar{1}\bar{1}$0) slab retains pronounced altermagnetic spin splitting, whereas the (0001) and (10$\bar{1}$0) slabs display nearly spin-degenerate bands. We demonstrate that dimensional reduction fundamentally changes the microscopic origin of altermagnetic spin splitting. Unlike bulk CrSb, altermagnetic spin splitting in thin films requires long-range inter-unit-cell coplanar Cr--Sb hopping, while Sb--Sb hopping provides an additional contribution. The preservation or suppression of these hopping pathways explains the strong surface dependence of the spin splitting. Our findings establish a microscopic mechanism for understanding altermagnetism in reduced dimensions and provide a general principle for engineering spin splitting in low-dimensional altermagnetic materials.

AI.tldr: The paper uses first-principles calculations to investigate CrSb thin films with different surface orientations, revealing that altermagnetic spin splitting in reduced dimensions requires long-range inter-unit-cell coplanar Cr-Sb hopping (with Sb-Sb hopping as an additional contribution), explaining the strong surface-orientation dependence where only the (2̄1̄10) slab retains pronounced spin splitting while (0001) and (101̄0) slabs become nearly spin-degenerate.
AI.motivation: Although bulk CrSb exhibits giant spin splitting and a high Néel temperature, the microscopic origin of distinct spin-splitting behaviors between bulk and thin-film CrSb remains unresolved, motivating a systematic investigation of how dimensional reduction affects altermagnetic ordering in this material.
AI.method: Systematic first-principles calculations of CrSb slabs with different surface orientations (2̄1̄10, 0001, and 101̄0), analyzing their spin-group symmetries and the role of specific hopping pathways (long-range inter-unit-cell coplanar Cr-Sb hopping and Sb-Sb hopping) in determining altermagnetic spin splitting.
AI.result: All slab orientations preserve spin-group symmetries compatible with altermagnetism, yet only the (2̄1̄10) slab retains pronounced altermagnetic spin splitting, while (0001) and (101̄0) slabs display nearly spin-degenerate bands. Dimensional reduction changes the microscopic origin: thin-film altermagnetic spin splitting requires long-range inter-unit-cell coplanar Cr-Sb hopping, with Sb-Sb hopping providing an additional contribution.
AI.conclusion: The findings establish a microscopic mechanism for understanding altermagnetism in reduced dimensions and provide a general principle for engineering spin splitting in low-dimensional altermagnetic materials.

title: Time-Reversal-Invariant Altermagnetic Acoustic Crystals
summary: Altermagnets have emerged as a new class of magnetic materials that combine spin-split electronic bands with zero net magnetization. Extending this paradigm to classical-wave systems has, however, been fundamentally challenging because conventional realizations require broken time-reversal symmetry (TRS). Here, we overcome this limitation by introducing two pseudospin degrees of freedom and constructing a pseudo-time-reversal operator that faithfully reproduces the action of its physical counterpart while preserving actual TRS. Building on this framework, we theoretically propose and experimentally realize the first time-reversal-invariant altermagnetic acoustic crystal. Acoustic measurements directly reveal pseudospin-dependent band splitting--a defining hallmark of altermagnetism--under strictly TRS-preserving conditions. Moreover, the altermagnetic acoustic crystal exhibits sublattice-pseudospin locking, enabling flexible control over acoustic pseudospin splitting and filtering. Our work establishes acoustic crystals as a versatile platform for exploring altermagnetic physics and opens new avenues for spin-inspired wave manipulation in nonmagnetic devices.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces pseudo-time-reversal symmetry using two pseudospin degrees of freedom to realize the first time-reversal-invariant altermagnetic acoustic crystal, experimentally demonstrating pseudospin-dependent band splitting and sublattice-pseudospin locking in a nonmagnetic classical-wave system.
AI.motivation: Altermagnets combine spin-split bands with zero net magnetization, but extending this concept to classical-wave systems is challenging because conventional implementations require broken time-reversal symmetry (TRS), which is difficult to achieve in acoustic or other classical wave platforms.
AI.method: The authors introduce two pseudospin degrees of freedom and construct a pseudo-time-reversal operator that mimics physical TRS action while preserving actual TRS. Based on this framework, they design and fabricate a time-reversal-invariant altermagnetic acoustic crystal and perform acoustic measurements.
AI.result: Acoustic measurements directly reveal pseudospin-dependent band splitting under strictly TRS-preserving conditions—the defining hallmark of altermagnetism. The crystal also exhibits sublattice-pseudospin locking, enabling controllable acoustic pseudospin splitting and filtering.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes acoustic crystals as a versatile platform for exploring altermagnetic physics and opens new avenues for spin-inspired wave manipulation in nonmagnetic devices.

title: Distribution of Relaxation Times analysis of evolution of Oxygen Reduction Pathways for ionic conductor infiltration on MIEC cathode
summary: Solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs) are promising electrochemical energy conversion devices; however, the sluggish cathodic oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) remains a major limitation for intermediate-temperature operation. ORR subprocesses can be modified by infiltrating ionic Sm0.2Ce0.8O2-delta (SDC) on mixed ionic electronic SrFe0.9Ti0.1O3-delta (STF). However, the processes are indistinguishable in most cases and poorly understood using conventional equivalent circuits. Distribution of Relaxation Times (DRT) analysis distinguishes these processes to identify the dynamics with temperature and surface reconstruction. Such analysis is being reported, revealing the connection between increase of active sites, temperature, and polarization resistance (RP). SDC infiltration preferentially accelerates oxygen surface exchange and activation processes over the relatively high frequency charge transfer process related to cathode surface at elevated temperatures for the infiltrated cells. RP was reduced substantially with the systematic redistribution of each process to as low as 0.04 ohm.cm2 at 800 degC. This work underlines the deconvolution of the processes using DRT as a tool, and SDC infiltrated STF as a model cathode system to provide a mechanistic insight of understanding ORR kinetics and design a rationale for developing high-performance SOFC air electrodes

AI.tldr: This study uses Distribution of Relaxation Times (DRT) analysis to deconvolute the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) subprocesses in Sm0.2Ce0.8O2-delta (SDC)-infiltrated SrFe0.9Ti0.1O3-delta (STF) solid oxide fuel cell cathodes, revealing that SDC infiltration preferentially accelerates oxygen surface exchange and activation processes over the higher-frequency charge transfer, reducing polarization resistance to 0.04 ohm·cm² at 800°C.
AI.motivation: SOFCs suffer from sluggish cathodic ORR kinetics at intermediate temperatures, and the underlying subprocesses are difficult to distinguish with conventional equivalent circuits, limiting mechanistic understanding and rational design of high-performance air electrodes.
AI.method: Distribution of Relaxation Times (DRT) analysis was applied to distinguish ORR subprocesses in SDC-infiltrated STF cathodes, tracking their dynamics as functions of temperature and surface reconstruction, and correlating active-site increases, temperature, and polarization resistance.
AI.result: SDC infiltration preferentially accelerates low-frequency oxygen surface exchange and activation processes over the high-frequency charge transfer process. Polarization resistance was substantially reduced, reaching as low as 0.04 ohm·cm² at 800°C, with systematic redistribution of each ORR subprocess.
AI.conclusion: DRT proves to be a powerful deconvolution tool for ORR analysis, and SDC-infiltrated STF serves as a model cathode system providing mechanistic insight into ORR kinetics and a design rationale for developing high-performance SOFC air electrodes.

title: Reliability-Safety Trade-off in AI Distillation: A Renormalization-Group Approach
summary: Knowledge distillation transfers more than task competence: it also transmits response propensities, refusal policies, error boundaries, and latent safety biases. We formulate this behavioral inheritance as a coarse-graining model grounded in statistical mechanics, in which the student's answer and refusal decisions define two macrostates, while the teacher induces an effective field that reshapes the student's free-energy landscape. The model yields a reliability-safety trade-off relation controlled by a single parameter K, which we term the hazard discrimination capability. The predicted trade-off is consistent with refusal-token data [arXiv: 2412.06748]. In knowledge distillation, a teacher with strong hazard discrimination improves the student's attainable reliability and safety, whereas poor discrimination limits the attainable trade-off. Repeated distillation acts as an iterated renormalization-group-like transformation, under which K follows a flow across generations. The flow exhibits a tricritical structure separating regimes of K loss, stable transmission, and threshold-dependent inheritance, and yields testable scaling predictions for multigenerational distillation.

AI.tldr: This paper models knowledge distillation as a statistical-mechanics-based coarse-graining process where student behavior (answers vs. refusals) forms two macrostates shaped by a teacher-induced effective field. It derives a reliability-safety trade-off governed by a single parameter K (hazard discrimination capability), and shows that repeated distillation behaves like an iterated renormalization-group transformation with a tricritical structure, yielding testable scaling predictions for multigenerational distillation.
AI.motivation: Knowledge distillation transfers not just task competence but also behavioral traits like response propensities, refusal policies, error boundaries, and safety biases. The authors aim to formally characterize this "behavioral inheritance" and understand how safety and reliability are transmitted across distillation generations.
AI.method: The authors formulate behavioral inheritance as a coarse-graining model grounded in statistical mechanics. Student answer and refusal decisions define two macrostates, while the teacher induces an effective field reshaping the student's free-energy landscape. This yields a reliability-safety trade-off controlled by a single parameter K (hazard discrimination capability). They analyze repeated distillation as an iterated renormalization-group-like transformation and study the flow of K across generations.
AI.result: The model predicts a reliability-safety trade-off consistent with refusal-token data from arXiv:2412.06748. A teacher with strong hazard discrimination improves attainable student reliability and safety, while poor discrimination limits it. The K flow across generations exhibits a tricritical structure separating regimes of K loss, stable transmission, and threshold-dependent inheritance, with testable scaling predictions for multigenerational distillation.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a principled statistical-mechanics framework for understanding how safety biases and reliability trade-offs propagate through knowledge distillation, identifying the hazard discrimination capability K as the governing parameter and revealing a tricritical phase structure in multigenerational distillation that yields falsifiable scaling predictions.

title: Electronic bistability, discontinuous switching and stochasticity in a two-dimensional semiconductor
summary: Bistability - two stable electronic states under the same bias - underlies switching and memory, but is usually absent in transistors and must be engineered through material means: doped tunnel junctions, filaments in memristors, or phase transitions. Here we demonstrate a transistor with intrinsic electronic bistability in a single chemically homogeneous crystal. In dual-gated black phosphorus, whose band gap narrows under a perpendicular electric field due to a giant Stark effect, the gates not only modulate carrier density but also reshape the band profile, forming interband tunnel junctions in the channel. Transport across the two-gate parameter space reveals competing conduction regimes - diffusive, two tunnelling channels and Zener breakdown - whose interplay produces negative differential conductance and transconductance, discontinuous switching, and hysteresis with the state set by gate history. Moreover, the switching remains intrinsically stochastic, yet statistically stable within a narrow range of gate voltages, providing an electrically programmable source of randomness. Devices based on this principle should be realisable in other two-dimensional semiconductors, opening a route to next-generation computing architectures in which nonlinearity, switching, memory and stochasticity are integrated within a single electrostatically programmable element.

AI.tldr: A dual-gated black phosphorus transistor exhibits intrinsic electronic bistability in a single chemically homogeneous crystal, enabling switching, memory, negative differential conductance, and programmable stochasticity without external material engineering.
AI.motivation: Bistability in electronic devices typically requires engineered materials such as doped tunnel junctions, memristive filaments, or phase-change materials. The authors seek intrinsic bistability in a simple, homogeneous transistor to integrate nonlinearity, switching, memory, and stochasticity into a single electrostatically programmable element for next-generation computing.

Gates simultaneously modulate carrier density and reshape the band profile, forming interband tunnel junctions in the channel. Transport mapping across the two-gate parameter space reveals competing conduction regimes (diffusive transport, two tunnelling channels, and Zener breakdown).

title: Light-Stabilized Metastable Electronic State in NiO with Enhanced Orbital Hybridization2
summary: Light-driven control of electronic structure in correlated metal oxides offers new opportunities for optimizing materials used in photovoltaic and photoelectrochemical technologies. We show that photoexcitation of NiO, a prototypical transparent semiconductor and hole-transport material, across its charge-transfer gap produces a long-lived metastable state with enhanced Ni 3d-O 2p orbital hybridization. We characterize this state using Ni K-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy, which probes how structural and electronic changes affect the unoccupied p density of states during continuous and pulsed ultraviolet excitation. Under pulsed excitation, high carrier densities of approximately 10^20 per cubic centimeter generate a state with a lifetime of approximately 600 picoseconds, in which enhanced hybridization coexists with lattice heating. By contrast, continuous ultraviolet irradiation at much lower carrier densities of approximately 10^13 per cubic centimeter stabilizes a similar electronic state with negligible lattice heating, demonstrating that its formation is not solely thermally driven. First-principles DFT+U+V calculations attribute the spectral changes to stronger Ni 3d-O 2p hybridization, which alters the unoccupied Ni 4p states probed by dipole-allowed K-edge transitions. We attribute this change to the dynamic screening of on-site electronic correlations following photoexcitation, which redistributes the charge density. Because orbital hybridization governs carrier transport and charge-transfer energetics, our results identify photoinduced screening as a mechanism for dynamically tuning correlated oxides and suggest new design principles for optoelectronic materials.

AI.tldr: Photoexcitation of NiO across its charge-transfer gap creates a long-lived metastable state with enhanced Ni 3d-O 2p orbital hybridization, as probed by Ni K-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy. This state persists ~600 ps at high carrier densities (~10^20 cm^-3) and is also stabilized under continuous low-density irradiation (~10^13 cm^-3) with negligible lattice heating, confirming it is not purely thermal. DFT+U+V calculations attribute the effect to dynamic screening of on-site electronic correlations that redistributes charge density and enhances hybridization.
AI.motivation: To identify mechanisms for dynamically tuning electronic structure in correlated metal oxides, which could lead to new design principles for photovoltaic and photoelectrochemical materials.
AI.method: Ni K-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy under both continuous and pulsed ultraviolet excitation, combined with first-principles DFT+U+V calculations to interpret the spectral changes.
AI.result: Pulsed excitation produces a ~600 ps lifetime state with enhanced hybridization coexisting with lattice heating at ~10^20 cm^-3 carrier density; continuous irradiation at much lower density (~10^13 cm^-3) stabilizes a similar state without significant lattice heating, proving non-thermal origin. DFT+U+V attributes the changes to stronger Ni 3d-O 2p hybridization altering unoccupied Ni 4p states.
AI.conclusion: Photoinduced screening of on-site electronic correlations is identified as a mechanism for dynamically tuning orbital hybridization and charge transport in correlated oxides, offering new design principles for optoelectronic materials.

title: Retained hidden excess generates memory in price-limited markets
summary: The daily return of a stock is often restricted to an exchange-imposed band to curb extreme fluctuations. Any attempted price movement beyond this band is clipped, leaving an unobserved excess. We introduce a minimal stochastic latent-state model in which a fraction of this hidden excess is retained for the next day. This retention generates memory, even though the daily stochastic driving shocks are independent. For symmetric driving shocks with regularly varying tails, the stationary latent return preserves the tail index of the noise, but has an enhanced tail amplitude. In the wide-band limit, a close of the daily return at either limit of the band admits a single-dominant-shock description. We show that after such an event, the mean return on the following day has the same sign and grows proportionally to the band width, while the probability of reaching the same limit again approaches a finite value. Reaching the opposite band limit on the following day requires a second extreme shock of opposite sign and is power-law suppressed. Simulations support these analytical predictions. Empirical data from stocks subject to daily price limits are qualitatively consistent with the predicted same-sign response and its increase across wider price bands.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a minimal stochastic latent-state model to capture the effect of exchange-imposed daily price limits (bands) on stock returns. When a price movement is clipped at the band, a fraction of the hidden excess is retained and carried to the next day, generating memory despite independent daily shocks. For heavy-tailed symmetric noise, the stationary latent return preserves the tail index but with an enhanced amplitude. In the wide-band limit, a return landing at a band limit admits a single-dominant-shock description, and the mean next-day return has the same sign growing linearly with band width, with finite probability of hitting the same limit again, while reaching the opposite limit is power-law suppressed. Simulations confirm the analytics, and empirical data from price-limit stocks show qualitative agreement with the same-sign response and its growth across wider bands.
AI.motivation: To understand how exchange-imposed price limits (bands) distort the observed return process. Clipping at the band creates hidden excess returns, and the paper seeks a parsimonious model that explains the memory and short-term predictability induced by this mechanism, as well as its statistical properties under heavy-tailed shocks.
AI.method: A minimal stochastic latent-state model is proposed where a fraction of excess return beyond the price band is retained for the next day, generating serial dependence. Analytical methods are applied to characterize the stationary distribution, tail behavior (tail index and amplitude), and the wide-band limit using a single-dominant-shock approximation. Monte Carlo simulations are used to validate the analytical results, and empirical stock data with daily price limits are compared qualitatively.
AI.result: The stationary latent return inherits the noise tail index with an enhanced tail amplitude. In the wide-band limit, after hitting a band limit, the next-day mean return is positive and proportional to band width; the probability of revisiting the same limit converges to a finite value, while reaching the opposite limit is power-law suppressed. Simulations support the predictions, and empirical price-limit stock data show a qualitatively consistent same-sign response that strengthens with wider bands.
AI.conclusion: The retention of clipped excess returns is a viable mechanism for generating short-term momentum-like effects and memory in daily return series under price-limit regulations. The model provides analytically tractable predictions for heavy-tailed return distributions and agrees qualitatively with empirical observations, offering insights into the microstructure of price-limited markets.

title: Relaxation-driven flat bands and topology in moiré transition metal dichalcogenide heterobilayers
summary: Moiré transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) heterobilayers are commonly modeled by a continuum theory that yields topologically trivial bands, in contrast to their homobilayer counterparts which host topological bands and fractional Chern insulators (FCI). We show this conclusion is an artifact of neglecting the pseudomagnetic field generated by lattice relaxation, an effect intrinsic to every moiré material. We develop a continuum model that resolves relaxation into three channels: a modified moiré potential with higher Fourier harmonics, a pseudoelectric (scalar deformation) potential, and a pseudomagnetic (vector) potential. Using WSe$_2$/WS$_2$ as a prototype, we find that the pseudomagnetic field alone gaps the third and fourth valence bands with Chern numbers $\pm 1$ over a broad range of twist angle and lattice mismatch, while the moiré potential correction and pseudoelectric potential narrow the bandwidth and enhance the bandgaps, which survive many-body interactions using neural-network variational Monte Carlo calculations. Relaxation also smoothens the Berry curvature and quantum metric relative to the rigid model, moving the band closer to the ideal Chern limit, beneficial for the quantum anomalous Hall effect, FCI states, and flat-band superconductivity when filled to higher bands. Our work establishes a new framework that connects first-principles calculations, through the continuum model, to many-body observables. Using this framework, we show moiré heterobilayers as a new class of topological materials whose topology is driven entirely by intrinsic lattice relaxation.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that topological bands in moiré TMD heterobilayers emerge from lattice relaxation via a pseudomagnetic field, making them topologically nontrivial — contrary to previous continuum models that predicted trivial bands. Using WSe2/WS2, they demonstrate Chern bands survive many-body interactions, establishing heterobilayers as a new class of relaxation-driven topological materials.
AI.motivation: Existing continuum models for moiré TMD heterobilayers yield topologically trivial bands, whereas homobilayers host topological bands and FCI states. The authors argue this discrepancy is an artifact of neglecting the pseudomagnetic field generated by lattice relaxation — an intrinsic effect in all moiré materials.
AI.method: They develop a continuum model that decomposes lattice relaxation into three channels: (1) a modified moiré potential with higher Fourier harmonics, (2) a pseudoelectric (scalar deformation) potential, and (3) a pseudomagnetic (vector) potential. They validate using WSe2/WS2 and many-body calculations via neural-network variational Monte Carlo.
AI.result: The pseudomagnetic field alone opens gaps in the third and fourth valence bands with Chern numbers ±1 across a broad range of twist angles and lattice mismatches. The moiré potential correction and pseudoelectric potential narrow bandwidths and enlarge bandgaps that survive many-body interactions. Relaxation also smooths Berry curvature and quantum metric, moving bands closer to the ideal Chern limit.
AI.conclusion: Moiré heterobilayers are a new class of topological materials whose topology is entirely driven by intrinsic lattice relaxation. The framework bridges first-principles calculations to many-body observables, relevant for quantum anomalous Hall effect, FCI states, and flat-band superconductivity in higher bands.

title: A Dataset of Equilibrium State Configurations of Adsorption in Zeolites
summary: Zeolites are crystalline nanoporous materials widely used in adsorption, separation, and catalytic processes. Molecular simulations are commonly used to predict adsorption properties, but most high-throughput adsorption datasets report only ensemble-averaged quantities such as loadings or isotherms, rather than the molecular configurations from which these averages are obtained. Here, we present AdsZeo, a coordinate-resolved dataset of equilibrium methane adsorption configurations in aluminium-substituted, sodium-containing zeolite frameworks. The processed release contains 4,775 framework realisations derived from 191 zeolite topologies. Each framework realisation was simulated at 13 methane pressures between 0.1 and 100 bar at 298 K using grand canonical Monte Carlo simulations, giving 62,075 production simulations in total. In addition to scalar adsorption records, the dataset stores production-frame methane pseudo-atom coordinates, mobile Na$^+$ cation coordinates, framework atomic coordinates, per-frame loading and energy statistics, and simulation metadata in a processed DuckDB database. The release contains 12,415,000 saved production-frame records and 1,245,376,215 saved particle-coordinate records. AdsZeo provides coordinate-resolved adsorption data across variations in framework topology, aluminium content and distribution, sodium cation arrangement, pressure, and methane loading, enabling reuse for adsorption analysis, spatial statistics, density estimation, and machine-learning models for molecular configuration generation in charged zeolite pores.

AI.tldr: AdsZeo is a coordinate-resolved dataset of equilibrium methane adsorption configurations in aluminium-substituted, sodium-containing zeolites, containing 62,075 GCMC production simulations across 4,775 framework realisations from 191 topologies, with over 1.2 billion saved particle-coordinate records stored in a DuckDB database.
AI.motivation: Most high-throughput adsorption datasets only report ensemble-averaged quantities (loadings, isotherms) rather than the molecular configurations from which these averages are derived, limiting reuse for spatial analysis, density estimation, and machine-learning model training on molecular configurations.
AI.method: Grand canonical Monte Carlo simulations of methane adsorption in aluminium-substituted, sodium-containing zeolites at 13 pressures (0.1-100 bar) at 298 K, across 4,775 framework realisations from 191 zeolite topologies. The dataset stores production-frame coordinates of methane pseudo-atoms, mobile Na+ cations, framework atoms, per-frame loading and energy statistics, and simulation metadata in a processed DuckDB database.
AI.result: 62,075 production simulations, 12,415,000 saved production-frame records, and 1,245,376,215 saved particle-coordinate records, covering variations in framework topology, aluminium content and distribution, sodium cation arrangement, pressure, and methane loading.
AI.conclusion: AdsZeo provides a uniquely coordinate-resolved adsorption dataset enabling reuse for adsorption analysis, spatial statistics, density estimation, and machine-learning models for molecular configuration generation in charged zeolite pores.

title: A Systematic Comparison of q-Gaussian Fitting Methods across Complex Systems
summary:
Nature exhibits a wide variety of nonlinear phenomena characterized by strong fluctuations that push the system away from equilibrium. Recent studies have shown that non-extensive statistics are more suitable for analyzing these phenomena, as they can capture long-range correlations and heavy-tailed distributions that conventional Boltzmann-Gibbs statistics cannot represent. However, estimating the non-extensiveness parameter ($q$) is not trivial, and methods vary significantly across disciplines.
  This paper presents a systematic and interdisciplinary comparison of three fitting methods: direct nonlinear fitting of the probability distribution function (PDF), linearization using the q-logarithm function, and numerical fitting of the cumulative distribution function (CDF). We applied this analysis to various phenomena, from areas such as geophysics, space weather and economics, analyzing the critical impact of discretization. The results show that $q$ estimates are highly sensitive to histogram binning, while the CDF-based method provides a bin-free alternative that yields more stable estimates for the datasets analyzed here. This contribution provides relevant information for the search for a method that allows the correct determination of the parameters of heavy-tailed distributions in various disciplines.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically compares three fitting methods (direct PDF nonlinear fitting, q-logarithm linearization, and CDF numerical fitting) for estimating the non-extensiveness parameter q in heavy-tailed distributions across geophysics, space weather, and economics, finding that q estimates are highly sensitive to histogram binning while the CDF-based bin-free method yields more stable estimates.
AI.motivation: Non-extensive statistics are increasingly used to analyze nonlinear phenomena with strong fluctuations, but estimating the non-extensiveness parameter (q) is non-trivial and methods vary significantly across disciplines. A systematic, interdisciplinary comparison of fitting methods is needed to establish reliable estimation approaches.
AI.method: The authors compare three fitting methods: (1) direct nonlinear fitting of the probability distribution function (PDF), (2) linearization using the q-logarithm function, and (3) numerical fitting of the cumulative distribution function (CDF). These are applied to multiple phenomena from geophysics, space weather, and economics, with particular attention to the impact of histogram discretization/binning on q estimates.
AI.result: The q estimates are highly sensitive to histogram binning when using PDF-based methods. The CDF-based method provides a bin-free alternative that yields more stable and reliable estimates across the datasets analyzed.
AI.conclusion: The CDF-based fitting method offers a more robust approach for determining the non-extensiveness parameter in heavy-tailed distributions, providing relevant guidance for researchers seeking reliable parameter estimation in non-extensive statistical analyses across disciplines.

title: Gradient-based optimization of non-Abelian fractional quantum states in patterned superlattices
summary: The realization of fractional Chern insulator (FCI) states in moiré heterostructures has attracted intense interest in the study of correlated states emerging from topological flat bands. So far, most experimentally realized FCI states may be interpreted as lattice analogues of fractional quantum Hall (FQH) states hosting Abelian anyonic excitations. Realizing non-Abelian FCI states is an important challenge in the field. Patterned dielectric superlattices provide a versatile platform for engineering topological flat bands. Such systems offer substantial structural flexibility and tunability, because their lattice patterns, periods, and other structural parameters can all be designed and fabricated. Here we propose to realize non-Abelian FCI states in patterned dielectric superlattices coupled to bilayer graphene. Specifically, we provide a realistic workflow based on a gradient-descent algorithm to design non-Abelian fractional states in bilayer graphene superlattices. The experimentally relevant structural parameters of the superlattices are gradient-optimized to favor a flat Chern band with quantum-geometric properties reminiscent of those of the first excited Landau level. Exact diagonalization calculations at 1/2 filling of the optimized flat Chern band naturally yield non-Abelian FCI states. We apply this workflow to triangular, honeycomb, and kagome patterned superlattices and find robust non-Abelian FCI states over a large region of the parameter space spanned by the superlattice constant and vertical potential drop. Our work thus establishes an experimentally feasible framework for exploring non-Abelian FCIs in realistic patterned-superlattice devices. It also demonstrates the potential of device-level inverse design to engineer correlated topological matter beyond the Abelian paradigm.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a gradient-descent-based inverse design workflow to realize non-Abelian fractional Chern insulator states in patterned dielectric superlattices coupled to bilayer graphene, demonstrating robust non-Abelian FCIs at 1/2 filling across triangular, honeycomb, and kagome superlattice geometries.
AI.motivation: Most experimentally realized FCI states in moiré heterostructures host Abelian anyonic excitations, while realizing non-Abelian FCI states remains an important open challenge. Patterned dielectric superlattices offer tunable platform for engineering topological flat bands, but how to design them for non-Abelian FCIs is unexplored.
AI.method: The authors use a gradient-descent algorithm to optimize structural parameters of patterned dielectric superlattices coupled to bilayer graphene, targeting a flat Chern band with quantum-geometric properties reminiscent of the first excited Landau level. They perform exact diagonalization at 1/2 filling to verify non-Abelian FCI states, applying the workflow to triangular, honeycomb, and kagome superlattice geometries.
AI.result: The optimized flat Chern bands naturally produce non-Abelian FCI states at 1/2 filling. Robust non-Abelian FCI states are found over a large region of parameter space spanned by the superlattice constant and vertical potential drop across all three investigated superlattice geometries (triangular, honeycomb, and kagome).
AI.conclusion: The work establishes an experimentally feasible framework for exploring non-Abelian FCIs in realistic patterned-superlattice devices and demonstrates device-level inverse design as a powerful approach to engineer correlated topological matter beyond the Abelian paradigm.

title: Energy-efficient spin Hall nano-oscillators using CoGd ferrimagnets
summary: Conventional spin Hall nano-oscillators (SHNOs) based on ferromagnets face practical limitations due to high threshold current densities and large external magnetic field requirements. Ferrimagnets provide an attractive alternative due to their unique magnetic dynamics and potential for energy-efficient spintronic devices. In this study, we report rare-earth-transition-metal (RE-TM) ferrimagnetic SHNOs utilizing Co1-xGdx alloys, in which compositional tuning enables high-performance operation near the magnetization compensation. The optimized SHNO operates at a low current density (1.43*10^7 A/cm^2), a small magnetic field (5 mT), and exhibits a narrow linewidth (0.61 MHz) simultaneously, showing an order-of-magnitude improvement over its ferromagnetic counterparts. This enhanced performance arises from high spin-orbit torque efficiency, low magnetic anisotropy, reduced effective magnetization, and minimized nonlinearity near the compensation point. These results establish RE-TM ferrimagnets as a promising materials platform for next-generation spintronic devices and offer new strategies for realizing energy-efficient, high-performance spintronic oscillators.

AI.tldr: The paper reports rare-earth-transition-metal (RE-TM) ferrimagnetic spin Hall nano-oscillators based on Co1-xGdx alloys that achieve high performance near the magnetization compensation point, operating at a low current density (1.43×10^7 A/cm²), small magnetic field (5 mT), and narrow linewidth (0.61 MHz)—an order of magnitude improvement over ferromagnetic counterparts.
AI.motivation: Conventional ferromagnetic spin Hall nano-oscillators suffer from high threshold current densities and large external magnetic field requirements, limiting their practical applications. Ferrimagnets offer an attractive alternative due to their unique magnetic dynamics and potential for energy-efficient spintronic devices.
AI.method: The authors fabricate RE-TM ferrimagnetic SHNOs using Co1-xGdx alloys and exploit compositional tuning to achieve optimal performance near the magnetization compensation point. The improvement stems from high spin-orbit torque efficiency, low magnetic anisotropy, reduced effective magnetization, and minimized nonlinearity at the compensation point.
AI.result: The optimized SHNO simultaneously achieves a low current density of 1.43×10^7 A/cm², a small magnetic field of 5 mT, and a narrow linewidth of 0.61 MHz—an order-of-magnitude improvement over conventional ferromagnetic SHNOs.
AI.conclusion: RE-TM ferrimagnets represent a promising materials platform for next-generation spintronic devices, offering new strategies for realizing energy-efficient, high-performance spintronic oscillators.

title: Scalene Yang--Baxter triples as a source of hidden symmetries beyond the ordinary Yang--Baxter equation
summary: We study a nearest-neighbor non-Hermitian spin chain obtained from one member of an exact non-braided scalene Yang--Baxter triple. Its local Hamiltonian density violates both the difference-form Reshetikhin condition and its general non-difference counterpart, obstructing its realization by a differentiable homogeneous regular solution of the ordinary Yang--Baxter equation. The transfer matrices constructed from the regular member do not commute among themselves at distinct spectral parameters. Nevertheless, the scalene Yang--Baxter relation implies cross-commutativity with another transfer matrix constructed from the third member of the scalene triple. We evaluate the latter for arbitrary chain length and show that, on even periodic chains, it is a finite generating function of a non-obvious staggered nilpotent symmetry. The resulting conserved hierarchy belongs entirely to the algebra generated by this single symmetry and hence does not constitute an extensive family of algebraically independent charges. Nevertheless, this example demonstrates that scalene Yang--Baxter triples can act as an algebraic symmetry-discovery mechanism beyond the ordinary self-commuting transfer-matrix framework.

AI.tldr: A nearest-neighbor non-Hermitian spin chain from a non-braided scalene Yang-Baxter triple, whose transfer matrices don't commute, nonetheless yields a staggered nilpotent symmetry via cross-commutativity, producing a conserved hierarchy generated by a single symmetry rather than an extensive family of charges.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether scalene Yang-Baxter triples can serve as a symmetry-discovery mechanism beyond the standard self-commuting transfer-matrix framework, particularly for chains whose Hamiltonian densities do not satisfy the Reshetikhin condition and thus cannot be realized by ordinary Yang-Baxter solutions.
AI.method: The authors study a nearest-neighbor non-Hermitian spin chain derived from a non-braided scalene Yang-Baxter triple. They construct transfer matrices from the regular member (which don't commute at distinct spectral parameters) and use the scalene Yang-Baxter relation to show cross-commutativity with a transfer matrix from the third member of the triple. They evaluate this transfer matrix for arbitrary chain length, focusing on even periodic chains.
AI.result: On even periodic chains, the cross-commuting transfer matrix acts as a finite generating function of a non-obvious staggered nilpotent symmetry. The conserved hierarchy generated lies entirely in the algebra of this single symmetry and does not form an extensive family of algebraically independent charges.
AI.conclusion: Despite the lack of an extensive conserved charge family, scalene Yang-Baxter triples provide a valid algebraic mechanism for discovering hidden symmetries (such as the staggered nilpotent symmetry) beyond the reach of ordinary self-commuting transfer matrices.

title: Hyperbolic exciton-plasmon polaritons in MoS$_2$/MoOCl$_2$ van der Waals heterostructures
summary: Polaritons formed by strong coupling between excitons and confined electromagnetic modes underpin emerging nanophotonic technologies, yet platforms based on isotropic metals or optical microcavities provide limited control over propagation direction. Here we predict that monolayer MoS$_2$ on the in-plane hyperbolic conductor MoOCl$_2$ supports hyperbolic exciton-plasmon polaritons governed by crystallographic direction, slab thickness, and hyperbolic mode order. Using an anisotropic transfer-matrix model coupled to a dissipative three-level Hamiltonian, we obtain wavevector-dependent anticrossings between the MoOCl$_2$ plasmons and the spin-orbit-split A and B excitons of MoS$_2$, yielding lower, middle, and upper polariton branches with coupling energies $g_A$ = 64.7 meV and $g_B$ = 61.2 meV. Rotating the in-plane wavevector tunes the plasmon-exciton detuning, while increasing the MoOCl$_2$ thickness activates higher-order hyperbolic Fabry-Pérot modes. Their coupling follows an approximate effective-mode-volume scaling. Strong coupling persists for excitonic linewidths up to 50 meV, with the normalised spectral-resolution ratio remaining above unity. These results establish MoS$_2$/MoOCl$_2$ as a lithography-free platform for directional and multimode exciton-plasmon polariton engineering in the visible spectral range.

AI.tldr: The paper predicts that monolayer MoS2 on the in-plane hyperbolic conductor MoOCl2 supports hyperbolic exciton-plasmon polaritons with directionality controlled by crystallographic orientation, slab thickness, and hyperbolic mode order. Using an anisotropic transfer-matrix model with a dissipative three-level Hamiltonian, the authors find strong coupling between MoOCl2 plasmons and MoS2 A/B excitons with coupling energies of ~62-65 meV, tunable by rotating the in-plane wavevector and increasing MoOCl2 thickness, persisting up to 50 meV excitonic linewidths. This establishes a lithography-free platform for directional multimode polariton engineering in the visible range.
AI.motivation: Existing polariton platforms based on isotropic metals or optical microcavities offer limited control over the propagation direction of polaritons. The authors seek a platform that enables directional and multimode control of exciton-plasmon polaritons, motivating their exploration of hyperbolic conductors coupled to monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides.
AI.method: The study uses an anisotropic transfer-matrix model coupled to a dissipative three-level Hamiltonian to compute the optical response of a monolayer MoS2 on MoOCl2. The model captures wavevector-dependent anticrossings between MoOCl2 plasmons and the spin-orbit-split A and B excitons of MoS2, giving lower, middle, and upper polariton branches. Parameter sweeps examine the role of in-plane wavevector rotation (detuning), MoOCl2 slab thickness (hyperbolic Fabry-Pérot mode order), and excitonic linewidth on coupling strength and strong-coupling criteria.
AI.result: The predicted coupling energies are gA = 64.7 meV and gB = 61.2 meV. Rotating the in-plane wavevector tunes plasmon-exciton detuning, and increasing MoOCl2 thickness activates higher-order hyperbolic Fabry-Pérot modes whose coupling follows an approximate effective-mode-volume scaling. Strong coupling persists for excitonic linewidths up to 50 meV, with the normalized spectral-resolution ratio remaining above unity.
AI.conclusion: The MoS2/MoOCl2 heterostructure is established as a lithography-free platform for directional and multimode exciton-plasmon polariton engineering in the visible spectral range, with control over propagation via crystallographic orientation, slab thickness, and hyperbolic mode order.

title: Pseudo-Distributions: Thermodynamic Geometry and an Empirical Application
summary: We develop a consistent pseudo-analytic framework based on $g$-calculus for constructing deformed statistical distributions. By mapping standard algebraic operations through a monotone generator function, we systematically derive the associated pseudo-logarithmic and pseudo-exponential structures. Applying this formalism, we introduce a new family of pseudo-distributions that generalizes nonextensive statistical mechanics at both the probability density and cumulative distribution levels, recovering classical and standard nonextensive statistics as limiting cases. We investigate the thermodynamic geometry of the proposed models using the Ruppeiner metric on the equilibrium manifold. A perturbative analysis around the classical limit reveals that, to leading order, the thermodynamic scalar curvature is governed solely by the generator deformation parameter, while the nonextensivity parameter remains decoupled. To evaluate the empirical robustness of the framework, we apply the model to analyze the absolute deviations of daily West Texas Intermediate crude oil prices from their hundred-day moving average. Model comparison based on information criteria demonstrates that the proposed pseudo-distributions provide a superior description of these high-frequency financial fluctuations and their heavy-tailed characteristics compared to standard benchmarks. These results suggest that $g$-calculus offers a flexible and physically grounded mathematical tool for generating deformed statistics and analyzing their geometric properties.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a pseudo-analytic framework based on g-calculus to construct deformed statistical distributions, generalizing nonextensive statistical mechanics via monotone generator functions. The proposed pseudo-distributions are analyzed through Ruppeiner thermodynamic geometry and applied to WTI crude oil price deviations, demonstrating superior fit over standard benchmarks.
AI.motivation: To create a systematic and consistent mathematical framework for constructing deformed statistical distributions that generalize nonextensive statistical mechanics, while also linking these distributions to their thermodynamic geometric properties.
AI.method: The framework uses g-calculus, mapping standard algebraic operations through a monotone generator function to derive pseudo-logarithmic and pseudo-exponential structures. This formalism generates a new family of pseudo-distributions at both probability density and cumulative distribution levels. Thermodynamic geometry is studied via the Ruppeiner metric on the equilibrium manifold, with a perturbative expansion around the classical limit. Empirical validation uses daily WTI crude oil absolute deviations from a hundred-day moving average, with model comparison via information criteria.
AI.result: The perturbative analysis shows the thermodynamic scalar curvature is governed solely by the generator deformation parameter to leading order, with the nonextensivity parameter decoupled. The pseudo-distributions outperform standard benchmarks in describing heavy-tailed high-frequency financial fluctuations of WTI crude oil prices based on information criteria.
AI.conclusion: g-calculus provides a flexible and physically grounded tool for generating deformed statistics and analyzing their geometric properties, with practical utility demonstrated in financial econometrics.

title: Phonon-assisted transport and hole-phonon coupling in GaAs double quantum dots
summary: Hole-phonon interactions play an important role in transport and decoherence processes in semiconductor quantum dots. Here we investigate hole-phonon coupling in a gate-defined GaAs double quantum dot integrated with a quantum point contact charge sensor. Under finite source-drain bias, pronounced oscillatory stripe patterns appear near specific charge transition regions in the charge stability diagram. We attribute these oscillations to phonon emission during inelastic interdot tunneling. A theoretical model including piezoelectric hole-phonon coupling reproduces the observed patterns. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the oscillations emerge only in particular charge configurations. Our results provide direct insight into phonon-assisted transport and coherent hole-phonon interactions in semiconductor quantum dots.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates hole-phonon coupling in a gate-defined GaAs double quantum dot with a QPC charge sensor, revealing oscillatory stripe patterns in charge stability diagrams under finite bias that are attributed to phonon emission during inelastic interdot tunneling, confirmed by a piezoelectric hole-phonon coupling model.
AI.motivation: Hole-phonon interactions are crucial for transport and decoherence in semiconductor quantum dots, yet direct experimental insight into phonon-assisted transport and coherent hole-phonon interactions remains limited.
AI.method: A gate-defined GaAs double quantum dot is integrated with a quantum point contact charge sensor. Measurements of the charge stability diagram are performed under finite source-drain bias, and a theoretical model incorporating piezoelectric hole-phonon coupling is used to reproduce and explain the observed oscillatory stripe patterns near specific charge transition regions.
AI.result: Pronounced oscillatory stripe patterns appear near specific charge transition regions in the charge stability diagram under finite bias. These are attributed to phonon emission during inelastic interdot tunneling, and the theoretical model reproduces the observed patterns. The oscillations emerge only in particular charge configurations.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide direct experimental insight into phonon-assisted transport and coherent hole-phonon interactions in semiconductor quantum dots, and reveal configuration-dependent emergence of these coupling signatures.

title: Wrinkling in Selected Polymer Thin Films Induced by Combined Ion Beam and Humidity Exposure
summary: This study investigates ion beam sputtering (IBS)-induced surface wrinkling phenomena in three polymers with varying hydrophilicity: poly-hydroxy-ethyl-methacrylate (pHEMA), poly-4-vinyl pyridine (p4VP), and poly-2,4,6,8-tetramethyl-2,4,6,8-tetravinylcyclotetrasiloxane (pV4D4). It is observed that pHEMA and p4VP films wrinkle only when exposed to ion bombardment and subsequent water vapor exposure. No wrinkling is observed in pV4D4 under these same conditions. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) are performed before IBS, after IBS, and after exposure to humidity. XPS shows that IBS drives chemical changes within the surface layer, creating a graphitized film at the surface. For the polymer films that exhibit wrinkling (pHEMA and p4VP), XPS and FTIR indicate water absorption in both the surface and the bulk of the films, resulting in swelling. We conjecture that the formation of wrinkles arises from this swelling being mechanically constrained by the rigid underlying silicon substrate and the stiff graphitized surface layer. In contrast, the absence of wrinkle formation in pV4D4 under the same experimental conditions can be attributed to its comparatively low water absorption and the correspondingly limited swelling response.

Wrinkling occurs only in hydrophilic polymers (pHEMA and p4VP) after IBS and water vapor exposure. XPS and FTIR reveal that IBS creates a graphitized surface layer, and water absorption causes swelling in the film bulk for wrinkling polymers. The proposed mechanism is that swelling is mechanically constrained by the rigid silicon substrate and stiff graphitized surface, leading to wrinkle formation. pV4D4 does not wrinkle due to its low water absorption and limited swelling.

XPS showed IBS creates a graphitized surface layer. For wrinkling polymers, XPS and FTIR confirmed water absorption in both surface and bulk, causing swelling. The absence of wrinkling in pV4D4 is attributed to its low water absorption and limited swelling.
AI.conclusion: Wrinkle formation in IBS-treated polymer films arises from water-induced swelling that is mechanically constrained between the rigid silicon substrate and the stiff graphitized surface layer. Polymer hydrophilicity governs water uptake and thereby determines whether wrinkling occurs, providing a mechanistic framework for this surface patterning phenomenon.

title: Ensemble-level loopy message passing with generalized-edge closure for percolation
summary: Predicting the percolation threshold of highly clustered networks from local statistics remains difficult, because short loops break the independence assumption underlying tree-like message passing. Existing remedies address loopy connectivity either through prescribed local motifs in random-graph ensembles or through a single network's realized topology, leaving an ensemble-level treatment of arbitrary connectivity patterns absent. Here, we develop a loopy message-passing framework for random clustered graph ensembles based on generalized-edge statistics, which characterize overlap patterns among the neighborhoods of different nodes. This yields a progressively refined approximation scheme based on neighborhoods of increasing size around each node. The low-order approximations recover previous equations for random network ensembles, and the new result that yields refined threshold prediction is developed by the second-order approximation. We show that the effectiveness of this framework depends not only on short-cycle density but also on the internal consistency of generalized edges. To diagnose this effectiveness, we introduce the generalized-edge closure coefficient (GECC) to quantify this consistency. Because GECC is computed entirely from local statistics and does not rely on any percolation calculation, it serves as an a priori diagnostic for the reliability of the approximation. Using synthetic and real networks, the threshold is evaluated via the second-order and lower-order approximations. Comparisons with Monte Carlo simulations show that GECC captures key structural features that strongly affect the percolation threshold. These results establish ensemble-based loopy message passing as an efficient route for predicting the percolation threshold in large clustered networks.

AI.tldr: A loopy message-passing framework for random clustered graph ensembles predicts percolation thresholds using generalized-edge statistics, introducing the generalized-edge closure coefficient (GECC) as an a priori diagnostic for approximation reliability, validated against Monte Carlo simulations on synthetic and real networks.
AI.motivation: Predicting percolation thresholds in highly clustered networks is difficult because short loops break the independence assumptions of tree-like message passing. Existing approaches either prescribe local motifs in random-graph ensembles or rely on a single network's realized topology, leaving no ensemble-level treatment of arbitrary connectivity patterns.
AI.method: The authors develop a loopy message-passing framework for random clustered graph ensembles using generalized-edge statistics that characterize overlap patterns among node neighborhoods. This produces a progressively refined approximation based on increasing neighborhood sizes, with the key threshold prediction arising from a second-order approximation. They introduce the generalized-edge closure coefficient (GECC) as a purely local statistic to diagnose approximation effectiveness. Thresholds are evaluated via second-order and lower-order approximations and compared against Monte Carlo simulations on synthetic and real networks.
AI.result: Low-order approximations recover previous equations for random network ensembles, while the second-order approximation yields refined percolation threshold predictions. The framework's effectiveness depends on both short-cycle density and the internal consistency of generalized edges, as quantified by GECC. Comparisons with Monte Carlo simulations show GECC captures key structural features strongly affecting the percolation threshold.
AI.conclusion: Ensemble-based loopy message passing provides an efficient, generalizable route for predicting percolation thresholds in large clustered networks, with GECC serving as a reliable a priori diagnostic for approximation quality without requiring percolation calculations.

title: Size-Dependent Band-Tail Localization in Oxide Semiconductors Revealed by Direct Density-of-States Mapping
summary: Disorder-induced localization is expected to become increasingly important as amorphous oxide semiconductor transistors are scaled toward low-dimensional channels, yet the electronic states responsible for this transport regime remain difficult to resolve experimentally. Here, we use a lock-in-based electric-field penetration technique to directly map the effective density of states (DOS) in In-based oxide semiconductor thin-film transistors (TFTs). The extracted quantum capacitance, carrier density, and chemical potential reveal a disorder-dominated transport regime in which band-tail states are not merely passive traps, but become screening-active and partially transport-active. Geometry-dependent DOS mapping shows an exponential suppression of the effective DOS with channel length, demonstrating size-dependent band-tail localization and providing a microscopic origin for a distinct localization-induced threshold-voltage roll-off mechanism. Temperature-dependent measurements show that the disorder-dominated DOS is strongly suppressed at low temperatures, while extended diffusive states remain nearly unchanged, confirming the localization origin. By tuning film thickness, O2 annealing, and In/Ga/Zn composition, we further demonstrate systematic suppression of disorder and effective-DOS localization. This work establishes direct DOS mapping as a device-level probe of localization physics and provides a pathway for engineering disorder in low-dimensional oxide semiconductor electronics.

The study shows geometry-dependent exponential suppression of effective DOS with channel length (size-dependent band-tail localization), temperature-dependent suppression of disorder-dominated DOS at low temperatures, and demonstrates systematic suppression of disorder through film thickness, O2 annealing, and composition tuning.

The authors aim to directly probe and map the effective density of states to understand localization physics in these materials.

They extract quantum capacitance, carrier density, and chemical potential. Geometry-dependent DOS mapping was performed as a function of channel length, and temperature-dependent measurements were conducted. title: Altermagnetism-Induced Spin-resolved electronic structure in Janus FeX0.5Y0.5 Monolayers (X, Y = S, Se, Te)
summary: Realizing the spin-resolved electronic properties in superconducting materials stands as a critical frontier, offering both novel fundamental physics and potential for dissipationless spin-based devices. Here, we predict a series of Janus FeX0.5Y0.5 monolayers derived from iron-based superconductors (e.g., FeSe, FeTe, and FeS) by using Kondo-type model and first-principles calculations. These Janus structures exhibit significant spin-splittingelectronic states, large topological band gaps (51.4 meV) and high Néel temperatures (415 K). We further reveal that valley polarization can be effectively tuned via applied in-plane strain and the resulting valley-polarized anomalous Hall conductivity can be manipulated by shifting the Fermi level. Our work suggests a new strategy based on altermagnetism for engineering spin-splitting states in superconducting systems and inspires further exploration of superconducting spintronics.
