AI.motivation: Realizing spin-resolved electronic properties in superconducting materials is a critical frontier for achieving dissipationless spin-based devices. The authors aim to engineer spin-splitting states in superconducting systems by designing novel Janus structures.
AI.method: The authors use Kondo-type model calculations combined with first-principles calculations to predict and characterize Janus FeX0.5Y0.5 monolayers derived from iron-based superconductors (FeSe, FeTe, and FeS).
AI.result: The Janus structures exhibit significant spin-splitting electronic states, large topological band gaps (up to 51.4 meV), and high Néel temperatures (up to 415 K). Valley polarization is effectively tunable via applied in-plane strain, and the resulting valley-polarized anomalous Hall conductivity can be manipulated by shifting the Fermi level.
AI.conclusion: The work suggests a new strategy based on altermagnetism for engineering spin-splitting states in superconducting systems, inspiring further exploration of superconducting spintronics.

title: Polarization engineered all 2D Graphene/Ferroelectric hybrid for persistence-free photoresponse
summary: Graphene-based van der Waals hybrid photodetectors typically work on trap-mediated photogating mechanism, exhibiting high sensitivity, but under-perform in the fast detection of repetitive optical signals. Designing photodetectors that are simultaneously fast and highly sensitive has therefore remained difficult. In this work, we realize both attributes by integrating atomically thin sliding ferroelectrics in the design architecture, thereby uniting semiconducting properties with intrinsic polarization fields capable of efficiently governing interfacial photocarrier dynamics. We report a bilayer graphene-bilayer MoS2 (with MoS2 in a rhombohedrally stacked (3R) configuration) van der Waals photodetector with edge-contacted dual-gated field-effect transistor architecture. The photo-induced modulation in spontaneous out-of-plane polarization of 3R-MoS2 and selective confinement of charge carriers in bilayer graphene under an out-of-plane displacement field results in a tunable persistence-free photoresponse. Here, the photoinduced polarization change in 3R-MoS2 produces an optically controlled gating effect that alters the electrostatic environment of bilayer graphene, resulting in a temperature-independent photoresponse with rapid response times of the order of 10's of milliseconds (limited by the measurement instrument). We demonstrate reproducible detection of optical signals and examine the photon-counting resolution of this structure in high-sensitivity regimes, where we determine its internal quantum efficiency to be 10 percent with minimum detectable photon number of 31 in single shot measurements. This work highlights the functionality of 3R-MoS2 in manipulating the interfacial charge dynamics and establishes the hybrid of graphene and ferroelectric 3R-MoS2 as a promising platform for ultra-sensitive optoelectronic devices.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates a bilayer graphene-bilayer 3R-MoS2 van der Waals hybrid photodetector that achieves both high sensitivity and fast response times by leveraging the intrinsic polarization of sliding ferroelectric MoS2. The device exhibits a tunable persistence-free photoresponse (~10 ms, instrument-limited), a temperature-independent response, an internal quantum efficiency of 10%, and a minimum detectable photon number of 31 in single-shot measurements.
AI.motivation: Conventional graphene-based van der Waals hybrid photodetectors rely on trap-mediated photogating, which provides high sensitivity but suffers from slow response to repetitive optical signals. Achieving simultaneous high sensitivity and fast response in a single photodetector has remained a fundamental challenge.
AI.method: The authors integrate atomically thin sliding ferroelectric 3R-stacked bilayer MoS2 with bilayer graphene in an edge-contacted dual-gated field-effect transistor architecture. The photoinduced modulation of the spontaneous out-of-plane polarization in 3R-MoS2, combined with selective charge carrier confinement in bilayer graphene under an out-of-plane displacement field, produces an optically controlled gating effect that yields a persistence-free photoresponse.
AI.result: The device achieves rapid response times on the order of tens of milliseconds (limited by the measurement instrument), a temperature-independent photoresponse, reproducible detection of optical signals, an internal quantum efficiency of 10%, and a minimum detectable photon number of 31 in single-shot measurements at high sensitivity.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes that 3R-MoS2 can effectively manipulate interfacial charge dynamics in van der Waals heterostructures, and positions the graphene/ferroelectric 3R-MoS2 hybrid as a promising platform for ultra-sensitive optoelectronic devices that are both fast and highly sensitive.

title: Self-induced crystalline fluctuation spin-glass state in Mn7C3 binary compounds
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures, 3 supplementary figures, 2 supplementary tables
summary: Crystalline spin glasses are attractive compounds owing to their unique nature and applications. Here, we synthesised a bulk Pnma-type Mn7C3 spin glass by a high-temperature, high-pressure method. Experimental characterisation including X-ray diffraction and magnetic susceptibility measurements demonstrated that the compound has a triangular Ising-model-based structure, high freezing temperature of 37.4 K, and novel competition mechanism. Theoretical calculations and simulations revealed that the triangular Mn units are spontaneously frustrated and bridge neighbouring Mn units via polarised C atoms and messenger Mn atoms. Triangular C units each share one electron within a three-pronged electron cloud. This electron is the direct cause of frustration and competition in Mn7C3. The competition within the triangular Mn units suggests that the possible magnetic configurations are highly degenerate and that the Mn7C3 spin glass has high robustness. This work introduces a new family of spin glasses with ordered microgeometries that drive electronic structure disorder, and an application-friendly spin-glass material for use in fields like high-efficiency hardware and algorithm design in artificial intelligence.

This material exhibits a triangular Ising-model structure with a high freezing temperature of 37.4 K and a novel competition mechanism. Theoretical work reveals that spontaneous frustration arises from triangular Mn units bridged by polarised C atoms and messenger Mn atoms, with shared electrons in triangular C units being the root cause of frustration. The resulting highly degenerate magnetic configurations confer high robustness, introducing a new family of spin glasses with ordered microgeometries driving electronic disorder, with potential applications in AI hardware and algorithm design.
AI.motivation: To discover and synthesize new crystalline spin-glass materials with unique properties (high freezing temperature, novel frustration mechanisms) that are application-friendly for fields such as high-efficiency hardware and AI algorithm design.
AI.method: High-temperature, high-pressure synthesis of bulk Pnma-type Mn7C3; experimental characterisation via X-ray diffraction and magnetic susceptibility measurements; combined theoretical calculations and simulations to investigate the electronic structure, frustration mechanisms, and magnetic configuration degeneracy.
AI.result: Mn7C3 was successfully synthesized as a bulk crystalline spin glass with a triangular Ising-model structure, a high freezing temperature of 37.4 K, and a novel competition mechanism. Triangular Mn units exhibit spontaneous frustration, bridged by polarised C atoms and messenger Mn atoms; each triangular C unit shares one electron within a three-pronged electron cloud, which is the direct cause of frustration and competition. The highly degenerate magnetic configurations indicate high robustness of the spin glass.
AI.conclusion: This work introduces a new family of spin glasses characterized by ordered microgeometries that drive electronic structure disorder, offering a promising application-friendly spin-glass material for high-efficiency hardware and AI algorithm design.

title: Magnetically induced Circular Photogalvanic Effect in Symmetric Two-dimensional Materials
summary: Photocurrents that depend on the helicity of the incident light can be generated in both bulk and low-dimensional materials lacking inversion symmetry, known as the circular photogalvanic effect (CPGE). We propose that by employing a magnetic effect, the limitation on the inversion symmetry broken materials can be overcome, such that helicity-dependent photocurrent can be generated in a symmetric material, i.e., a magneto-circular photogalvanic effect (MCPGE). As a proof of principle, we elucidate the mechanism of such an MCPGE through an effective Hamiltonian of a monolayer SbH on a magnetic substrate with an adjustable magnetization. Moreover, the associated response in optical absorption is analyzed, both single-particle and excitonic, through a Bethe-Salpeter equation to describe the Coulomb interaction in excitons. Our result broadens the mechanism of CPGE and opens new opportunities for optoelectronic devices.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a novel magneto-circular photogalvanic effect (MCPGE) that enables helicity-dependent photocurrent generation in inversion-symmetric materials by leveraging magnetism, demonstrated theoretically using a monolayer SbH on a magnetic substrate, with analysis of both single-particle and excitonic optical absorption via the Bethe-Salpeter equation.
AI.motivation: The conventional circular photogalvanic effect (CPGE) requires materials lacking inversion symmetry, which limits its application. The authors aim to overcome this restriction by introducing a magnetic mechanism that allows helicity-dependent photocurrents to be generated even in symmetric materials.
AI.method: The mechanism is demonstrated through an effective Hamiltonian model of a monolayer SbH on a magnetic substrate with adjustable magnetization. Optical absorption responses are analyzed at both single-particle and excitonic levels, with the Bethe-Salpeter equation used to incorporate Coulomb interactions between electrons and holes in excitons.
AI.result: The MCPGE is shown to produce helicity-dependent photocurrents in a symmetric material (monolayer SbH on a magnetic substrate), thereby extending the CPGE mechanism. The optical absorption response, including excitonic effects, is characterized within this framework.
AI.conclusion: The work broadens the underlying mechanism of the CPGE by introducing magnetism as a symmetry-breaking alternative to inversion symmetry breaking, opening new possibilities for optoelectronic device applications.

title: Multitask Scanning Probe Microscopy
summary: Scanning probe microscopy provides nanoscale access to structural, electrical, electromechanical, magnetic, and mechanical properties of materials. Its increasing use for wafer-scale characterization and combinatorial materials exploration creates a need to distribute measurements efficiently across large spatial domains. This is particularly important when available modalities differ in acquisition time and potential for tip and sample damage, making exhaustive multimodal mapping over spatial grids impractical. Here, we demonstrate multitask scanning probe microscopy, a live, closed-loop workflow in which a multitask Gaussian process learns spatial and cross-modal relationships and autonomously selects both the next measurement location and the next experimental protocol. The approach is implemented on an automated large-sample atomic force microscope and demonstrated on a composition-spread AlScN wafer using tapping-mode and Dual AC Resonance Tracking (DART) measurements. Paired initial measurements establish the relation between the tasks, after which noncoincident measurements are used to update both response landscapes. The resulting workflow extends active learning in scanning probe microscopy from spatial sampling to autonomous allocation of measurement modalities and provides a basis for combining rapid, weakly perturbative imaging with slower contact, electrical, electromechanical, magnetic, or spectroscopic measurements.

AI.tldr: This paper presents multitask scanning probe microscopy (SPM), a closed-loop workflow where a multitask Gaussian process learns both spatial and cross-modal relationships to autonomously select both the next measurement location and the next experimental protocol. Implemented on an automated large-sample atomic force microscope and demonstrated on a composition-spread AlScN wafer using tapping-mode and Dual AC Resonance Tracking measurements, this approach extends active learning from spatial sampling to autonomous allocation of measurement modalities.
AI.motivation: As scanning probe microscopy is increasingly used for wafer-scale characterization and combinatorial materials exploration, exhaustive multimodal mapping over spatial grids becomes impractical due to differing acquisition times and potentially damaging modalities across spatial domains.
AI.method: A live, closed-loop multitask Gaussian process learns spatial and cross-modal relationships, autonomously selecting both the next measurement location and the next experimental protocol. Paired initial measurements establish the relation between tasks, after which noncoincident measurements update both response landscapes. The workflow is implemented on an automated large-sample AFM using tapping-mode and DART measurements on an AlScN composition-spread wafer.
AI.result: The workflow successfully demonstrated autonomous allocation of measurement modalities during atomic force microscopy characterization, enabling efficient distribution of measurements across large spatial domains while combining rapid, weakly perturbative imaging with slower contact/electrical/electromechanical/magnetic/spectroscopic measurements.
AI.conclusion: This approach extends active learning in scanning probe microscopy from spatial sampling alone to autonomous allocation of measurement modalities, providing a basis for combining rapid imaging with slower, potentially damaging measurement protocols in large-area characterization.

title: Parity-Resolved Quantum Capacitance and Quantum Inductance in Topological, Trivial, and Normal Nanowire Interferometers
summary: Quantum-capacitance measurements convert the curvature of a quantum-dot energy in a flux-threaded nanowire loop into fast parity-sensitive signals and, therefore, have become a promising readout tool for Majorana devices. However, Majorana-like quantum-capacitance responses can also arise from topologically trivial Andreev bound states, making capacitance alone insufficient to identify a topological phase. To analyze this problem, we consider a quantum dot coupled to both ends of four nanowire realizations: a topological nanowire hosting Majorana bound states, non-topological superconducting nanowires hosting one or two Andreev bound states, and a fully normal nanowire. Motivated by proposals to use quantum inductance as an additional phase-sensitive probe, we compute both the parity-resolved quantum capacitance $C_\mathrm{Q}$ and inverse quantum inductance $L_\mathrm{Q}^{-1}$ as functions of the magnetic flux by exact diagonalization. We show that signatures associated with zero-energy Majorana bound states, such as $h/e$ periodicity and an $h/(2e)$ flux shift between even and odd parity sectors in $C_\mathrm{Q}$ and $L_\mathrm{Q}^{-1}$, are not sufficient indicators of topological superconductivity. In certain realistic parameter regimes, similar Majorana-like behavior can arise from a trivial Andreev bound state and even from a purely normal nanowire. By contrast, two nearly zero-energy Andreev bound states can generate a pronounced $h/(2 e)$-periodic component associated with charge-$2e$ transfer, providing a clear non-Majorana signature. A low-energy projection shows that the Majorana, single-Andreev-state, and normal cases can be mapped onto the same minimal low-energy model explaining their similar flux-dependent responses despite their different physical origins.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes whether quantum-capacitance and quantum-inductance measurements can reliably distinguish topological Majorana bound states from trivial Andreev bound states in quantum-dot coupled nanowire loops. Using exact diagonalization on four nanowire realizations, the authors show that Majorana-like signatures (h/e periodicity and h/(2e) parity shifts) can also arise from trivial Andreev states and even normal nanowires, but that two nearly zero-energy Andreev bound states produce a distinct h/(2e)-periodic charge-2e signature. A low-energy projection reveals all cases map onto the same minimal model, explaining their similar responses.
AI.motivation: Quantum-capacitance measurements are a promising parity-sensitive readout for Majorana devices, but Majorana-like capacitance responses can also come from topologically trivial Andreev bound states, making capacitance alone insufficient to identify topological phases. The paper aims to investigate whether additional phase-sensitive probes (quantum inductance) can resolve this ambiguity.
AI.method: The authors compute parity-resolved quantum capacitance C_Q and inverse quantum inductance L_Q^{-1} as functions of magnetic flux via exact diagonalization for a quantum dot coupled to both ends of four nanowire configurations: a topological Majorana nanowire, non-topological superconducting nanowires with one or two Andreev bound states, and a fully normal nanowire. A low-energy effective model projection is also used to explain similarities between cases.
AI.result: Majorana-like signatures (h/e periodicity and h/(2e) flux shifts between even and odd parity sectors in both C_Q and L_Q^{-1}) are not sufficient indicators of topological superconductivity. These behaviors can also be reproduced by trivial Andreev bound states and even a purely normal nanowire in certain realistic parameter regimes. However, two nearly zero-energy Andreev bound states generate a pronounced h/(2e)-periodic component from charge-2e transfer, offering a clear non-Majorana fingerprint.
AI.conclusion: Capacitance and inductance measurements alone cannot unambiguously identify topological Majorana phases, since Majorana, single-Andreev-state, and normal cases map onto the same minimal low-energy model. The presence of a strong h/(2e)-periodic charge-2e signature from two Andreev bound states can serve as a distinguishing non-Majorana indicator, but further discriminative probes are needed for reliable topological identification.

title: All-Electron Single-Atom Reference Correction for Absolute Transition Energies in Fixed-Reference PAW-XCH Calculations
summary: The transition energy of a core-loss spectrum comprises a transferable atomic core-reference contribution and a material-dependent response that determines chemical shifts. Density functional theory calculations commonly underestimate absolute transition energies. In VASP, the same PAW dataset is used for the ground and core-excited occupations, retaining the ground-state atomic reference when the core occupation changes and thereby omitting the associated all-electron atomic reference change. We evaluate this change using self-consistent single-atom calculations and construct a residual atomic reference correction from the valence reference change and isolated-atom total-energy response. Comparisons with an independent ultrasoft-pseudopotential implementation demonstrate numerical consistency of the all-electron reference for K, L1, and L2,3 core holes, while representative corrected spectra approach the experimental absolute energy scale. For a fixed element, edge, and core-hole scheme, the atomic reference terms cancel from energy differences, showing that same-element chemical shifts are governed by the double difference of the supercell total energy. At the Al and Si L2,3 edges, the near-edge spectral shape additionally depends strongly on the PAW representation of low-lying 3d-like unoccupied states.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the systematic underestimation of absolute transition energies in density functional theory (DFT) core-loss spectra calculations using the PAW method in VASP. The authors identify that using the same PAW dataset for ground and core-excited occupations omits an all-electron atomic reference change, and they construct a residual atomic reference correction from valence reference changes and isolated-atom total-energy responses. The correction is validated against an independent ultrasoft-pseudopotential implementation for K, L1, and L2,3 core holes, bringing corrected spectra near experimental absolute energies. They also show that same-element chemical shifts are governed by the double difference of supercell total energies, and that Al/Si L2,3 near-edge spectral shapes depend strongly on the PAW representation of 3d-like unoccupied states.
AI.motivation: DFT calculations of core-loss spectra systematically underestimate absolute transition energies, which limits their direct comparison with experiments. The authors aim to understand and correct the source of this error in the PAW implementation within VASP, specifically the omission of the all-electron atomic reference change when core occupations are modified.
AI.method: The authors evaluate the atomic reference change using self-consistent single-atom calculations and construct a residual atomic reference correction combining the valence reference change and the isolated-atom total-energy response. They validate this correction against an independent ultrasoft-pseudopotential implementation and test the formalism across K, L1, and L2,3 core holes, as well as Al and Si L2,3 edges.
AI.result: The residual atomic reference correction demonstrates numerical consistency with an independent ultrasoft-pseudopotential implementation for K, L1, and L2,3 core holes. Corrected spectra approach the experimental absolute energy scale. For fixed element, edge, and core-hole scheme, atomic reference terms cancel from energy differences, confirming that same-element chemical shifts are controlled by double differences of supercell total energies. The near-edge spectral shape at Al and Si L2,3 edges depends strongly on how low-lying 3d-like unoccupied states are represented in the PAW dataset.

The work also highlights the importance of PAW dataset quality for describing unoccupied states in near-edge spectral shapes.

title: Noisy Braiding of Majorana Modes: A Comparison of Nanowire Trijunction and Quantum-Dot-Assisted Architectures
summary: Majorana zero modes have emerged as one of the most promising platforms for topological quantum computation, since their non-Abelian braiding statistics allow quantum information to be encoded nonlocally and manipulated through braiding operations that are, in principle, protected against local perturbations. In practice, however, a braid is only as robust as its physical implementation: finite-time operation, residual couplings, and environmental noise can all convert local excitations into logical errors during the exchange process. Here, we address this question through a microscopic comparison of two representative braiding architectures, a nanowire trijunction and a quantum-dot-assisted setup, simulating the full time-dependent Bogoliubov--de Gennes dynamics under both noiseless and noisy conditions. We show that the dot-assisted architecture consistently achieves a lower error over a shorter timescale than the trijunction, owing to its more localized exchange mechanism. This advantage persists in the presence of noise, and a spatially resolved analysis further reveals that, in the dot-assisted geometry, fast noise localized on the dot produces a smaller error than equivalent noise on the wires, whereas slow, quasi-static noise on the dot becomes the dominant limitation. Taken together, these findings link the different error contributions directly to device geometry, pointing to concrete design principles for noise-resilient Majorana-based quantum gates.

AI.tldr: The paper microscopically compares two Majorana braiding architectures—a nanowire trijunction and a quantum-dot-assisted setup—via full time-dependent Bogoliubov-de Gennes simulations under noiseless and noisy conditions, finding that the dot-assisted architecture achieves lower error over shorter timescales due to a more localized exchange mechanism, with noise resilience depending on noise localization and device geometry.
AI.motivation: While Majorana zero modes promise topologically protected quantum computation through non-Abelian braiding, practical braiding implementations suffer from errors induced by finite-time operation, residual couplings, and environmental noise. Understanding how different braiding architectures perform under realistic conditions is essential for designing robust topological quantum gates.
AI.method: The authors perform a microscopic comparison of two braiding architectures—a nanowire trijunction and a quantum-dot-assisted setup—by simulating the full time-dependent Bogoliubov-de Gennes dynamics under both noiseless and noisy conditions, including spatially resolved noise analysis.
AI.result: The dot-assisted architecture consistently achieves lower braiding error over a shorter timescale than the trijunction due to its more localized exchange mechanism. This advantage persists under noise. Spatially resolved analysis shows that fast noise on the dot produces smaller errors than equivalent noise on wires, while slow quasi-static noise on the dot becomes the dominant limitation.
AI.conclusion: The findings link different error contributions directly to device geometry, pointing to concrete design principles for creating noise-resilient Majorana-based quantum gates.

title: Machine-learning octet $AB$-type binary compounds across chemical space with domain knowledge of the interatomic bond
summary: The prediction of the structural stability of octet $AB$-type binary compounds is a classical materials informatics problem. The challenge is to capture the relative stability of 4-fold coordinated atoms in zincblende ($β$-ZnS) structure and 6-fold coordinated atoms in rocksalt (NaCl) structure, modulated by charge transfer and atomic-size differences. Previous structure maps and machine-learning approaches used atomic features such as valence-electron count, ionization potential and atomic radii, using either physical intuition or symbolic regression. Here, we demonstrate that explicitly incorporating the domain knowledge of the interatomic bonds can significantly and systematically improve the prediction of $β$-ZnS/NaCl stability. We encode this bonding information through a coarse-grained representation of the local electronic structure obtained by a recursive solution of a tight-binding bond model. The underlying pairwise Hamiltonians are taken from downfolded eigenstates of density-functional theory calculations for diatomic molecules and thereby include domain knowledge of the bond between specific $A-B$ pairs. The benefit of this description is demonstrated with an ensemble of independently trained Kernel Ridge or symbolic regression models combined with sequential feature selection. The obtained models are compared to a previous symbolic-regression model using the same set of \emph{ab initio} calculations for octet binaries as training data. We find a significant improvement in the prediction of the formation energy difference of $AB$ compounds as compared to previous works and demonstrate that an increasing amount of bond-informed recursion features improves the predictive accuracy.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a bond-informed machine-learning approach for predicting the relative stability of octet AB-type binary compounds between zincblende and rocksalt structures. By encoding chemical bonding information through a coarse-grained tight-binding bond model derived from density-functional theory, the authors show significant improvement over previous structure maps and symbolic regression models using atomic features alone.
AI.motivation: Predicting structural stability of octet AB-type binary compounds (zincblende vs. rocksalt) is a classical materials informatics problem. Previous approaches relied on atomic features like valence-electron count, ionization potential, and atomic radii, but failed to explicitly incorporate interatomic bonding information, limiting predictive accuracy.
AI.method: The method explicitly incorporates domain knowledge of interatomic bonds via a coarse-grained representation of local electronic structure, obtained by a recursive solution of a tight-binding bond model. Pairwise Hamiltonians are derived from downfolded eigenstates of DFT calculations for diatomic molecules, capturing A-B bond-specific domain knowledge. Models are built using ensembles of independently trained Kernel Ridge or symbolic regression models combined with sequential feature selection.
AI.result: The bond-informed models significantly improve prediction of the formation energy difference of AB compounds compared to previous symbolic-regression models using the same ab initio training data. Increasing the amount of bond-informed recursion features systematically improves predictive accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly incorporating interatomic bonding information through a recursive tight-binding representation systematically enhances the predictive capability of machine-learning models for structural stability of octet binary compounds, outperforming previous atomic-feature-based approaches.

title: Quantum sensing composite excitations in an anisotropic ferromagnet via a qubit
summary: Ordered magnets harbor intrinsically squeezed ground states and magnonic excitations characterized by entanglement between spins and nonclassical magnon number composition. A pathway to detecting the superpositions of noneigenmode magnon number states underlying these nonclassical magnetic ground states has recently been demonstrated by utilizing a qubit coupled to the magnon mode via a direct dispersive interaction. Here, we theoretically develop this qubit spectroscopy further delineating the capabilities and limitations of this qubit spectroscopy for sensing the quantum superpositions that underlie the excited states. We demonstrate that the spectroscopy lends itself naturally to unraveling the superpositions that underlie the various quantized squeezed-magnon number states. However, excited states comprising superpositions of multiple squeezed Fock states become increasingly hard due to the large number of possible transitions, and resulting peaks, in the qubit spectroscopy thereby requiring qubits with narrower linewidths. Along the same lines, we theoretically demonstrate the qubit spectroscopy of a low amplitude coherent squeezed-magnon state analyzing the tradeoff between frequency crowding due to multiple transitions and peak linewidths. Our work lays the groundwork and design equations for deploying high-quality qubits towards sensing the composite nature of spin excitations in magnetic systems.

AI.tldr: This paper theoretically develops and analyzes qubit spectroscopy as a tool for detecting quantum superpositions of magnon number states in ordered magnets, demonstrating its capability to unravel squeezed-magnon number states while identifying limitations for complex superpositions and tradeoffs between frequency crowding and linewidth requirements.
AI.motivation: Ordered magnets possess intrinsically quantum ground states with nonclassical magnon number composition. A qubit coupled to magnon modes via dispersive interaction has been demonstrated as a pathway to detect superpositions of noneigenmode magnon number states. This work aims to further develop this qubit spectroscopy to understand its capabilities and limitations for sensing the quantum superpositions underlying excited states in magnetic systems.
AI.method: The authors theoretically develop qubit spectroscopy for detecting quantum superpositions in magnonic excitations. They analyze the spectroscopy applied to various quantized squeezed-magnon number states, study excited states composed of superpositions of multiple squeezed Fock states, and examine the spectroscopy of a low-amplitude coherent squeezed-magnon state. They analyze the tradeoff between frequency crowding from multiple transitions and peak linewidths requiring narrower qubit linewidths.
AI.result: The qubit spectroscopy naturally unravels superpositions underlying quantized squeezed-magnon number states. However, excited states with superpositions of multiple squeezed Fock states become increasingly difficult to resolve due to the large number of possible transitions and resulting spectral peaks, requiring qubits with narrower linewidths. For low-amplitude coherent squeezed-magnon states, a tradeoff exists between frequency crowding due to multiple transitions and peak linewidths.
AI.conclusion: The work lays groundwork and provides design equations for deploying high-quality qubits toward sensing the composite nature of spin excitations in magnetic systems.

title: Long-range exchange interaction controls the fine structure of excited trion states in semiconductor quantum dots
summary: We develop a microscopic theory of the long-range electron-hole exchange interaction in charged excitons (trions) confined in semiconductor quantum dots. While the ground-state singlet trion remains degenerate in the spin component of unpaired charge carrier by time-reversal symmetry, excited trion states exhibit a rich fine structure resulting from the interplay of electron-electron and electron-hole exchange interactions. We derive the effective long-range exchange Hamiltonian for both the spin-$3/2$ heavy-hole and a simple spin-$1/2$ valence band models. The long-range exchange interaction mixes singlet and triplet trion configurations, giving rise to anisotropic fine-structure splittings and related polarization-dependent optical spectra determined by the quantum-dot shape. Analytical expressions are obtained for the long-range exchange parameters. The developed theory establishes a unified microscopic description of the fine structure of excited trions in semiconductor quantum dots and provides a framework for interpreting polarization-resolved optical spectroscopy of charged excitonic complexes.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a microscopic theory of long-range electron-hole exchange interaction in charged excitons (trions) confined in semiconductor quantum dots, deriving an effective exchange Hamiltonian that explains the fine structure of excited trion states and its polarization-dependent optical signatures.
AI.motivation: To establish a unified microscopic description of the fine structure of excited trions in semiconductor quantum dots, which arises from the interplay of electron-electron and electron-hole exchange interactions, and to enable interpretation of polarization-resolved optical spectroscopy of charged excitonic complexes.
AI.method: The authors derive the effective long-range exchange Hamiltonian for both spin-3/2 heavy-hole and spin-1/2 valence band models, obtaining analytical expressions for the long-range exchange parameters, and analyze how the exchange interaction mixes singlet and triplet trion configurations.
AI.result: The ground-state singlet trion remains degenerate by time-reversal symmetry, while excited trion states exhibit anisotropic fine-structure splittings from the long-range exchange interaction, with polarization-dependent optical spectra determined by quantum-dot shape.
AI.conclusion: The theory provides a unified microscopic framework for the fine structure of trions in quantum dots and serves as a foundation for interpreting polarization-resolved optical spectroscopy of charged excitonic systems.

title: Time-resolved study of carbonization and growth of ultrathin 3C-SiC on Si(111) under ultra-high vacuum
summary: The early-stage formation of silicon carbide (SiC) on Si(111) by ethylene exposure under ultra-high vacuum (UHV) was investigated to resolve the time-dependent chemical and morphological evolution of an ultrathin layer. Clean Si(111) substrates were exposed to C$_2$H$_4$ at 800 °C for 2 min to 4 h, and the surfaces followed by in-situ X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and ex-situ AFM, SEM, AES, SIMS and TEM. Si 2p and C 1s peak analysis shows the progressive conversion of elemental silicon into a carbidic Si-C phase, the SiC fraction overtaking the elemental component between 120 and 160 min and saturating near 80-81% beyond 180 min, leaving about 19-20% residual elemental silicon. Correlative SEM and AFM reveal a parallel morphological progression, from sparse isolated islands to a coalesced, near-continuous layer. AES depth profiling confirms carbon incorporated into the near-surface region rather than weakly adsorbed as contamination, assigning the islands to early SiC nuclei. TEM confirms the zinc-blende lattice and the presence of cubic silicon carbide (3C-SiC). Together, these results provide a time-resolved picture of SiC nucleation, coalescence and layer growth on Si(111), relevant to 3C-SiC heteroepitaxy, and can be utilized in the optimization of SiC/Si(111) templates for growth of III-nitride and other carbide systems on silicon (e.g. Mo$_2$C).

AI.tldr: This study investigates the time-dependent evolution of ultrathin silicon carbide layers formed on Si(111) by ethylene exposure at 800°C under UHV, revealing progressive conversion of elemental silicon into carbidic SiC (saturating ~80-81% after ~180 min), with morphological progression from isolated islands to a near-continuous layer, confirming 3C-SiC formation via multi-technique analysis.
AI.motivation: To resolve the time-dependent chemical and morphological evolution of ultrathin SiC layers formed on Si(111), which is critical for optimizing 3C-SiC heteroepitaxy and SiC/Si(111) templates for subsequent growth of III-nitride and other carbide systems on silicon.
AI.method: Clean Si(111) substrates were exposed to C2H4 at 800°C for 2 min to 4 h under UHV, then characterized by in-situ XPS (Si 2p and C 1s peak analysis) for chemical speciation, and ex-situ AFM, SEM, AES, SIMS and TEM for morphology, depth profiling, and crystallography.
AI.result: XPS shows progressive conversion of elemental Si into carbidic SiC, with the SiC fraction surpassing the elemental component between 120-160 min and saturating near 80-81% beyond 180 min (leaving ~19-20% residual elemental Si). Correlative SEM/AFM show morphological progression from sparse isolated islands to a coalesced, near-continuous layer. AES depth profiling confirms carbon incorporation into the near-surface region (not surface contamination), and TEM confirms zinc-blende 3C-SiC lattice structure.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a time-resolved picture of SiC nucleation, coalescence and layer growth on Si(111), offering insights relevant to 3C-SiC heteroepitaxy and enabling optimization of SiC/Si(111) templates for III-nitride and other carbide systems on silicon (e.g., Mo2C).

title: Buried germanium quantum well proximitised by magnetic field-resilient superconducting platinum iridium germanosilicide
summary: Hybrid superconductor-semiconductor systems provide a versatile platform for quantum technologies, ranging from superconducting-spin interfaces to topological quantum devices. Progress toward scalable implementations requires superconductors that exhibit high critical fields ($>1$T) at accessible temperatures integrated with low-disorder semiconductor heterostructures. Here we demonstrate a superconducting platinum iridium germanosilicide (PtIrSiGe), with critical out-of-plane magnetic field up to $B_{\perp} = 1.9$T and critical temperature of $T_c\sim 1.85$K, integrated with planar germanium with mobility $μ= 1.3\times 10^6$cm$^{2}$/Vs via top-down lithography fabrication. We show that the integrity of the germanium quantum well and mobility and density of the 2D hole gas are preserved despite annealing at $500°$C, a temperature comparable to that used for strained germanium epitaxy. We further demonstrate proximitisation of a buried germanium quantum well in a gate-defined Josephson junction/SQUID on a Ge/SiGe heterostructure.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates a superconducting platinum iridium germanosilicide (PtIrSiGe) with high critical out-of-plane magnetic field (1.9T) and critical temperature (~1.85K), integrated with high-mobility planar germanium, preserving the quantum well integrity and demonstrating proximitised gate-defined Josephson junctions/SQUIDs.
AI.motivation: Progress toward scalable hybrid superconductor-semiconductor quantum technologies requires superconductors with high critical fields (>1T) at accessible temperatures that can be integrated with low-disorder semiconductor heterostructures.
AI.method: Demonstration of a superconducting PtIrSiGe material with B_perp = 1.9T and Tc ~1.85K, integrated with planar Ge (mobility 1.3x10^6 cm2/Vs) via top-down lithography, with 500°C annealing, and proximitisation of a buried Ge quantum well in a gate-defined Josephson junction/SQUID on a Ge/SiGe heterostructure.
AI.result: PtIrSiGe exhibits B_perp = 1.9T and Tc ~1.85K; the germanium quantum well integrity, mobility, and 2D hole gas density are preserved after 500°C annealing; proximitisation of a buried Ge quantum well is demonstrated in a Josephson junction/SQUID.
AI.conclusion: PtIrSiGe is a viable superconductor for integration with germanium-based semiconductor heterostructures for scalable quantum technology applications.

title: A spin-bond theory unifying non-relativistic spin splitting and emergent spin-orbit textures
summary: Magnetic order with vanishing net magnetization can produce non-relativistic spin-split bands, broadly categorized into even-parity altermagnets and odd-parity \(p\)-wave magnets. Here, we introduce a spin-bond theory that unifies these seemingly distinct phenomena into a single algebraic framework. We demonstrate that non-relativistic spin textures are fundamentally governed by two components of the electronic bond: unitary spin phases and Hermitian spin amplitudes. The unitary sector generates odd-parity p-wave and emergent spin-orbit-like textures, while the Hermitian sector generates even-parity spin fields, including the uniform \(Γ\)-split and bond-structured altermagnetic limits. Beyond unifying known phases, our theory uncovers a mixed non-commuting regime that emerges when the unitary and Hermitian sectors fail to commute, revealing an underlying non-commuting spin-bond structure. This regime generates a non-coplanar spin texture characterized by an even-in-momentum transverse spin polarization, providing a direct spectroscopic fingerprint for spin- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. Furthermore, we establish that this synthetic spin-orbit coupling can be dynamically tuned by geometrically controlling the non-commutation of the bond sectors. By providing a microscopic foundation for such tuning, our theory paves the way for advanced applications, including field-free spin qubits.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a spin-bond theory that unifies even-parity altermagnets and odd-parity p-wave magnets into a single algebraic framework. It shows that non-relativistic spin textures are governed by unitary spin phases and Hermitian spin amplitudes, and uncovers a novel non-commuting regime that produces a non-coplanar spin texture with an even-in-momentum transverse spin polarization—a spectroscopic fingerprint observable via spin-resolved ARPES, with potential applications in field-free spin qubits.
AI.motivation: To unify two seemingly distinct classes of magnetic orders—even-parity altermagnets and odd-parity p-wave magnets—that both produce non-relativistic spin-split bands via magnetic order with vanishing net magnetization, and to reveal deeper underlying principles governing these phenomena.
AI.method: The authors develop a spin-bond theory that decomposes the electronic bond into two components: unitary spin phases (generating odd-parity p-wave and emergent spin-orbit-like textures) and Hermitian spin amplitudes (generating even-parity spin fields such as uniform Γ-split and bond-structured altermagnetic limits). The theory also identifies and analyzes a mixed non-commuting regime where these two sectors fail to commute.
AI.result: The theory unifies known magnetic spin-split phases and uncovers a novel non-commuting regime producing non-coplanar spin textures with even-in-momentum transverse spin polarization, providing a direct spectroscopic fingerprint for spin- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. It also demonstrates that this synthetic spin-orbit coupling can be dynamically tuned by controlling geometric non-commutation of the bond sectors.
AI.conclusion: By providing a microscopic foundation for tuning synthetic spin-orbit coupling through geometric control of non-commuting bond sectors, the theory paves the way for advanced applications such as field-free spin qubits.

title: Symmetry Breaking by Interfacial Dead Layers: Observation of Forbidden Self-Induced Spin-Orbit Torque in Symmetric Ferromagnets
summary: Conventionally, spin-orbit torques (SOTs) in ferromagnets require heavy-metal layers or engineered structural asymmetry to break inversion symmetry. In this work, we report the observation of robust, self-generated SOTs in a nominally symmetric, heavy-metal-free MgO/NiFe/MgO trilayer - a geometry where such torques are theoretically forbidden. By combining harmonic Hall measurements with SQUID magnetometry and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, we identify the symmetry-breaking origin: a 1.8 nm magnetic dead layer at the bottom interface. Crucially, we demonstrate a quantitative agreement between our data and the drift-diffusion theory predicted by Kim and Lee, yielding a theoretically extracted dead-layer thickness (1.2 nm) which matches structural characterization. Furthermore, density-functional calculations confirm that NiFe possesses sufficient intrinsic spin Hall conductivity to support the observed spin currents. These results reframe the parasitic dead layer as a functional spintronic component, establishing a universal, all-ferromagnetic route to SOTs in standard magnetic heterostructures.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the observation of self-generated spin-orbit torques (SOTs) in a nominally symmetric, heavy-metal-free MgO/NiFe/MgO trilayer, contrary to conventional theory. The symmetry-breaking is attributed to a 1.8 nm magnetic dead layer at the bottom interface, confirmed by harmonic Hall measurements, SQUID magnetometry, and XPS. Quantitative agreement with Kim and Lee's drift-diffusion theory yields a predicted dead-layer thickness (1.2 nm) consistent with structural data, and DFT confirms sufficient intrinsic spin Hall conductivity in NiFe. The study reframes parasitic dead layers as functional spintronic components, establishing an all-ferromagnetic route to SOTs.
AI.motivation: Conventional wisdom holds that spin-orbit torques require heavy-metal layers or engineered structural asymmetry to break inversion symmetry. This work challenges this paradigm by demonstrating that a naturally occurring magnetic dead layer—previously considered a parasitic artifact—can serve as the symmetry-breaking element, potentially enabling universal SOT functionality in standard symmetric ferromagnetic heterostructures without heavy metals.
AI.method: The authors combine harmonic Hall measurements with SQUID magnetometry and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to characterize the trilayer structure and quantify the magnetic dead layer. They compare their experimental data against the drift-diffusion theory of Kim and Lee to extract the dead-layer thickness, and perform density-functional theory (DFT) calculations to verify the intrinsic spin Hall conductivity of NiFe.
AI.result: Robust self-generated SOTs are observed in the symmetric MgO/NiFe/MgO trilayer. The symmetry-breaking mechanism is identified as a 1.8 nm magnetic dead layer at the bottom interface. The theoretically extracted dead-layer thickness (1.2 nm) from the Kim-Lee drift-diffusion model quantitatively matches structural characterization, and DFT confirms sufficient intrinsic spin Hall conductivity in NiFe to support the observed spin currents.
AI.conclusion: Magnetic dead layers, traditionally regarded as parasitic defects, can be repurposed as functional spintronic components that generate spin-orbit torques. This establishes a universal, all-ferromagnetic route to SOTs in standard magnetic heterostructures, eliminating the need for heavy-metal layers or engineered inversion-symmetry breaking.

title: Preserved metallicity and tunable magnetism in Zr-based Janus MXenes
comment: 9 pages, Physical Chemistry Chemical Physics (2026). Published by the Royal Society of Chemistry. DOI: 10.1039/d6cp00440g
summary: Janus MXenes provide a chemically asymmetric platform to tailor the properties of two-dimensional transition metal carbides. Here, we present a systematic first-principles study of the structural, electronic, mechanical, and magnetic properties of Janus ZrMCX2 MXenes (M = Cr, Hf, Nb, Sc, Ti; X = F, Cl, S). All compositions exhibit negative formation energies and satisfy the Born stability criteria, supporting the energetic and mechanical stability of the Janus structures. In contrast to the metal-tosemiconductor transitions frequently reported for functionalized MXenes, we find that the metallic character is preserved in nearly all ZrMCX2 systems, despite the strong chemical asymmetry introduced by the Janus configuration. Surface functionalization nevertheless plays a key role in modulating the electronic density near the Fermi level and strongly influences the magnetic and mechanical responses. Several compounds exhibit ferromagnetic or antiferromagnetic ground states, three display halfmetallicity, and sizable magnetic anisotropy energies are obtained, with Neel temperatures exceeding room temperature in selected cases. Functionalization also enhances the elastic stiffness of the Janus structures. These results demonstrate that chemical asymmetry and surface termination provide effective control over magnetic and mechanical properties while maintaining a robust metallic framework, identifying Zr-based Janus MXenes as promising model systems for metallic and spindependent two-dimensional materials.

AI.tldr: A systematic first-principles study of Janus ZrMCX2 MXenes (M = Cr, Hf, Nb, Sc, Ti; X = F, Cl, S) reveals that all compositions are energetically and mechanically stable, retain metallic character, and exhibit tunable magnetic properties including ferromagnetic/antiferromagnetic ground states, half-metallicity, and high Néel temperatures, while surface functionalization enhances elastic stiffness.
AI.motivation: Janus MXenes offer a chemically asymmetric platform to tailor 2D transition metal carbide properties, but a systematic understanding of how chemical asymmetry and surface termination control their electronic, magnetic, and mechanical behavior was lacking.
AI.method: Systematic first-principles (density functional theory) calculations of structural, electronic, mechanical, and magnetic properties of Janus ZrMCX2 MXenes across five transition metals (Cr, Hf, Nb, Sc, Ti) and three surface terminations (F, Cl, S). Stability was assessed via formation energies and Born stability criteria; magnetic properties via ground-state determination, magnetic anisotropy energies, and Néel temperatures.
AI.result: All compositions have negative formation energies and satisfy Born stability criteria. Metallic character is preserved in nearly all systems despite chemical asymmetry. Several compounds show ferromagnetic or antiferromagnetic ground states, three exhibit half-metallicity, sizable magnetic anisotropy energies are found, and Néel temperatures exceed room temperature in select cases. Functionalization enhances elastic stiffness.
AI.conclusion: Chemical asymmetry and surface termination provide effective control over magnetic and mechanical properties while maintaining a robust metallic framework, identifying Zr-based Janus MXenes as promising model systems for metallic and spin-dependent two-dimensional materials.

title: Predictive Simulation of Interphases on Li Metal Surface
summary: Interphases remain the least understood components in advanced batteries. Although their properties dictate whether a new battery chemistry could perform as designed, there has never been a reliable way to predict what an interphase could arise from a new electrolyte system due to the absence of atomistic level knowledge about interphasial formation process. In this work, we attempt to develop a simulation method that can universally predict interphasial chemistries formed on Li metal surface, so that the electrolyte engineering would no longer need lengthy Edisonian approaches. By combining a transferable universal polarizable force field and a universal machine learning force field, we simulate interphasial chemistry across chemically diverse electrolyte formulations, and successfully replicate the experimental observation that fluorinated solvents promote the formation of LiF-rich interphases, whereas interphases of more organic origin arise from conventional carbonate-based electrolytes. By directly capturing these spontaneous interfacial reactions behind these interphasial chemistries, our simulations establish molecular-level relationships between electrolyte chemistry, salt concentration, decomposition pathways, and SEI properties, and opens a route toward universal and high-throughput predictive simulation of interphases that is the foundation for AI-driven electrolyte discoveries.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a universal simulation framework combining a transferable polarizable force field and a machine learning force field to predict interphase (SEI) chemistries formed on Li metal surfaces across diverse electrolyte formulations, replicating experimental observations that fluorinated solvents yield LiF-rich interphases while carbonate-based electrolytes produce organic-rich interphases, enabling high-throughput predictive simulation for AI-driven electrolyte discovery.
AI.motivation: Interphases are the least understood components in advanced batteries, and there has been no reliable way to predict what interphase a new electrolyte system will form due to the lack of atomistic-level understanding of the interphasial formation process, forcing researchers to rely on lengthy, trial-and-error (Edisonian) approaches in electrolyte engineering.
AI.method: The authors combine a transferable universal polarizable force field with a universal machine learning force field to simulate spontaneous interfacial reactions and interphasial chemistry across chemically diverse electrolyte formulations on Li metal surfaces, capturing decomposition pathways and SEI properties at the molecular level.
AI.result: The simulations successfully replicate experimental observations: fluorinated solvents promote LiF-rich interphases, while conventional carbonate-based electrolytes produce interphases of more organic origin. The simulations directly capture spontaneous interfacial reactions and establish molecular-level relationships between electrolyte chemistry, salt concentration, decomposition pathways, and SEI properties.
AI.conclusion: The work opens a route toward universal and high-throughput predictive simulation of interphases, providing a foundation for AI-driven electrolyte discoveries and eliminating the need for lengthy Edisonian approaches in electrolyte engineering.

title: Polar-vortex-driven interfacial strain coupling in PbTiO3/SrRuO3 Heterostructures
summary: Interfacial coupling in oxide heterostructures is a central problem in condensed-matter physics, as it typically emerges at the atomic scale through local interactions mediated by lattice polarization and strain. In this work, we investigate nanoscale polar-supertexture-driven interfacial strain coupling in (PbTiO3)16/(SrRuO3)9/(PbTiO3)16 heterostructures grown on DyScO3(110) substrates. Under appropriate epitaxial strain conditions, the PbTiO3 layers form polar vortex superstructures with a periodicity of approximately 10 nm. We demonstrate that the resulting in-plane nanoscale strain modulation propagates into the SrRuO3 layer. Using element-specific resonant X-ray reflectivity, we probe the nanoscale strain modulations of the strontium and ruthenium sublattices at the interface, revealing strong interfacial strain coupling between the ferroelectric and ferromagnetic layers. These findings provide new insights into engineering nanoscale magnetic modulations through interfacial strain and polarization control.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates nanoscale polar-supertexture-driven interfacial strain coupling in (PbTiO3)16/(SrRuO3)9/(PbTiO3)16 oxide heterostructures grown on DyScO3(110) substrates. Polar vortex superstructures (~10 nm periodicity) in the PbTiO3 layers induce in-plane nanoscale strain modulations that propagate into the SrRuO3 layer, confirmed via element-specific resonant X-ray reflectivity probing of strontium and ruthenium sublattices. Strong interfacial strain coupling between ferroelectric and ferromagnetic layers is demonstrated.
AI.motivation: Interfacial coupling in oxide heterostructures is a central problem in condensed-matter physics, as it typically emerges at the atomic scale through local interactions mediated by lattice polarization and strain. The authors aim to understand how nanoscale polar superstructures can drive interfacial strain coupling across dissimilar oxide layers.
AI.method: The authors grow (PbTiO3)16/(SrRuO3)9/(PbTiO3)16 heterostructures on DyScO3(110) substrates under appropriate epitaxial strain conditions to form polar vortex superstructures (~10 nm periodicity) in the PbTiO3 layers. They use element-specific resonant X-ray reflectivity to probe nanoscale strain modulations of the strontium and ruthenium sublattices at the interface.
AI.result: The in-plane nanoscale strain modulation from the PbTiO3 polar vortex superstructures propagates into the SrRuO3 layer, revealing strong interfacial strain coupling between the ferroelectric (PbTiO3) and ferromagnetic (SrRuO3) layers.
AI.conclusion: These findings provide new insights into engineering nanoscale magnetic modulations through interfacial strain and polarization control in oxide heterostructures.

title: Spatially resolved elastic strain and lattice rotation at threading dislocations in HgCdTe/CdZnTe epilayers by dark-field X-ray microscopy
summary: Threading dislocations (TDs) propagating from a Cd$_{1-y}$Zn$_{y}$Te (CZT) substrate into a liquid-phase-epitaxy Hg$_{1-x}$Cd$_{x}$Te (MCT) epilayer set the minority-carrier lifetime and dark-current floor of mid-wave infrared focal-plane arrays, yet at device-grade densities their local strain fields have been accessible only through topography, which conflates lattice tilt and elastic strain. We apply dark-field X-ray microscopy in reflection geometry to a \SI{7}{\micro\metre}-thick (111) MCT/CZT epilayer. Shallow Bragg angle and absorption makes the signal layer dominated while the numerical aperture of the objective keeps the layer and substrate rocking curves convolved, so weak-beam images on either side of the rocking curve and their difference image the correlated defects in a single frame: dot-like substrate TDs and the elongated, in-plane island features they nucleate in the layer. Kernel average misorientation resolves each TD as a \SI{7}{\micro\metre} signature, the layer thickness, alongside axial strain lobes of $\pm(4$ to $5)\times10^{-5}$.

AI.tldr: This paper applies dark-field X-ray microscopy in reflection geometry to image threading dislocations in an MCT/CZT epilayer, distinguishing substrate dislocations from the island features they nucleate, and resolving their strain lobes.
AI.motivation: Threading dislocations propagating from CZT substrates into MCT epilayers limit minority-carrier lifetime and dark current in infrared focal-plane arrays. Existing topography conflates lattice tilt and elastic strain, so a technique is needed to access local strain fields at device-grade densities.
AI.method: Dark-field X-ray microscopy in reflection geometry is applied to a 7 µm-thick (111) MCT/CZT epilayer. Shallow Bragg angle and absorption make the signal layer dominant, while the objective's numerical aperture keeps layer and substrate rocking curves convolved. Weak-beam images on either side of the rocking curve and their difference image correlated defects in a single frame, revealing dot-like substrate TDs and elongated in-plane island features they nucleate. Kernel average misorientation is used to resolve strain signals.
AI.result: Kernel average misorientation resolves each threading dislocation as a 7 µm signature (matching layer thickness) along with axial strain lobes of ±(4 to 5)×10⁻⁵. The imaging reveals both dot-like substrate TDs and the elongated in-plane island features they nucleate in a single frame.
AI.conclusion: Dark-field X-ray microscopy in reflection geometry successfully decouples lattice tilt from elastic strain, enabling direct measurement of local strain fields around threading dislocations in device-grade MCT/CZT epilayers without topography's limitations.

title: Substrate-dependent thermally driven morphological evolution of Pt$_{0.9}$Ni$_{0.1}$ thin films on sapphire and langasite
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures in the main manuscript; 4 pages, 5 figures in the Supplemental Material
summary: We examine the thermal evolution of 100-nm-thick Pt$_{0.9}$Ni$_{0.1}$ alloy films on sapphire and langasite substrates with a 10-nm Zr adhesion layer. Sequential vacuum annealing from room temperature to 800 $^\circ$C produces a substrate-dependent morphological pathway that is quantified by atomic force microscopy, image segmentation, height-distribution analysis, and effective coarsening metrics. Both types of films remain densely granular up to 400 $^\circ$C, undergo a sharp coarsening transition between 400 and 600 $^\circ$C, and evolve into coalesced faceted crystallites by 800 $^\circ$C. The mean projected feature area increases from $7.84 \times 10^2$ to $1.09 \times 10^5$ nm$^2$ on langasite and from $3.32 \times 10^2$ to $1.67 \times 10^5$ nm$^2$ on sapphire. Sapphire therefore develops the larger faceted crystallites, while langasite exhibits the larger roughness maximum at 600 $^\circ$C. Area distributions reveal that the 400-600 $^\circ$C transition does not uniformly shift the initial granular population but instead replaces it with a distinct large-feature ensemble. Height and roughness measurements show a pronounced maximum at 600 $^\circ$C, followed by partial smoothing at 800 $^\circ$C, consistent with rapid coalescence followed by faceting-limited growth. An effective Arrhenius analysis based on $Δ\langle r^2\rangle$, with $\langle r^2\rangle = \langle A\rangle/π$, identifies the 400-600 $^\circ$C interval as the dominant coarsening window. These results show that the thermal stability of PtNi/Zr films on sapphire and langasite is governed by the coupled influence of alloy mobility, interfacial energetics, and substrate-dependent morphological selection.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates the thermal evolution of 100-nm Pt0.9Ni0.1 alloy films on sapphire and langasite substrates with a Zr adhesion layer, using sequential vacuum annealing from room temperature to 800°C. Both films remain granular up to 400°C, undergo a sharp coarsening transition between 400-600°C, and form coalesced faceted crystallites by 800°C. Substrate-dependent behavior emerges: sapphire produces larger faceted crystallites (mean area up to 1.67×10^5 nm²) while langasite shows a larger roughness maximum at 600°C. The coarsening is characterized by population replacement rather than uniform shift, with the 400-600°C interval identified as the dominant coarsening window via Arrhenius analysis.
AI.motivation: To understand the thermal stability and morphological evolution of PtNi/Zr thin-film systems on different piezoelectric substrates (sapphire and langasite), which is relevant for high-temperature device applications requiring stable metallization layers.
AI.method: Sequential vacuum annealing from RT to 800°C was performed on 100-nm Pt0.9Ni0.1 films with 10-nm Zr adhesion layers on sapphire and langasite. Characterization employed atomic force microscopy, image segmentation, height-distribution analysis, and effective coarsening metrics. An effective Arrhenius analysis based on Δ〈r²〉 (with 〈r²〉=〈A〉/π) was used to identify the dominant coarsening temperature window.
AI.result: Both film types remain densely granular up to 400°C, undergo a sharp coarsening transition between 400-600°C, and form coalesced faceted crystallites by 800°C. Mean projected feature area increases from 7.84×10² to 1.09×10⁵ nm² on langasite and from 3.32×10² to 1.67×10⁵ nm² on sapphire. Sapphire develops larger faceted crystallites, while langasite exhibits larger roughness at 600°C. Area distributions indicate population replacement rather than uniform shifting during the transition. Roughness peaks at 600°C with partial smoothing at 800°C.
AI.conclusion: The thermal stability of PtNi/Zr films on sapphire and langasite is governed by the coupled influence of alloy mobility, interfacial energetics, and substrate-dependent morphological selection. The 400-600°C interval is the dominant coarsening window, and the coarsening mechanism involves rapid coalescence followed by faceting-limited growth.

title: AES-Debye: an Accurate, Efficient, and Scalable Engine for Debye Scattering Calculations
summary: Total scattering models are essential for characterizing the structure and disorder of nanoscale materials. The Debye scattering equation (DSE) provides a rigorous route to elastic total scattering, but its direct evaluation is computationally demanding because pairwise contributions must be accumulated at every scattering vector, whereas common acceleration strategies based on binned pair-distance distributions or gridded fast Fourier transforms can introduce discretization and aliasing artifacts that compromise diffuse-scattering accuracy. Here, we present AES-Debye, an accuracy-preserving DSE framework that aggregates pair distances into a pair distribution function (PDF) using corrected bin centers and numerically robust accumulation to suppress discretization and summation errors. A data-locality-aware parallel design enables efficient execution on CPUs and GPUs. We demonstrate strong scalability by computing a high-resolution total scattering profile for a system of 90 million atoms, $(0.1,μ\mathrm{m})^{3}$, in minutes on a distributed-memory CPU platform. These capabilities extend accurate elastic total scattering calculations to large, complex systems while simultaneously providing high-resolution PDFs for downstream structural analysis.

AI.tldr: AES-Debye is an accuracy-preserving Debye scattering equation framework that uses corrected bin centers and numerically robust accumulation to compute high-resolution total scattering profiles, scaling to 90 million atoms on distributed-memory CPU platforms in minutes.
AI.motivation: Total scattering models are essential for characterizing nanoscale materials, but the direct evaluation of the Debye scattering equation is computationally demanding. Existing acceleration strategies (binned pair-distance distributions or gridded FFTs) introduce discretization and aliasing artifacts that compromise diffuse-scattering accuracy.
AI.method: AES-Debye aggregates pair distances into a pair distribution function using corrected bin centers and numerically robust accumulation to suppress discretization and summation errors, combined with a data-locality-aware parallel design for efficient CPU and GPU execution.
AI.result: The framework demonstrates strong scalability by computing a high-resolution total scattering profile for a 90-million-atom system (0.1 μm)³ in minutes on a distributed-memory CPU platform.
AI.conclusion: The approach extends accurate elastic total scattering calculations to large, complex systems while simultaneously providing high-resolution PDFs for downstream structural analysis.

title: Determination of acoustic nonlinearity parameters using thermal modulation of ultrasonic waves
comment: Published in Applied Physics Letters 116, 241901 (2020), DOI: 10.1063/5.0014975
summary: This study presents a test method and its theoretical framework to determine the acoustic nonlinearity parameters ($α,β,δ$) of material using thermal modulation of ultrasonic waves. Temperature change induced thermal strain excites the nonlinear response of the material and modulates the ultrasonic wave propagating in it. Experimental results showed a strong correlation between the relative wave velocity change and the temperature change. With a quadratic polynomial model, the acoustic nonlinearity parameters were obtained from the polynomial coefficients by curve fitting the experimental curves. Their effects on thermal-induced velocity change were discussed. The parameters $α,β,δ$ govern the hysteretic gap, average slope, and curvature of the correlation curve, respectively. The proposed theory was validated on aluminum, steel, intact and damaged concrete samples. The obtained nonlinear parameters show reasonable agreements with values reported in the literature. Compared to other nonlinear acoustic methods using vibration or acoustic excitation, the thermal modulation method generates more uniform, slow changing, and larger strain field in the test sample. Employing thermal effect as the driving force for nonlinearity instead of an undesired influencing factor, this method can measure the absolute values of $α,β,δ$ with good accuracy using a simple ultrasonic test setup.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a novel test method and theoretical framework for determining acoustic nonlinearity parameters (α, β, δ) of materials by using thermal modulation of ultrasonic waves. Temperature-induced thermal strain excites nonlinear responses and modulates propagating ultrasonic waves. The parameters are extracted from quadratic polynomial curve fitting of the wave velocity-temperature correlation, where α, β, and δ govern the hysteretic gap, average slope, and curvature respectively. Validation on aluminum, steel, and concrete (intact and damaged) samples showed values consistent with literature. Compared to vibration or acoustic excitation methods, thermal modulation produces a more uniform, slower-changing, and larger strain field, enabling accurate measurement of absolute nonlinearity parameters with a simple setup.
AI.motivation: Existing nonlinear acoustic methods for measuring material nonlinearity parameters typically use vibration or acoustic excitation, which can produce non-uniform strain fields and are limited in their ability to measure absolute values of the nonlinearity parameters. This work aims to develop a method that uses thermal strain as the driving force to more uniformly excite material nonlinearity and accurately extract the absolute values of α, β, and δ.
AI.method: The method involves heating the test sample to induce thermal strain, which modulates ultrasonic wave propagation through the material. The relative wave velocity change is measured as a function of temperature change. A quadratic polynomial model is used to fit the experimental velocity-temperature curves, and the acoustic nonlinearity parameters (α, β, δ) are obtained from the polynomial coefficients. The theoretical framework connects each parameter to specific features of the correlation curve: α to the hysteretic gap, β to the average slope, and δ to the curvature.
AI.result: The proposed theory was validated on aluminum, steel, intact concrete, and damaged concrete samples. The extracted nonlinear parameters (α, β, δ) showed reasonable agreement with values reported in the literature. The method successfully distinguished between intact and damaged concrete through the nonlinearity parameters, demonstrating sensitivity to material condition.
AI.conclusion: Thermal modulation of ultrasonic waves is an effective approach for determining absolute acoustic nonlinearity parameters with good accuracy using a simple ultrasonic test setup. By treating thermal effects as a driving force for nonlinearity rather than a parasitic factor, this method offers advantages over vibration- or acoustic-excitation-based techniques, including more uniform, slower-changing, and larger strain fields in the sample. The method provides a practical path toward quantitative material characterization based on nonlinear acoustic parameters.

title: 200 mm Wafer-Scale Monolithic 3D Integration of Atomic Layer-Deposited Oxide Semiconductors
summary: Monolithic 3D (M3D) integration offers a pathway to overcome the scaling limits of conventional silicon complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) technology by extending dense vertical stacking of multifunctional logic and memory devices. Here, we demonstrate wafer-scale M3D integration of three tiers of atomic-layer-deposited (ALD) indium oxide (InOx)-based devices (>100,000 fabricated), including ferroelectric, enhancement-mode, and depletion-mode field-effect transistors, on 200 mm silicon wafers. We achieve threshold voltage standard deviation as low as 0.04 V, average electron mobility up to 91.6 cm2V-1s-1, and fully functional cross-tier circuits. A four-tier 3D computing-in-memory (CIM) accelerator targeting large language model workloads is developed using a custom InOx process design kit, delivering 1.4x to 2.9x speedup and comparable energy-delay product improvements over 2D baselines. These results establish ALD InOx M3D integration as a scalable and CMOS-compatible platform for next-generation artificial intelligence hardware and advanced electronics.
